## Purpose

Living home for Wardnet's **go-to-market and monetization strategy**. This is a tracking/discussion issue, not a code task — it captures the durable commitments and the evolving execution plan. The engineering work it implies is tracked in #609 (premium tier + entitlement) and #610 (bridge decoupling).

## Durable commitments (decided — see `docs/adr-premium-tier-and-entitlement.md`)

- **Free tier is the growth engine and is permanently free.** Self-host + bring-your-own-domain = full features, zero cost to us. Premium never gates the self-hostable product.
- **Premium gates a real cost centre** (DDNS + Tunneler run on our infra), so it is paid **from public availability** — never given away free and later charged for (clawback is the cardinal sin).
- **Beta is free but explicitly labelled** "free during beta → premium at GA, with advance notice." Never silently free.
- **Stripe-native trial at GA.** Stripe is the payment processor only; the account master record is ours (tenant management).
- **Positioning: transparent-but-quiet.** Free/self-hostable product and the mission are the hero; premium is an honest, secondary "supports the project" tier. The solo-OSS identity is a trust asset, leaned into — not a slick SaaS launch.

- [ ] Launch copy + the explicit beta-pricing notice wording
- [ ] Pricing (amount, monthly/annual, trial length) — defer until closer to GA
- [ ] Channels / community launch plan (privacy + self-hosting communities)
- [ ] GA cutover plan: beta → premium transition, advance-notice mechanics
- [ ] Decide where the "manage subscription" surface lives (Stripe Customer Portal vs in-app)

## Why an issue, not a Discussion

Solo + pre-launch: Discussions earn their keep when there's a community conversing. This repo standardized on issues (impl-docs retired in favour of issues, d8ed6c83), so a long-lived `strategy`-labelled issue is the idiomatic home. Revisit if/when a public community forms.

title: CostTracker governance gaps: WARN overrun is silent, OBSERVE waives new-paid-tool approval, approved tools lost on resume
body_excerpt:
**Category:** Bug — budget-governance contract violations (\`tools/cost_tracker.py\`)

Three related defects in \`reserve()\` and persistence undermine the spend-governance contract that AGENT_GUIDE.md leans on.

**1. WARN mode never signals a budget overrun** — \`tools/cost_tracker.py:143-148\`
\`\`\`python
if estimated > self.usable_budget_usd:
    if self.mode == BudgetMode.CAP:
        raise BudgetExceededError(...)
# WARN falls straight through and reserves — no log, no flag, no return signal
\`\`\`
The module docstring promises "Budget overruns trigger pauses (in warn/cap mode)." In WARN mode an overrun produces **nothing** the orchestrator can detect. Fix: emit \`logging.warning(...)\` and/or set \`entry["budget_warning"] = True\` (surfaced in \`cost_snapshot()\`).

**2. \`BudgetMode.OBSERVE\` silently waives BOTH approval gates** — \`tools/cost_tracker.py:127-140\`
The single-action-threshold check (127) and the new-paid-tool check (135) are both gated on \`self.mode != BudgetMode.OBSERVE\`. So \`require_approval_for_new_paid_tool=True\` becomes a no-op the moment mode is OBSERVE, and a brand-new paid provider runs unapproved. Spend-cap mode and consent are orthogonal and should not be coupled. Fix: keep new-paid-tool / single-action approval active regardless of budget mode (or add a separate flag).

**3. \`_approved_tools\` is not persisted — resume re-prompts for already-approved tools** — \`tools/cost_tracker.py:59, 155-157\`, \`_save()/_load()\`
\`_approved_tools\` is an in-memory \`set\` never written by \`_save()\` nor restored by \`_load()\`. On any pipeline resume (a fresh \`CostTracker\` built from an existing \`cost_log.json\`), every previously approved paid tool is forgotten and \`reserve()\` raises \`ApprovalRequiredError\` again — breaking resumability of paid stages. Fix: persist approved tool names in the saved JSON and rehydrate in \`_load()\`.

title: Logical Reasoning with Outcome Reward Models for Test-Time Scaling
body_excerpt:
**Paper**: [Logical Reasoning with Outcome Reward Models for Test-Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19903v1)

## TL;DR

Paper trains Outcome Reward Models for deductive text-LLM reasoning + test-time scaling. Repo is inference-only VLM spatial-reasoning eval — no trainer, no reward-model path, no logic benchmark, no scoped call site. Decide fit.

## Suggested experiment

Scope a test-time-selection harness that fits the existing inference-only path: for each spatial-reasoning benchmark item, have the VLM generate N candidate answers, score each with a lightweight proxy reward (reuse `evaluation.py`'s ground-truth scoring as a stand-in for a learned ORM), and measure the accuracy lift from best-of-N selection over the single-shot baseline. This tests whether ORM-style test-time scaling transfers to the spatial VLM setting before investing in training a real reward model.

## Engineering analysis

The paper contributes three things, all centered on **text LLMs doing deductive logic**:

- A set of trained **Outcome Reward Models (ORMs)** that score whether an LLM's reasoning trace reaches a correct conclusion on deductive-reasoning tasks.
- A **training recipe** for those ORMs (needs a trainer, supervised/RL data, and a model head).
- A **test-time scaling recipe**: generate N candidate reasoning traces, score each with the ORM, select the best.

This is fundamentally an LLM logical-reasoning method: text in, text out, built on a reward-modeling + training pipeline.

### What blocks a clean implementation

- **Modality and domain mismatch.** vqasynth is an **inference + evaluation pipeline for visual spatial reasoning** over VLMs (`benchmarks.py`, `evaluation.py`, `inference.py`, plus `depth`/`localize`/`scene_fusion`). The paper targets **deductive logical reasoning** over text LLMs. There is no logical-reasoning benchmark, no text-only LLM path, and no spatial ↔ deductive bridge in the repo.
- **No training infrastructure.** The paper's core contribution is *training* ORMs and *selecting among candidates via reward scores*. vqasynth is inference-only — there is no trainer, no reward-model head, and no candidate-generate + score + select harness. `r1_reasoning.py` does reasoning prompting but not ORM-scored best-of-N selection.
- **No scoped call site identified.** No candidate-selection rationale named a subset or call site against this module layout, so there is no implementable slice that drops into existing code. The most realistic implementation

The `bounty-agent-usable` migration's branding check was `grep -rni tuskboard`, which returns clean because **grep can't see into a binary `.webp`**. The text was all migrated; the wordmark *image* still carries the old brand. Caught during the Alpine surface port's browser verification.

## Impact
This is a **live Tuskboard mark in the surface**, which violates the `bounty-agent-usable` success criterion *"No live Tuskboard string remains in the bounty spell surface/contract."* That criterion was explicitly **deferred** for the migration branch (per maintainer) and split out here as a follow-up.

## Fix
Regenerate a **Bounty** wordmark asset (image generation — imago / media-forge, not a find-replace) matching the surface palette, and replace `assets/wordmark.webp`.

## Context
Follow-up from the bounty house-pattern migration (`docs/projects/bounty-agent-usable/`); tracked as merge-gate item **W1** in that project's `backlog.md`.

title: feat(reward): normalize reward scores and add temporal decay
body_excerpt:
## Summary
`memory-core` already exposes reward-related types including `AdaptiveRewardCalculator`, `DomainStatistics`, and `DualRewardScore`, so the next improvement is to prevent old successes from dominating retrieval forever.

## Problem
Static reward accumulation can bias retrieval toward stale episodes, even when more recent lower-volume evidence is more relevant.

## Proposed Code Changes

### 1. Add temporal decay
Extend reward computation with a decay component:
- exponential decay by age
- configurable half-life by task domain

### 2. Normalize by task distribution
Use `DomainStatistics` to normalize reward relative to:
- task type
- agent type
- complexity band

### 3. Separate raw vs effective reward
Add fields:
- `raw_reward`
- `normalized_reward`
- `decayed_reward`
- `effective_reward`

### 4. Use effective reward in ranking
Update retrieval ranking so effective reward is used instead of raw score.

### 5. Backfill migration
Provide migration or lazy recomputation path for existing episodes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Reward calculator supports decay
- [ ] Reward normalization uses domain statistics
- [ ] Retrieval ranking uses effective reward
- [ ] Existing data can be recomputed safely
- [ ] Tests cover age and domain normalization behavior

title: [Feature]: Native on-device iMessage adapter via the imsg CLI (no cloud relay), plugin or core?
body_excerpt:
## Problem or Use Case

I want to run iMessage from Hermes on an always-on Mac without any cloud service or relay in the loop. No managed line, no webhook, no public URL. Just the local Messages.app database plus the [`imsg`](https://github.com/nicholasstephan/imsg) CLI, which drives IMCore directly on the machine.

I'm filing this before opening a PR because iMessage clearly already has attention here, and I'd rather check direction than burn review cycles on something that fights your roadmap:

- Photon (`plugins/platforms/photon/`, author NousResearch) is the managed Spectrum service. Plugin-based, and from the README it reads like the path you recommend to most people.
- BlueBubbles (`gateway/platforms/bluebubbles.py`) is the self-hosted Mac relay.
- Linq picked up channel docs recently.

So it isn't a duplicate (there's no imsg-CLI adapter in the tree), but it is a fourth iMessage path, and it leans on the local-Mac model rather than the managed-service direction Photon represents. Your contributor guide says to ask about exactly this kind of thing before building, so here I am.

## Proposed Solution

A native `imsg` adapter that shells out to the CLI:

- Inbound through `imsg watch --json --since-rowid`, with persistent resume state so a restart doesn't replay or drop messages.
- Outbound through `imsg send`; attachments through `imsg send --file`.
- Typing indicators and read receipts via IMCore, with `imsg launch` arming the bridge when the adapter connects.
- A small declarative rules engine for group access: top-down, first match wins, with `silent_drop` as the default deny so the bot never leaks its existence to an unauthorized sender. A legacy flat allowlist auto-synthesizes into rules, so existing configs keep working with no migration.

I already have the whole thing built and tested on a private branch: 68 passing tests, clean compile, adapter plus config/run/status/cron/send_message wiring plus a desktop setup card. I can open the PR today if you're interested.

The question I actually want answered: would you take an on-device, no-cloud iMessage path at all? And if yes, do you want it as a plugin under `plugins/platforms/` to match Photon, instead of wired into core `gateway/platforms/`? I'm glad to repackage it as a standalone plugin before submitting if that's the shape you'd prefer.

## Alternatives Considered

Photon covers the managed case well, but it's a third-party service on a shared or paid line. I specifically want zero external

title: Decide the fate of the model-reward bandit (wire it, or remove + drop wake_session replay)
body_excerpt:
## Context
The model-reward bandit (`router/bandit.py`, MCP tools `route_to_model` / `record_model_reward` / `bandit_stats`, the `model_rewards` table) has **zero recorded data** — `bandit_stats` returns "No bandit data yet". It looked like dead weight, but a reference audit showed it is **not cleanly removable**:

- `wake_session()` crash-recovery replays in-flight `record_model_reward` events (imports `bandit.record_reward` / `bandit.bucket`).
- `tests/test_wake_session.py` has 4 acceptance tests asserting that replay against the `model_rewards` table.
- 3 public MCP tools are registered in the capability list.
- `store.py` creates the `model_rewards` table at startup (dropping it needs a schema migration).
- Config keys `router_bandit_enabled` / `router_bandit_epsilon` + a settings-UI group reference it.

## Decision needed
- **Wire it** — actually seed rewards from real routing outcomes so the bandit influences model selection (today nothing calls `record_model_reward` in the normal path; only crash-recovery replays it), **or**
- **Remove it** — delete the module + 3 MCP tools + config + settings UI, **and** rewrite/remove the `wake_session` reward-replay step and its 4 tests, **and** drop the `model_rewards` DDL via a migration.

Either path is a deliberate design decision, not a mechanical edit — hence this follow-up rather than an inline change.

title: Why Building a One‑Person SaaS with Zero Customer‑Acquisition Cost Beats Scaling a Ten‑Person Team on a $100K Monthly Budget
body_excerpt:
## The Counterintuitive Landscape

It was a rainy Thursday in Berlin. I was sitting across from a venture‑capitalist who just closed a $50 million fund. He asked me how many engineers I needed to “hit $10 million ARR in 18 months.” My answer was a single sentence: “Zero.” He stared, then laughed, assuming I was joking. In the next 12 months, a solo developer I know—let’s call her Maya—launched a niche analytics tool, spent nothing on paid ads, and quietly grew to $1.2 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). Meanwhile, a well‑funded competitor with a ten‑person engineering and sales team, $100 k a month in acquisition spend, still struggles to break even.

The intuition that “more people, more money” is baked into every pitch deck. Yet the economics of digital products have shifted. When the marginal cost of reaching another customer approaches zero, the classic growth equation—*Revenue = Users × Price*—must be paired with a new factor: *Acquisition Cost per User (ACU)*. If ACU is zero, the breakeven point slides dramatically leftward, and the optimal team size shrinks.

## The Economics of Zero‑Acquisition Products

Below is a simplified comparison of two hypothetical SaaS businesses over a 12‑month horizon.

| Metric | Solo Founder (Zero ACU) | Ten‑Person Team ( $100k/mo ACU) |
|--------|------------------------|---------------------------------|
| Monthly Salary & Overhead | $8,000 (my own salary) | $150,000 (engineers, sales, ops) |
| Marketing Spend | $0 | $100,000 |
| Total Monthly Burn | $8,000 | $250,000 |
| Monthly New Users | 200 (organic referrals) | 5,000 (paid ads) |
| Average Revenue per User (ARPU) | $15 | $15 |
| Monthly Revenue | $3,000 | $75,000 |
| Cumulative ARR after 12 mo | **$36,000** | **$900,000** |
| Net Cash Flow after 12 mo | **+$240,000** (profit) | **‑$2,100,000** (loss) |

*Key observations*:

1. **Acquisition Cost Dominates Burn** – The ten‑person team spends $100 k each month just to acquire users, dwarfing salary costs.
2. **User Quality vs Quantity** – Organic users tend to be higher‑intent, lower churn, because they arrived via recommendation rather than a cheap ad impression.
3. **Scalability of Marginal Cost** – Adding another user to a zero‑ACU product costs nothing; adding another ad click costs money.

The numbers are stylized, but they illustrate a principle: when ACU is near zero, the optimal capital allocation is to keep the team lean, focus on product depth, and let the market discover you.

title: Payment currency is not normalized to lowercase before processing
body_excerpt:
Parent Algora bounty: #743

## Bug
`paymentService.createPaymentIntent` stores `payload.currency ?? 'usd'` as-is. Payment processors such as Stripe require currency codes in lowercase (e.g. `'usd'`). Passing `'USD'` or `'GBP'` would cause the downstream Stripe integration to fail with a validation error once implemented.

## Reproduction
1. Send `POST /api/payments` with body `{ "amount": 100, "currency": "USD" }`.
2. Response includes `currency: 'USD'` instead of the normalized `'usd'`.

## Expected behavior
Normalize the currency to lowercase in `createPaymentIntent` before storing or forwarding to Stripe: `currency: (payload.currency ?? 'usd').toLowerCase()`.

## Scope
Fix `apps/api/src/services/paymentService.js` only. Do not change the controller or routes.

title: Platform observability — metrics audit, gaps & alerting (SSB platform)
body_excerpt:
> This issue consolidates #1647, #1648, and #1661 into a single unified observability work item. Those issues are now closed and tracked here.

## Purpose

Define the full observability picture for the SSB platform — covering both **business / product metrics** and **operational / system metrics** — what we have today, the gaps, and the alerting required. This also incorporates the metrics audit action from the Lean Coffee session (Jun 24).

This is a requirements issue. It deliberately does not prescribe _how_ to deliver it (build it natively, use a third-party platform, etc.) — that is the implementer's decision. The goal is to state clearly **what we need to be able to see and be alerted on**.

---

## Context & background

Raised during the Lean Coffee session on Jun 24, the team recognised that there is currently no clear picture of what metrics are being collected across the Alpha platform, or whether those metrics are sufficient for understanding platform health and performance.

---

## Two cross-cutting gaps (apply across both business and system metrics)

**No common observability tool / single pane.** Where logs and metrics exist at all, they are fragmented across separate places with no unified view. Answering one question today means stitching several sources together by hand. There is no single place a person — technical or not — can open to understand how the platform is doing.

**No proper alerting when a metric flags a problem.** Capturing a metric or a log is not the same as being told when it goes wrong. Today there is no reliable path that turns a problem signal into an alert a human actually receives — so problems are found manually, late, or from a citizen/agency complaint.

Both points are in scope here: all metrics defined below need a common place to live and a dependable alerting path to a human.

---

## What we have today

### Business / product metrics
- **Chatbot** — usage, traffic, latency, RAG-degraded %, error rate: metrics + alerting exist.
- **Landing** — basic page/event analytics.

- **Forms funnel analytics** — instrumented in the code (via Umami) but not active in production (produces zero data).

title: Contract: Batch vulnerability verification for gas optimization
body_excerpt:
## Description

The `verify_vulnerability` and `verify_emergency_vulnerability` functions operate on individual reports. For bulk operations (e.g., a batch of 50 reports from an automated scanner), this creates excessive transaction costs and poor UX.

## Requirements

1. Add a `batch_verify_vulnerabilities` function:
   ```rust
   pub fn batch_verify_vulnerabilities(
       env: Env,
       admin: Address,
       report_ids: Vec<u64>,
       bounty_amounts: Vec<i128>,
   ) -> Result<Vec<u64>, ContractError>
   ```
2. Requirements:
   - All report IDs must be unique (reject duplicates with `InvalidInput`)
   - `report_ids` and `bounty_amounts` must have equal length
   - Batch size is limited to 50 (configurable via `MAX_BATCH_SIZE` constant)
   - Each verification follows existing permission checks (multi-sig for high bounties)
   - Return list of successfully verified report IDs; skip failures with event emission
3. Add a `batch_verify_vulnerabilities_test` test function
4. Gas benchmarking: compare gas cost of N individual calls vs 1 batch call

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `batch_verify_vulnerabilities` implemented with all safety checks
- [ ] Batch size limit enforced (max 50)
- [ ] Duplicate rejection works
- [ ] Partial failure handling with event emission
- [ ] Gas cost benchmark shows batch is cheaper than N individual calls
- [ ] `cargo test` passes
- [ ] `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` passes
- [ ] `cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release` succeeds

title: ## 🔴 P0 — #559 · Reward-Deckel: eligible Trials saturieren auf `+5.0`, Winner-Gradient kollabiert
body_excerpt:
**Symptom.** Alle 18 eligiblen Trials (9 je FlashCrash-Lauf) erhalten `reward == 5.0` bit-identisch, obwohl ihr `oos_total_return` von 0.0118 bis 0.0177 streut (Faktor 1.5). TPE erhält am oberen Rand der Landschaft ein **flaches Plateau** und kann den robustesten Kandidaten nicht selektieren. Der willkürlich (first-found / sampler-order) gewählte Vektor überfittet → `REJECTED_ON_HOLDOUT`.

**Root-Cause (Mathematik).** `base = clip(oos_sortino, ±5.0)`. Der Sortino ist mit `√8766 = 93.63` annualisiert. Ein per-Bar-Sortino von nur `5/93.63 = 0.0534` erreicht bereits den annualisierten Wert 5.0 → **jeder** evaluable Trial mit minimalem positiven Edge klemmt auf `base = 5.0`. Für die eligiblen Trials gilt zusätzlich `overfit_gap = max(0, is_sortino_median − 5) = 0`, `dd_excess = 0` (DD ≈ 0.02 ≪ 0.30), `param_pen = 0` (#565) ⇒ `reward = 5.0 − 0 − 0 − 0 − 0 = 5.0` **konstant**. Die harte `min/max`-Klemmung ist eine **stückweise konstante** Funktion mit Gradient 0 oberhalb der Klemmgrenze — genau dort, wo die Winner leben.

**Fix.** Die harte Klemmung durch eine **glatte, streng monotone, kompressive** Transformation ersetzen, die oberhalb der bisherigen Grenze *weiterhin Ordnung trägt*, plus einen **performance-basierten Tie-Breaker** für eligible Trials.

1. **Weiche Sättigung** statt Hard-Clip (empfohlen: `asinh` — linear nahe 0, logarithmisch in den Extremen, überall streng monoton, unbeschränkt aber gedämpft):

   ```
   base = c · asinh(oos_sortino / c),   c = sortino_soft_scale (z. B. 5.0)
   ```

   `asinh(x) = ln(x + √(x²+1))`. Für |Sortino| ≤ c ≈ linear (kein Informationsverlust), für |Sortino| = 50 (RATIO_CAP): `base = 5·asinh(10) = 5·3.0 = 15.0` — komprimiert, aber die Ordnung `50 > 10 > 5` bleibt erhalten. Alternative bei gewünschter Beschränktheit: `base = c·tanh(oos_sortino/c)` (asymptotisch ±c, Gradient → 0 aber nie exakt 0).

2. **Tie-Breaker** für den eligiblen Ast (bricht Restplateaus ökonomisch sinnvoll auf):

   ```
   reward_eligible = base − overfit_gap·w_of − dd_excess·w_dd − param_pen − turnover
                     + w_ret · oos_total_return          # NEU, w_ret klein (z. B. 2.0)
   ```

   Da `oos_total_return` bei eligiblen Trials ∈ [0.012, 0.018] streut, liefert `w_ret·return` einen Diskriminator von ≈ 0.024–0.036 Reward-Einheiten — genug, damit TPE den return-stärksten Winner bevorzugt, ohne die Sortino-Ordnung zu überstimmen.

3. `sortino_soft_scale`, `w_ret` deklarativ in `optimizer.json` (Zero-Hardcoding). Fehlen ⇒ Legacy-Hard-Cli

title: ## 🔴 P0 — #560 · Near-Miss-Gradient: performance-tragender Return-Term wird von kosten-saturierten Termen erschlagen
body_excerpt:
**Symptom.** 695 ineligible Trials, `corr(reward, oos_total_return) = −0.005`. Der TPE hat auf 97,5 % der Landschaft **keine verwertbare Richtung** Richtung Eligibility. Alle Strategien außer FlashCrash finden 0 Winner — nicht weil kein Winner existiert, sondern weil der Sampler ihn nicht finden *kann*.

**Root-Cause (Mathematik).** `_constraint_distance_penalty` aggregiert 6 Distanz-Terme als **Mittelwert der aktiven Terme** (#534). Rekonstruktion der Term-Beiträge über die geloggten `oos_gate_deltas` (distance_term_cap=3.0):

| Distanz-Term | aktiv % | Ø aktiver Wert |
|---|---:|---:|
| Return (scale 0.1) | 83.0 | **0.101** |
| Expectancy (scale 0.002) | 100.0 | **0.965** |
| Win-Rate (scale 0.25) | 100.0 | **0.973** |
| ANY (Sortino/PF) | ~100 | ~1.0 |
| Drawdown | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| Trades | ~0 | 0.0 |

Expectancy, Win-Rate und ANY sind **kosten-getrieben bei ≈ 1.0 gesättigt** (siehe #563). Der **einzige** Term, der mit der ökonomischen Zielgröße mitläuft — der Return-Term — trägt Ø 0.101 und wird durch den 4er-Mittelwert auf ≈ 0.101/4 ≈ **2,5 % des Penalty-Betrags** verdünnt. Ergebnis: `penalty ≈ const`, `reward ≈ const`, Gradient ≈ 0.

**Fix.** Den Failure-Reward an **eine gut konditionierte, ökonomisch monotone Skalarzahl** verankern statt an einem von Sättigungen dominierten 6-Term-Mittel. Zwei kombinierbare Optionen:

1. **Return-verankerter Failure-Reward** (empfohlen, mathematisch am saubersten). Unterhalb des Feasible-Floors einen glatten, streng monotonen Term in `oos_total_return` verwenden:

   ```
   failure_reward = (−c − ε) − softplus( −(oos_total_return − oos_min_total_return) / s ) · w
   softplus(z) = ln(1 + e^z)
   ```

   `softplus` ist überall streng monoton, C∞, und bildet den *Rest-Gap zum Return-Gate* stufenlos ab. Ein Trial mit `return = 0.004` (knapp unter 0.005) liegt messbar höher als einer mit `return = −0.05`. Damit ist `corr(reward, return | ineligible)` konstruktionsgemäß > 0.

2. **Falls Multi-Constraint-Distanz beibehalten wird:** vom **Mittelwert** auf **gewichtete Norm mit Dominanz der Performance-Dimensionen** wechseln und die gesättigten Nebendimensionen nur als kleinen additiven Malus führen:

   ```
   penalty = w_perf · d_return_expectancy_combined + w_side · mean(d_winrate, d_any, d_dd)
   ```
   mit `w_perf ≫ w_side`. Da Return und Expectancy nach Kosten-Fix (#562/#563) de-saturieren, tragen sie dann echten Gradienten.

3. Aggregations-Modus (`failure_reward_mode ∈ {"return_anchored", "weighted_mean", "legacy_mean"}

title: [P0] Zero Security Documentation — Enterprise Adoption Blocker and Credibility Risk
body_excerpt:
Labels: documentation, P0, security, enterprise, smart-contracts, critical-gap, compliance

Bug Description
The XDC documentation contains ZERO security-related content. There is no smart contract security section, no common vulnerability catalog, no secure coding patterns, no audit preparation guide, no key management documentation, and no incident response playbook. This is a credibility-killing omission that prevents enterprise adoption and puts all XDC dApps at risk.

Competitor Benchmark:
- Ethereum: 20+ security pages including SWC registry, Secureum, OpenZeppelin guides
- Solana: Security best practices, common exploit patterns, audit checklist
- Polygon: Security standards, bug bounty program, formal verification guides
- Cosmos: Validator security, node hardening, threat model documentation

Security is not optional for enterprise blockchain adoption. Fortune 500 companies, financial institutions, and government entities will not build on XDC without security documentation.

Affected Pages & Features

| Page/Feature | File Path (Guessable) | Impact/Symptom |
|--------------|----------------------|----------------|
| Security Section | /docs/security/ (DOES NOT EXIST) | Entire section missing |
| Smart Contract Security | /docs/security/smart-contracts.md (N/A) | No secure coding guidance |
| Vulnerability Catalog | /docs/security/vulnerabilities.md (N/A) | No known attack vectors documented |
| Audit Preparation | /docs/security/audit-prep.md (N/A) | No pre-deployment checklist |
| Key Management | /docs/security/key-management.md (N/A) | No HSM/custody guidance |
| Incident Response | /docs/security/incident-response.md (N/A) | No breach playbook |

Blast Radius: 100% of enterprise prospects, 100% of DeFi protocols, 100% of institutional custody solutions. This is a deal-breaker for regulated industries.

Root Cause Analysis
The documentation strategy prioritized feature documentation (what XDC can do) over operational security (how to use XDC safely). This is a common mistake in infrastructure-focused projects — the assumption that "security is the developer's responsibility."

However, in blockchain, the documentation IS the security standard. Developers copy patterns from official docs. Without security guidance, they copy vulnerable patterns from StackOverflow or Ethereum docs that don't account for XDC-specific risks.

Specific risks unique to XDC:
1. XDPoS consensus has different finality guarantees than Ethereum PoS
2. Masternode set is

title: Fund tracking error vs its benchmark index
body_excerpt:
Per-**fund** tracking error: how closely a fund's return tracks the **benchmark index it reports against** — a fund-quality metric on the Explore / fund-detail side. It applies across the **whole catalog, global-first** (US, global, regional, and Thai funds alike); the Thai SEC factsheet is just one input, not the focus. Distinct from the portfolio-vs-benchmark overlay (that's portfolio-area).

## What it answers

- **Index / passive funds:** is replication tight, or is there drift and cost leakage?
- **Active funds:** how much active risk — and the **closet-tracker** tell (active fees for near-index tracking error).

## Why SEC summary stats aren't enough

Where a fund publishes a benchmark return + volatility (e.g. the Thai SEC factsheet, `SEC_INGEST_PERFORMANCE`), those are two summary numbers. A *true* tracking error is the **standard deviation of the periodic return differences** between fund and index — which needs the aligned daily **index series**, not the summaries. And most of the catalog isn't Thai-SEC, so the general path can't lean on factsheet stats at all.

## Needs (general)

- **Each fund's own declared benchmark** — an S&P 500 fund → S&P 500, a global fund → MSCI ACWI, a SET50 fund → SET50, a bond fund → its bond index. #127 captured the per-fund index family — that's the fund → benchmark mapping hook.
- **A total-return index series per benchmark.** #81 shipped a `benchmark_tr` source (tracking-ETF adjusted close) for a curated set; full coverage needs TR series for whatever indices funds actually track (any index with no free deep source — e.g. SET's own TRI is XLS/paid — likely uses an ETF proxy too).
- **Fund NAV series** — already deep via `prewarm-nav`.
- **TE computation + display** — a fund-detail stat and/or a screener column.

## Not this

- Portfolio-vs-benchmark comparison on the "All" chart (the VS toggle) — portfolio-area.
- Benchmark selection / blend → #26.

title: Compile-time blowup for modulated-clock patches: inlining duplicates shared subtrees (hash-cons the IR)
body_excerpt:
## Summary

Compiling a deeply-nested patch whose **clock is modulated by an oscillator**
(e.g. a through-zero flanger: an LFO sweeping a comb of `ModalVoice`s) is ~4×
slower to compile than a *larger* patch with static clocks. The emitted kernel
is correct and small — the cost is entirely a compile-time **build-then-dedup**
of a duplicated expression tree. The fix is to preserve sharing in the IR
(hash-consing) instead of recovering it late via CSE.

This surfaced during the fixed-point clock work (Phase 1), but it is **not a
flanger bug** — it will hit every clock-modulating effect on the roadmap
(chorus, PM/FM, per-oscillator-clock instruments), since they all place an
oscillator in a clock path.

## Reproduction

- `patches/flanger_probe.json` (`ThroughZeroFlangerProbe` → `ThroughZeroFlanger`
  → `ReversibleComb` → 3× `ModalVoice` → 4× `ClockPhasor` each), LFO-modulated
  delay.
- `time diffcli compile patches/flanger_probe.json` → **~7.0–7.25s**.
- Contrast `patches/reverse_reverb.json` (5× `ModalVoice`, **static** offset
  clocks) → **~1.9s**, despite *more* oscillators.

The only structural difference is that the flanger's tap clock is `clk ± d`
where `d` carries an oscillator (`Sin`∘`ClockPhasor`); the reverb's offset is a
constant.

## Root cause: tree-representing-a-graph

`ClockPhasor` reads its clock `clk` twice (the fixed-point split-multiply:
`thi = clk >> 32`, `tlo = clk & mask`). `ModalVoice` feeds the same `clk` to 4
partial `ClockPhasor`s → 8 uses of `clk` per voice. `ReversibleComb` passes a
**modulated** clock into 3 `ModalVoice`s. The whole patch is fully inlined
(`sessionInlineNested = true`), and inlining is *substitution*: each `clk`
use-site gets a **copy** of the modulated-clock expression, so the LFO subtree
(`Sin` polynomial + a phasor) is duplicated ~16×. The pre-CSE strata/partition
passes then walk that bloated tree; emit-time structural CSE collapses it back
to a small plan. So the denotation never duplicated anything (`clk` is one
value used many times) — the *tree* representation lost the sharing the meaning
always had.

## What was ruled out (with evidence)

- **Output / codegen volume** — the fused flanger plan (112KB) is *smaller*
  than the static reverb's (171KB). Not a codegen-size problem.
- **`structuralId` emit-CSE memo** — the TS emitter had a per-node `hashCache`
  (WeakMap node→id) that the Lean port intentionally dropped
  (`lean/Tropical/Ir/Emit.lean:29`). Restoring it (value-keyed `Std.HashMap
  CoreExpr Nat

title: [Bug] expeditious reward functions: inverted sign in linear/quad, wrong-direction exponential in exp, crash in const
body_excerpt:
All observations are against current `main` (986bf86), `bluebird-gymnasium` 0.2.0, in [`bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py`](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py).

### 1. `expeditious_linear` rewards moving *away* from the exit (sign inverted)

[expeditious.py#L87-L89](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py#L87-L89):

```python
dist_diff = curr_dist - prev_dist
reward = np.clip(dist_diff, -DIFF_THRESHOLD, DIFF_THRESHOLD)
```

When the aircraft makes progress toward its exit, `curr_dist < prev_dist`, so `dist_diff` is **negative** and the function returns a **negative** reward. This is the opposite of the docstring, which says progress should yield a positive reward up to +1.0. An agent trained with this reward is incentivised to fly away from its sector exit.

**Suggested fix** — negate the difference:

```python
reward = np.clip(-dist_diff, -DIFF_THRESHOLD, DIFF_THRESHOLD)
# or equivalently: dist_diff = prev_dist - curr_dist
```

### 2. `expeditious_quad` has the same inverted sign

[expeditious.py#L150-L153](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py#L150-L153):

```python
dist_diff = curr_dist - prev_dist
reward = np.clip(dist_diff, -DIFF_THRESHOLD, DIFF_THRESHOLD)
sign = np.sign(reward)
```

`sign` is taken from the raw `dist_diff`, so progress (negative `dist_diff`) again produces a negative final reward, contradicting the docstring. Same fix: negate `dist_diff` (or the final `sign`).

### 3. `expeditious_exp` exponential grows in the wrong direction (and exceeds its documented range)

[expeditious.py#L217-L222](https://github.com/project-bluebird/BluebirdATC/blob/986bf868da76feda1e2d0f458f03d87dec70544f/bluebird-gymnasium/bluebird_gymnasium/rewards/expeditious.py#L217-L222):

```python
if dist_diff < 0:
    dist_diff = max(dist_diff, -DIFF_THRESHOLD)
    # the closer `dist_diff` is to -1.0, the higher the reward
    reward = np.exp(dist_diff + DIFF_THRESHOLD)
```

This one gets the sign convention right (progress → positive reward), but `np.exp(dist_diff + DIFF_THRESHOLD)` is *increasing* in `dist_diff`:

- maximal progress (`dist_diff = -1.0`) → `exp(0) = 1.0`
- minimal progress (`dist_diff → 0⁻`) → `e

title: Add `.coderabbit.yaml` template + multi-file sync enforcement recipe
body_excerpt:
## Problem

The boilerplate has **no `.coderabbit.yaml` config or recipe**. CodeRabbit (the AI code review tool) is the workhorse for low/medium-risk PR auto-review in `nyc-re-tracker-2`, but more importantly, its **path-instruction system enforces multi-file consistency** in ways that no other tool currently does.

The pattern that's emerged: when one file changes, certain other files must also change. CodeRabbit blocks the PR if they don't. This catches an entire class of "I forgot to update the docs/taxonomy/test" bugs at review time.

## The multi-file sync pattern

`nyc-re-tracker-2` `.coderabbit.yaml` enforces three classes of cross-file consistency:

1. **Events ↔ Taxonomy ↔ LLM events** — if `events.ts` changes, `event-taxonomy.md` must too. If `event-taxonomy.md` LLM-events section changes, `posthog_llm.py` must too. If `prompts.py` changes a template materially, `<NAME>_PROMPT_VERSION` must bump.
2. **Memory budget guards (ETL)** — flag steps accumulating >100K rows, missing empty-batch guards on `full_replace`, large-geometry datasets without streaming.
3. **Path-specific instructions** — different review prompts for `api/` vs `ui/` vs `etl/` vs `transforms/` vs `schemas/`.

Without these, sync drift is a constant tax — a developer changes one side, ships, and the other side rots until someone notices.

## Why it matters

Concrete examples of bugs CodeRabbit caught in `nyc-re-tracker-2` (each would have shipped without it):
- New tracked button added to `events.ts` but no row in `event-taxonomy.md` → CodeRabbit blocked the PR until the taxonomy was updated
- Prompt template materially changed but `PROMPT_VERSION` not bumped → CodeRabbit caught it; would otherwise have polluted PostHog eval data
- Inngest step added with `for row in rows:` accumulating into a list → CodeRabbit flagged the OOM risk on the 2048MB Fly VM

title: [Bug] Reward CPU tests fail during collection in lightweight dev environments
body_excerpt:
## Bug Description

Reward-related CPU unit tests fail during pytest collection in a lightweight contributor environment, before any test body runs.

The failure is caused by import-time dependency coupling. A reward test imports the math reward utilities, Python executes the reward model hub package initializer first, and that initializer imports runtime dependencies such as `aiohttp`. The math reward utilities also import symbolic / LaTeX parsing packages such as `sympy` and `pylatexenc` at module import time.

This makes local CPU validation fragile: a contributor who wants to run reward string-normalization or boxed-answer tests can be blocked by unrelated runtime-only dependencies.

This is not a reward-scoring correctness bug. It is a test dependency / import-boundary issue.

## Steps to Reproduce

From a lightweight local environment with pytest installed, but without the full Vime runtime dependency stack:

1. Check out latest `main`.
2. Install only lightweight test tooling, for example `pytest`.
3. Run:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=$PWD python -m pytest -q tests/test_rm_math.py
```

## Expected Behavior

Reward CPU tests should either:

1. collect and run when they only exercise local reward utility behavior, or
2. skip with a clear message if a dependency is genuinely required for the behavior under test.

Running math reward utility tests should not require unrelated remote reward runtime dependencies.

## Actual Behavior

The test suite fails during collection before any tests run:

```shell
tests/test_rm_math.py:21: in <module>
    from vime.rollout.rm_hub.math_utils import (
vime/rollout/rm_hub/__init__.py:5: in <module>
    import aiohttp
E   ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'aiohttp'
```

In the same lightweight environment, these reward-test-related packages are also absent:

```text
aiohttp: missing
pylatexenc: missing
sympy: missing
```

## Environment

- vime version: latest `main`, commit `d679c755`
- Python version: 3.11.15
- PyTorch version: not installed in this lightweight CPU test environment
- CUDA version: not applicable
- GPU type and count: not applicable
- OS: macOS arm64 / Darwin 25.4.0
- vLLM version: not installed
- vllm-router version: not installed
- Megatron-LM version (if relevant): not installed

## Logs

```shell
============================= test session starts ==============================
platform darwin -- Python 3.11.15, pytest-9.1.1, pluggy-1.6.0
rootdir: /Users/bytedance/opensource/vime
configfile: pyproject.toml

title: Create 3 example agent templates (fork-and-run)
body_excerpt:
## Summary

Create 3 production-quality example agent templates that developers can fork and immediately run. These templates serve as both documentation and starting points for building Neunode-integrated agents.

## Templates

### 1. Inference Agent (`examples/inference-agent/`)
An agent that discovers available models, requests inference, and manages payments.

**Features:**
- Auto-discovers models via knowledge graph
- Sends inference requests with retry logic
- Pays with nCompute tokens automatically
- Streams results to stdout
- Configurable model preferences and budget

**Tech stack:** TypeScript, `@neunode/sdk`, commander.js

### 2. Bounty Hunter Agent (`examples/bounty-agent/`)
An agent that monitors open bounties, claims matching work, submits results, and collects payment.

**Features:**
- Watches for new bounties matching skill profile
- Auto-claims when requirements match capabilities
- Submits completed work with verification
- Collects payment upon acceptance
- Configurable: max concurrent bounties, reward minimums, skill filters

**Tech stack:** TypeScript, `@neunode/sdk`, event emitter

### 3. Model Publisher Agent (`examples/model-agent/`)
An agent that registers models on the network, sets pricing, and manages lineage.

**Features:**
- Registers model with metadata (architecture, size, benchmarks)
- Sets per-token pricing (nCompute per 1K tokens)
- Links to parent models for lineage tracking
- Updates model metadata (new version, pricing changes)
- Monitors inference requests and revenue

**Tech stack:** TypeScript, `@neunode/sdk`

## Template Structure (each)
```
examples/<name>/
├── README.md            # Quick-start guide (fork, configure, run)
├── package.json         # Dependencies, scripts
├── tsconfig.json        # TypeScript config
├── src/
│   ├── index.ts         # Entry point
│   ├── config.ts        # Configuration (env vars + defaults)
│   └── agent.ts         # Agent logic
├── .env.example         # Required env vars
└── Dockerfile           # Optional containerization
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All 3 templates work end-to-end with a running agnetd daemon
- [ ] README with fork-and-run instructions (< 5 minutes to first action)
- [ ] TypeScript strict mode, no `any` types
- [ ] `.env.example` with all required configuration

title: LYB data-integrity: FFMI differs across surfaces — Share card 17.7 vs home/Timeline 18.5 for same snapshot
body_excerpt:
**Problem:** The same body-comp snapshot shows two different FFMI values depending on screen. On a paid measurement app, the headline number contradicting itself destroys trust. **Evidence (Tim screenshots, 2026-06-21, #product):** * 'Share Body Score' card: Weight 170.4 lbs, Body Fat 12.1%, **FFMI 17.7**. * Home/Timeline (Oct 28 2024 selected): Weight 170.4 lbs, Body Fat 12.1%, **FFMI 18.5**.
Same weight, same BF%, same 30-day deltas ('+1 lbs last 30d', 'No change last 30d') = same snapshot. FFMI = lean mass ÷ height² — for fixed weight + BF it depends ONLY on height, so it MUST be identical across surfaces. **Severity/Priority:** P1 — visible self-contradiction on the headline metric; data-integrity bug, not cosmetic. **MRR opportunity:** HIGH (trust). Reach=anyone who views both home + share; Annoyance=high (looks broken / untrustworthy); Effort=low (single source of truth for the calc). Trust is the whole value prop of a measurement app. **Root-cause hypothesis (high conf):** two different FFMI computations/inputs — likely one surface applies the height-normalized/adjusted FFMI (e.g. +6.1×(1.8−height_m)) and the other the raw FFMI, OR one reads a stale/default height. Inspect the FFMI calc in MetricsInterpolationService / GlobalTimelineService vs the share-card builder; unify to one function. **Proposed fix:** single canonical FFMI function consumed by home, share card, and stats; add a unit test asserting all surfaces return identical FFMI for the same input. **Acceptance:** FFMI identical across home, Share card, and stats for a given snapshot; unit test guards it. **Issue shape & model:** Small, well-spec'd → Kimi K2 / DeepSeek. **Note:** also observed — the Body Fat % chart already has a working Smoothed/Raw toggle and reads reasonably smooth (re: JovieInc/Jovie#11352 'charts need smoothing', confirm WHICH charts are jagged); and the home full-bleed Avatar/Photo layout looks strong (JovieInc/Jovie#10880 delivered visually). Share-card crops the torso oddly vs home full-body — minor framing polish, not filed separately. **Related:** JovieInc/Jovie#10241 (unified timeline aggregation), JovieInc/Jovie#10226 (paid launch).

title: feat(skills): curated skills/community/ + bode skills install <repo>#<path>
body_excerpt:
## Problem

Wave 6.6 (#37) gives us a per-model skill converter. Wave 6's `.bode/skills/` resolver picks the right flavor per CLI. But there's no story for **community-contributed skills**:

- A dev writes a great `refactor-component.neutral.md` for React work — there's no path to share it.
- A team wants to standardize "Jira hand-off skill" across their org — they copy-paste into every repo's `.bode/skills/`.
- A new bode user discovers the tool but has no skill library beyond what ships in `src/skills/`.

The full marketplace (Wave 9) is too heavy for current adoption — it needs hosting, moderation, search, ratings. The **curated** path is what `homebrew-core` was for Homebrew in the early days: one repo, PR-reviewed additions, git-ref versioning, no servers.

## Proposal

### Curated folder in this repo

```
skills/
  community/
    react-component-refactor/
      skill.neutral.md
      README.md            # purpose, usage, examples
      VERIFIED.md          # date + reviewer notes
    jira-handoff/
      skill.neutral.md
      README.md
  built-in/                # existing bundled skills move here
    planning/...
    implementation/...
```

Acceptance for `skills/community/`: PR template, two-reviewer policy, manual smoke test, version pinned via the merge commit SHA.

### `bode skills install <repo>#<path>`

- `bode skills install KakunynQA/bode#skills/community/react-component-refactor`
- Downloads via `git archive` (sparse) or `gh api repos/.../tarball`.
- Lands in `~/.bode/skills/<slug>/` with a `.install.json`:

  ```json
  {
    "source": "KakunynQA/bode#skills/community/react-component-refactor@<sha>",
    "installed_at": "2026-08-01T00:00:00Z",
    "version": "<sha>"
  }
  ```

- `bode skills list` shows installed skills, source, install date, update available.
- `bode skills update <slug>` re-pulls from source, diffs, asks before overwriting local edits.
- `bode skills remove <slug>`.

### Resolver precedence (extends Wave 6)

1. Project `.bode/skills/<name>` (already)
2. Global `~/.bode/skills/<name>` (new — community-installed)
3. Built-in `src/skills/<name>` (already)
4. Flavored variants per CLI (already)
5. Neutral fallback (already)

### Versioning

- No central registry. Each install pins to a git SHA.
- Bode never auto-updates community skills (would change AI behavior silently).
- `bode skills update --all` runs interactively.

- `bode skills search react` greps `skills/community/*/README.md` headings in the bode re

title: Pay down remaining test quarantine debt + structural CI improvements to prevent recurrence
body_excerpt:
## Context

PR #1730 (issue #1729) paid down the bulk of the CI quarantine debt — fixing the production `save_plan` projection bug, resolving ~40 cross-platform test failures, and driving 3 of 4 quarantine lists to zero. However, **11 entries remain across 3 lists**, and the effort exposed systemic gaps that allowed the debt to accumulate undetected for months. This issue tracks both the remaining debt and the structural fixes needed to prevent recurrence.

## Current quarantine state (on main post-#1730)

| List | Active entries | Root cause category |
|---|---|---|
| quarantined-tests.txt | 5 | Knowledge-system test failures (pre-existing, unrelated to #1729) |
| quarantined-tests-macos.txt | 4 | Lean-turbo worktree provisioning — macOS-only lane mock issue |
| quarantined-tests-windows.txt | 0 | Clean |
| quarantined-integration-tests.txt | 2 | Ubuntu CI-only: read-only fs semantics + injection-budget shared-state |

---

## Part A — Diagnose and fix the 11 remaining quarantined tests

### A1. macOS lean-turbo worktree tests (4 files)

**Files:**
```
tests/unit/turbo/lean/integration-worktree.test.ts
tests/unit/turbo/lean/runner.test.ts
tests/unit/turbo/lean/runner.adversarial.test.ts
tests/unit/turbo/lean/retroactive-adversarial.test.ts
```

**Failure signature (from merge_group run 28806176287):**
```
expect(received).toBeGreaterThan(expected)
Expected: > 0
Received: 0
```
The tests mock `provisionWorktree` via `_internals.bunSpawn` and assert it was called at least 1 time during `runPhase`. On macOS it's called **0 times** — `runPhase` takes a different code path. These tests pass on ubuntu and Windows.

**Suspected root causes to investigate:**
- `checkPathBudget` (src/worktree/core.ts:326) may behave differently on macOS, changing the provisioning path. It's Windows-only in intent but may short-circuit on non-Windows in an unexpected way.
- `git worktree add` porcelain output format or branch creation semantics may differ on the macOS runner's git version, causing the mock to not match.
- A race condition that only manifests on the macOS runner's slower I/O — the `provisionWorktree` call may be async and the mock may not be installed by the time it runs.

title: [TESTING] No property-based or fuzz testing
body_excerpt:
## Background

All existing tests use example-based testing — specific inputs are hardcoded and specific outputs are asserted. For a financial application handling bounty state machines and reward amounts that can range from 1 to 1 billion stroops, property-based testing (generating random inputs and verifying invariants) catches edge cases that example-based tests miss. The Soroban contract's state machine (7 states, 8 transitions) is a perfect candidate for property-based testing.

## Evidence

**All tests use hardcoded values:**
```rust
// apps/contracts/src/lib.rs
let amount: i128 = 1000;
client.initialize(&owner, &amount, &token_address, &arbitrator);
```

**`apps/backend/src/bounties/dto/bounty.dto.spec.ts` — example-based:**
```ts
it.each(['0', '-1', '10.5', 'not-a-number', ...])
```

## Problem

- Edge cases at the boundaries of valid input ranges are not tested
- State machine transitions: not all 64 possible paths (7 states × 8 functions + transitions) are verified
- Reward amount range (1 to 1,000,000,000 XLM in stroops) has untested boundaries
- Contract invariants (funds always equal deposited amount, status always valid) are not verified

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Property-based tests are added for backend DTO validation using `fast-check`
- [ ] Property-based tests are added for contract state machine using `proptest` crate
- [ ] Property: "any valid CreateBountyDto passes validation" — generate random valid DTOs
- [ ] Property: "initialize → fund → start_work → submit → approve always results in Completed with correct funds" — generate random amounts and addresses
- [ ] Property: "no sequence of valid contract calls causes unwrap panic" — fuzz test all function sequences
- [ ] Property-based tests run in CI alongside existing tests

## Implementation Steps

1. Add `fast-check` to backend devDependencies
2. Add `proptest` to contracts dev-dependencies
3. Write fast-check test: generate random valid CreateBountyDto and verify `validate()` returns no errors
4. Write proptest: generate random amounts (1..1B), random addresses, verify full happy path
5. Write proptest: generate random sequences of contract function calls, verify no panics
6. Add property tests to CI

## Files to Modify

- `apps/backend/package.json`
- `apps/backend/src/bounties/dto/bounty.dto.spec.ts`
- `apps/contracts/Cargo.toml`
- `apps/contracts/src/lib.rs`

## Verification

- [ ] `fast-check` test runs 100+ random DTOs without failure
- [ ] `proptest` runs 100+ random co

# Archon fantasy RTS/FPS v0 technical prototype plan

[[index]] [[archon-fantasy-rts-fps-v0-prototype-spec-2026-05-20]] [[archon-fantasy-rts-fps-v0-unit-sheet-2026-05-20]] [[archon-fantasy-rts-fps-v0-map-blockout-2026-05-20]]

Goal: `9171b100de33` — Design and prototype a fantasy Archon RTS/FPS hybrid.

## Technical thesis
Build the smallest networked simulation where human-controlled FPS bodies and RTS-controlled AI squads interact with the same resources, objectives, and base core.

The hard technical problem is not fancy faction content. It is one authoritative match state that accepts both first-person inputs and shared RTS commands.

## Engine recommendation
For a serious multiplayer FPS/RTS prototype, start in Unreal if the team is comfortable with it. Unreal gives stronger defaults for replicated characters, movement, animation, AI navigation, and dedicated-server thinking.

Unity is viable if the team already has networking and FPS experience there. Godot is viable for a lean local/limited prototype but becomes riskier for networked FPS plus RTS at this scope.

Do not choose the engine for faction art. Choose it for multiplayer character control, AI pathing, and authoritative server workflow.

## Network authority model
Use server authority for:
- player body spawning
- player movement validation
- damage and death
- RTS command acceptance
- AI squad movement/orders
- production queues
- resource income
- capture zones
- hero availability
- base core health
- match end

Clients send inputs:
- FPS movement/combat inputs while controlling a body
- RTS commands while using a map table
- respawn body selections

The server owns final state. This matches the design rule: many teammates can input RTS commands, and the resulting team state resolves like normal RTS control.

## Milestone 0: project shell
Goal: create a runnable empty multiplayer test map.

Must have:
- one listen-server or dedicated-server test flow
- two teams
- join team command or auto-assignment
- placeholder player

title: [REVIEW] gcp-review: refresh CIS GCP v5 baseline and scope fields
body_excerpt:
## Skill Being Reviewed
**Skill name:** `gcp-review`
**Skill path:** `skills/cloud/gcp-review/`

## False Positive Analysis

**Benign GCP posture report that can be over-reported under the old baseline:**
```text
Framework: CIS Google Cloud Platform Foundation Benchmark v2.0.0
Sections evaluated:
  1 Identity and Access Management
  2 Logging and Monitoring
  3 Networking
  4 Virtual Machines
  5 Storage
  6 Cloud SQL
  7 BigQuery
Overall compliance: 92%
```

**Why this can be misleading:**

The skill hard-codes CIS Google Cloud Platform Foundation Benchmark v2.0.0 in the description, frontmatter, overview, process, output format, section map, references, and changelog. The NIST National Checklist Program now lists CIS Google Cloud Platform Foundation Benchmark v5.0.0 as a final checklist with an original publication date of 05/09/2026, and the CIS benchmark landing page lists Google Cloud Platform Foundation 5.0.0.

A current GCP posture report should not emit v2.0.0 recommendation IDs, section totals, or compliance percentages without stating that the organization intentionally requested a legacy benchmark. Otherwise teams may treat an outdated seven-section control map as current CIS GCP coverage.

## Coverage Gaps

**Missed variant 1: the framework version is pinned in metadata and output**
```yaml
frameworks: [CIS-GCP-v2.0.0]
```

The report template also emits `Framework: CIS Google Cloud Platform Foundation Benchmark v2.0.0`. The skill should require `benchmark_version`, `benchmark_source_date`, and `legacy_baseline` fields so auditors can distinguish current v5.0.0 evidence from historical v2.0.0 evidence.

**Missed variant 2: project-vs-organization scope is not tied to the benchmark source**
```text
Project/Organization: <identifier>
```

The current NIST checklist summary for v5.0.0 says most recommendations in this release cover individual project-level security considerations, not organization-level scope. The skill currently accepts either project or organization as a generic field, and it can produce one aggregate score without explicitly identifying which findings came from project-level controls, organization-level policy evidence, or not-evaluable org evidence.

This should be made explicit in the selected benchmark preflight and output, especially because an existing organization-level finding may be informative without proving v5.0.0 benchmark coverage.

**Missed variant 3: stale section totals can produce false compliance percentages**

title: test: lock the casing contract on projectKeyFromIssueKey
body_excerpt:
Followup from PR #55 review (https://github.com/aaronsb/jira-cloud/pull/55#issuecomment-4425735490 / #55 item 4).

`projectKeyFromIssueKey(issueKey: string): string` in `src/handlers/issue-handlers.ts:425` is private — both call sites (handleGetIssue:465, handleUpdateIssue:578) go through it, but the contract that it always uppercases the result isn't asserted anywhere. A future "simplification" that drops `.toUpperCase()` would not be caught by the test suite.

## Why it matters

The uppercase normalization keeps two things deterministic regardless of agent input casing:

1. The rendered breadcrumb URI emitted by `markdown-renderer.ts:206` (`jira://custom-fields/{proj}/{type}`) — an agent caching by URI string sees the same key for `paid-192` and `PAID-192`.
2. The cache key passed to `field-discovery.ts:209` (`issueTypesCache`) — already self-normalizes via its own `.toUpperCase()`, but if the helper drops uppercase, the two layers fall out of sync.

## Options

- **Cheapest:** add `// @internal` comment + export `projectKeyFromIssueKey`, write a 4-row test in `src/handlers/issue-handlers.test.ts` (or co-locate in a new `*.test.ts` next to the source). Cases: `PAID-192 → PAID`, `paid-192 → PAID`, `Mixed-1 → MIXED`, `noprefix → NOPREFIX` (documents the no-dash fallback).
- **Cleaner but heavier:** move the helper to `src/utils/jira-keys.ts`, export from there, test it there. Justifies the move only if a third call site appears.
- **Don't:** lean on review to catch any future drop of `.toUpperCase()`. Reviewer flagged this as acceptable given the small surface.

## Acceptance

`projectKeyFromIssueKey('paid-192')` returns `'PAID'`, asserted in a unit test that runs as part of `npm test`.

Low priority — nothing observable breaks today, this is just a contract-locking exercise.

title: [low-medium · needs-decision] Conditional regex (?(id)yes|no) build-rejected & mis-categorized; Python builds and matches (H7-3)
body_excerpt:
## Background

A Python `re` group-existence conditional `(?(1)yes|no)` is rejected at **build** by lark-rs and mis-categorized as a backtracking-only lookaround refusal, where Python Lark *builds* the terminal and matches with it.

- `start: A` / `A: /(a)(?(1)b|c)/` on `"ac"`. Python: builds, parses → `start [Token A "ac"]`. lark-rs: build fails — `Invalid regex pattern '(a)(?(1)b|c)': regex parse error … unrecognized flag (and the lookaround analyzer cannot parse it either; note that backtracking-only syntax is not supported — see docs/LOOKAROUND_SCOPE.md)`. XFAIL: `h7_3_conditional_group_reference_build_accepted`.

Two faults: (a) it rejects a Python-accepted construct, and (b) the refusal category is wrong — a conditional is not a backreference and not "backtracking-only."

Fix site: `grammar/terminal.rs::PatternRe::new` (the generic `Regex::new` → lookaround-analyzer fallback) (verified — the build error text originates here).

## Decision needed

The fix contract is a genuine fork:

1. **Support and match Python** — lower the group-existence conditional into the DFA. A conditional `(?(id)yes|no)` is a regular-ish alternation a linear engine could in principle host, but lowering it is real engine work and may interact with the lookaround-scope taxonomy (`LOOKAROUND_SCOPE.md`). This is the ADR-0017-default direction (match the oracle).
2. **Categorized refusal (diverge-with-divergence)** — keep rejecting it but re-categorize from the generic backtracking-only/lookaround bucket to a clean dialect `NotYetImplemented` (or `OutOfScope`) refusal with an honest message. Rejecting a Python-accepted construct is a *more-restrictive* divergence (the safe direction, unlike accepting what Python rejects), so it is defensible if documented by ADR.

## Recommendation

Lean toward **option 2** (categorized refusal) near-term: conditionals are rare in Lark grammars, and a correct category + honest message is cheap, whereas lowering conditionals is engine work with unclear payoff. Promote to option 1 if a real grammar needs it. Either way the current generic InvalidRegex/"backtracking-only" mislabel should be fixed.

## Consequences

Option 2 leaves the XFAIL asserting the *support* behavior, so it would be re-pointed (assert a categorized refusal) or kept as a promotion tripwire. Option 1 closes it as written.

title: Expand merchant catalog: integrate x402 Bazaar discovery + seed broader categories
body_excerpt:
## Summary

Grow the merchant catalog beyond its current seed so `haven_discover_tools` / the dashboard surface a useful set of pay-per-call x402 (and MPP) merchants — and, more importantly, make growth **sustainable** by tapping the x402 ecosystem's discovery layer instead of hand-curating forever.

## Current state

The catalog ships with **4 seed rows** (migration [`019_merchant_catalog.ts`](packages/backend/src/db/migrations/019_merchant_catalog.ts)):

| Name | Category | Rail | Protocol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Soundside — text generation | media | x402 | mcp |
| Soundside — image generation | media | x402 | mcp |
| Soundside — song generation | media | x402 | mcp |
| Haven MPP demo resource | demo | mpp | http |

So today the only *real* third-party merchant is Soundside, and only one category (`media`) is represented. Each entry is validated by the read-only probe in [`lib/merchant-catalog.ts`](packages/backend/src/lib/merchant-catalog.ts) (expects HTTP 402 + parsable challenge; degrades after `DEGRADE_AFTER_FAILURES`). That probe is the asset we should lean on: **anything we add gets price/availability verified automatically**, so the cost of adding a candidate is low and a bad entry self-degrades rather than misleading users.

## Recommendation 1 (strategic): integrate the x402 Bazaar discovery layer

Coinbase's **x402 Bazaar** is now the canonical discovery index for x402 resources, with a machine-readable catalog and an MCP discovery endpoint:

- Paginated catalog: `GET https://api.cdp.coinbase.com/platform/v2/x402/discovery/resources` (limit/offset)
- Semantic search: `GET …/v2/x402/discovery/search`
- MCP endpoint: `https://api.cdp.coinbase.com/platform/v2/x402/discovery/mcp`

Reportedly ~10k paid resources across Base/Solana. Instead of (or alongside) hand-seeding rows, Haven could pull candidates from Bazaar, run each through our existing `probeCatalogEntry`, and persist only the ones that verify. This turns the catalog from a static seed into a self-refreshing index and is a natural extension of the existing `refreshCatalog` cron.

**Proposed shape:** a `lib/catalog-discovery.ts` that fetches Bazaar pages, maps each resource → `CatalogRow` shape (name/description/category/resource_url/rail/protocol/tool_name), and feeds them through the probe before insert. Keep it opt-in / rate-limited; respect Base vs Solana network support (we're Base/Gnosis today — filter to chains we can actually pay on).

[REVIEW] aws-review: refresh CIS AWS v5 control mapping
body_excerpt:
## Skill Being Reviewed
**Skill name:** `aws-review`
**Skill path:** `skills/cloud/aws-review/`

## False Positive Analysis

**Benign AWS posture report that can be over-reported under the old baseline:**
```text
Framework: CIS Amazon Web Services Foundations Benchmark v3.0.0
Total CIS recommendations evaluated: 62/62
Section scores:
  1 Identity and Access Management: 20/22
  2 Storage: 9/10
  3 Logging: 10/11
  4 Monitoring: 15/16
  5 Networking: 5/6
Overall compliance: 95%
```

**Why this can be misleading:**

The skill is hard-coded to CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v3.0.0 and a fixed `62` recommendation denominator. AWS Security Hub CSPM now supports CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v5.0.0 and recommends using v5.0.0 to stay current. AWS also publishes a version comparison showing different control-to-requirement mappings across v5.0.0, v3.0.0, v1.4.0, and v1.2.0.

A report generated today should not present v3.0.0 recommendation counts and mappings as current CIS AWS coverage unless legacy v3.0.0 was explicitly requested. Otherwise a team may get stale compliance percentages or miss controls that exist in v5.0.0, such as the v5 EFS encryption-at-rest control listed in AWS Security Hub CSPM.

## Coverage Gaps

**Missed variant 1: the benchmark version and denominator are pinned**
```text
Framework: CIS Amazon Web Services Foundations Benchmark v3.0.0
Total CIS recommendations evaluated: <N>/62
```

The output should record `benchmark_version`, `benchmark_source_date`, `security_hub_standard_arn_or_version`, and `legacy_baseline`. The denominator should come from the selected benchmark/control mapping, not from the skill's v3.0.0 constant.

**Missed variant 2: v5-only or remapped controls can be omitted from current scoring**
```text
Skill section map:
  2 Storage: 10 recommendations
```

AWS's v5.0.0 control list includes current supported controls and the version-comparison table maps controls differently across benchmark versions. If the skill only walks the v3.0.0 section map, it can omit or mislabel current v5.0.0 controls and produce a compliance score that does not match Security Hub CSPM's current CIS standard.

**Missed variant 3: removed or unsupported requirements can be reported as current failures**
```text
Finding: CIS 3.3 - CloudTrail log bucket is publicly accessible
Status: Fail under current benchmark
```

AWS's version-comparison guidance includes cases where controls are not supported for later versions because CIS removed a requirement

title: Why a Fixed $1,000 Position Size Beats the Classic “Never Lose More Than 2 %” Rule in Turbulent Markets
body_excerpt:
### The Counter‑Intuitive Trade

Imagine you own a small‑cap tech stock that has just broken out of a long‑term downtrend. Your portfolio sits at $50,000 and the usual risk‑management mantra tells you to risk no more than 2 % on any single trade—$1,000 in this case. That feels comfortable, right?  

Now picture the same stock entering a three‑month period of extreme volatility, with daily swings of 8 % to 12 % as earnings, regulatory news, and macro data clash. You stick to the 2 % rule, buying a modest $1,000 position each time you see a pull‑back. Over the next three months you make five entries, each of which gets whipsawed down to a 15 % loss before you finally exit. Your cumulative loss is roughly $750.

Now flip the script: you decide instead to size every entry at a flat $1,000, regardless of your portfolio’s current value, and you *only* take a trade when the odds, measured by a disciplined edge (e.g., a 60 % win probability with an average win of $300 and an average loss of $150), are strongly in your favor. You make just two such high‑certainty bets before the volatility subsides, each yielding a $300 profit. Your net result is a $600 gain, despite risking the same dollar amount per trade.

The difference isn’t the dollar amount—it’s the *relationship* between position size, portfolio equity, and the quality of the edge you’re betting on. In volatile regimes, a fixed‑dollar size can actually protect you better than a percentage‑of‑equity rule, because it forces you to be selective about when you trade, and it caps the impact of equity swings on your willingness to stay in the game.

Below, I unpack why a rigid $1,000 position size can be a superior risk‑control mechanism when markets are noisy, and how you can translate that insight into a simple, repeatable process.

---

## 1. The Mechanics of Risk: Percentage vs. Fixed Dollar

|                     | %‑of‑Equity Rule (2 %) | Fixed Dollar Rule ($1,000) |
|---------------------|------------------------|----------------------------|
| **Initial Portfolio** | $50,000                | $50,000                    |
| **Position Size**   | $1,000 (2 % of equity) | $1,000 (constant)          |
| **After 10 % loss** | $45,000 → $900 (1.8 % of equity) | $50,000 → $1,000 (still 2 % of equity) |
| **After 20 % gain** | $60,000 → $1,200 (2 % of equity) | $50,000 → $1,000 (still 2 % of equity) |
| **Decision Pressure** | Increases as equity falls (you may feel forced to “double‑down”) | Remains constant – yo

title: feat(events): type EventId and event advancement reward references
body_excerpt:
## Summary

Move advancement-backed event IDs and event reward-function references onto Sand's typed resource-location / function-reference APIs instead of accepting bare strings on the normal event authoring path.

## Problem

Verified against current `main`, the open issue list, recent PRs, and `docs/typedness-audit.md`:

- The typedness audit still classifies `sand-core/event/mod.rs` as only **Mostly typed** because `EventAdvancement`/event IDs are raw strings and should use `ResourceLocation`.
- `sand-core/src/event/mod.rs` models `EventId::Explicit(&'static str)` and `EventId::resolve(...) -> String`, so invalid resource locations can remain in the event configuration until a later command/export boundary.
- `sand-core/src/event/builder.rs` exposes `EventBuilder::id(id: impl Into<String>)`, then leaks the string into `EventId::Explicit(...)`; this is not a typed boundary and makes invalid IDs look like normal API usage.
- `EventConfig::advancement(advancement_id: impl Into<String>, reward_fn: impl Into<String>)` parses the advancement ID internally but still accepts raw string inputs, and forwards `reward_fn` into `AdvancementRewards::function(...)` as a raw function reference.
- #183 covers the general advancement component surface for display/icon/rewards/parent IDs, but it does not explicitly cover the event builder API that generates advancement-backed event components.
- #194 covers typed function macro arguments; it is related to function calls/macros but does not type event reward function references.

For a strongly typed event framework, normal event authoring should not allow malformed advancement IDs or reward function IDs to travel as arbitrary strings.

## Suggested design

- Replace or supplement `EventId::Explicit(&'static str)` with a typed resource-location-backed form, for example `EventId::Explicit(ResourceLocation)` or `EventId::Explicit(AdvancementId)` if a dedicated advancement ID wrapper exists.
- Add typed constructors such as:
  - `EventId::explicit(id: impl TryInto<ResourceLocation>) -> Result<Self, ...>` or a panicking `new` plus fallible `try_explicit` depending on existing Sand conventions.
  - `EventBuilder::id(ResourceLocation)` / `EventBuilder::advancement_id(...)` with a clearly named raw/custom escape hatch only if needed.
- Update `EventConfig::advancement(...)` so the advancement ID and reward function argument use typed resource/function reference types on the normal path, reusing `ResourceLocation`, `FunctionRef`,

title: Grading: `path:`-style jsonpath assertions are not evaluated in Docker mode (runner has no JSONPath engine)
body_excerpt:
## Summary

In Docker grading mode, `state_checks.jsonpaths` assertions using `path:` (JSONPath
into the env-state DB, e.g. `$.db.orders[0].id`) are **not evaluated by the
grader**. Only `path_glob:` (filesystem glob) assertions are. Authors who write
careful `path:` assertions get them silently ignored — verdicts are driven entirely
by other grading components (hash, transcript), with the JSONPath assertions
producing 0 contribution regardless of state.

After PR #66 these assertions now produce a clear `FAIL: ... graded host-side` in
the reasons text, so the symptom is *visible*. But the underlying gap remains: the
assertions still don't actually evaluate the state they describe.

## Root cause: two parallel grading evaluators that don't speak the same language

- **Host-side** (`tolokaforge/core/grading/state_checks.py`,
  `StateChecker.check_jsonpaths`): understands both shapes — `path:` (JSONPath into
  env-state) AND `path_glob:` (filesystem glob). Has `jsonpath_ng` + the
  `equals` / `equals_ci` / `contains` / `contains_ci` operator logic.
- **Runner-side** (`tolokaforge/runner/grading.py`,
  `evaluate_jsonpath_file_checks`): only understands `path_glob:` + `contains_ci:`
  on the container filesystem. Has no JSONPath engine.

In Docker mode the orchestrator delegates grading to the runner (it owns the
env-state DB at grade time). The runner receives the full `state_checks.jsonpaths`
list — including any `path:` assertions — and silently skips everything it can't
evaluate. PR #66 makes that skip loud, but the assertions still don't run.

## Repro (deterministic, no LLM)

Write a task with mixed-shape jsonpaths:

```yaml
state_checks:
  jsonpaths:
    - path: "$.db.orders[0].status"
      equals: "paid"
      description: "Order status is paid"
    - path_glob: "/env/fs/agent-visible/notes/*"
      contains_ci: "shipped"
      description: "Notes mention shipping"
```

Run under Docker grading. The `path:` assertion will report
`FAIL: assertion uses 'path' ... graded host-side` even when `$.db.orders[0].status`
is genuinely `"paid"` in the runner's env-state. The `path_glob:` assertion
evaluates correctly.

## Impact

- Task authors ship grading.yaml configs that read as strict but evaluate as
  no-ops for any `path:`-style assertion. Tested via PR #66's diagnostic surface;
  every `path:` assertion across the repos is currently a no-op under Docker mode.
- Verdicts can be misleading: a task may pass on hash + transcript while its

title: Host a prebuilt olean cache so contributors fetch instead of building (73 min → ~3 min)
body_excerpt:
## Problem

A new contributor's first build is the onboarding bottleneck. Measured from a clean clone on a 12-core machine (Lean `v4.31.0-rc1`):

| Phase | Time |
|---|---|
| `git clone --depth 1` | 2 s |
| `cache get` (mathlib oleans) | seconds–minutes (download, not compile) |
| **`lake build LeanPool` — 2038 modules from source** | **72.8 min** |

The build dominates, and it is paid **in full on every fresh checkout** because Lean Pool publishes no olean cache for its own code. (mathlib only *feels* fast because contributors download its prebuilt oleans; compiled from source on the same machine mathlib takes ~135 min.)

The fix is the same one mathlib uses: **host a prebuilt olean cache and fetch it.**

## Why this is the right lever

- Build is CPU-bound and embarrassingly parallel (90 independent projects on mathlib); per-file tuning has a realistic ceiling of ~10–15%.
- The olean payload is **1.5 GB raw → ~460 MB gzipped**. Fetching ~460 MB (1–5 min) instead of a 72.8 min compile is a **~20–30× onboarding win**.
- CI already builds the whole pool on every PR — we just discard the output instead of keeping it.

## Proposal

### Tier 1 — whole-pool tarball keyed by commit (ship first, ~80% of value)
- [ ] On merge to `main`, CI tars `.lake/build/lib/lean/LeanPool` (~460 MB gz) and uploads it keyed by `<lean-toolchain>+<commit-sha>`.
- [ ] Add `make cache-get`: download the tarball for `HEAD`, unpack into `.lake/build`, fix mtimes + trace hashes so `lake` treats the oleans as fresh.
- [ ] Storage backend: Cloudflare R2 (zero egress) preferred; Azure or GitHub Releases (460 MB < 2 GB/file) acceptable. Retain last N commits.
- Outcome: fresh `main` checkout 73 min → ~3 min. Editing one project rebuilds only that subtree.

### Tier 2 — per-module content-addressed cache (only if needed later)
- [ ] Adapt mathlib's `Cache` exe to hash each LeanPool module by (source + transitive imports + toolchain) and store per-module tarballs, so any branch fetches every olean except the few its change invalidates.
- Defer until Tier 1's "rebuild the whole edited project" proves too slow for projects people actually touch.

## Gotchas (all solved by mirroring mathlib's cache)
- [ ] **Freshness:** `lake` rebuilds unless a stored hash/trace matches — the client must write those (the one fiddly part).
- [ ] **Toolchain keying:** oleans are toolchain-+-mathlib-specific; the key must include both, and **every version bump must re-upload** or everyone cache-misses. Wire the up

title: [Research] Asset-generation pipeline: using Claude + paid AI tools for consistent art/audio/store/text assets
body_excerpt:
Research findings from a `/deep-research` run (2026-07-02) on **how to use Claude to generate
high-quality, stylistically-consistent assets** across all four categories: visual/game art, audio,
store/marketing, and in-game text/narrative. Priority was **quality & consistency across a large asset
set**, with Claude orchestrating paid AI tools (Midjourney/Flux/ElevenLabs) where useful.

Filed to pursue later — this is a **backlog/research** issue, not a scoped code change. No production
code is touched by filing it.

**Method:** 5 search angles → ~15 sources fetched → claims extracted → **3-vote adversarial
verification** per claim (2/3 refutes kills it) → synthesis. **20 claims survived, 5 refuted.** Every
finding below carries its source + confidence; refuted claims are listed at the end so we don't act on
them. Time-sensitive items (2025–26 tool behaviour) are flagged for re-verification at implementation.

---

## Headline insight (reframes the whole approach)

**The battle renderer already draws 100% procedurally in Kotlin/Canvas — zero raster sprites.** Verified
against our own code: enemies are `drawRect` (`EnemyEntity.kt:130`), projectiles/orbs are `drawCircle`,
the ziggurat is stacked `drawRect` layers (`ZigguratEntity.kt:108`), biome skies are `LinearGradient`
shaders (`BackgroundRenderer.kt`), HP bars/floating text via `drawRect`/`drawText`; **no `drawBitmap` in
main**. [Confidence: **high** — primary Android docs + our codebase]

Consequence for the #1 goal (consistency): **code-drawn art is deterministic and governed by a single
source of truth** — a stochastic image generator fights consistency, a Kotlin function does not. So split
the asset problem in two:

- **Code-drawable** (in-battle entities, projectiles, particles, biome backgrounds, many UI shapes) →
  **Claude writes/refactors Kotlin.** Perfect consistency, free, version-controlled, no licensing questions.
- **Raster-only** (app icon, Play feature graphic, marketing art, detailed illustrated UI icons) →
  **Claude orchestrates Midjourney/Flux** with the consistency techniques below.

---

**Procedural (default for in-battle visuals):**
- Canvas primitives cover a large class of needs — `drawText`, `drawRect`/`drawOval`/`drawArc`,
  `Path`/`drawPath`, `LinearGradient`+`setShader`, `drawBitmap`. UI icons, projectiles, biome background
