title: Earn + redeem reward (idempotent) + receipt
body_excerpt:
# 07 — Earn + redeem reward (idempotent) + receipt

Label: ready-for-agent · Type: AFK
Source: docs/prd-loyalty-mvp.md

## What to build

Closing the loop. Reaching N stamps creates a discrete `reward` in state `available` and notifies the customer by WhatsApp. On the staff card screen a **Redeem button appears only when a reward is available**. Redemption is **idempotent** (`available → redeemed`, never reversible, never double-redeemable) and **deducts the threshold while carrying the remainder**. Each redemption is attributed to the staff PIN and fires a **WhatsApp receipt** to the customer — the anti-self-dealing control.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Reaching N creates an `available` reward and sends a bilingual "reward earned" message.
- [ ] Redeem button is shown only when a reward is available.
- [ ] Redemption transitions `available → redeemed` idempotently; a second attempt is a no-op (verified by test).
- [ ] Threshold is deducted and any surplus stamps carry over.
- [ ] Redemption is attributed to staff and a WhatsApp receipt is dispatched to the customer.
- [ ] No receipt is sent for an opted-out enrollment.
## Blocked by

- #6

Fetch and analyze https://www.foxmortgage.ca/smm in full detail:
- What is the current value proposition and how clearly is it communicated?

### 1B. Review FOX-4 and FOX-9
Pull context from both issues and summarize:
- What SMM growth strategies were previously identified or attempted
- What was decided or built
- What remains unresolved or untested
- Flag anything that contradicts or should be updated based on current findings

---

## Phase 2 — Platform and Onboarding Research

### 2A. Free Onboarding and Enrollment Platforms
Research and compare the best free or freemium platforms for managing a subscriber/member onboarding flow. Evaluate each on:
- Ease of setup
- Automation capability (welcome sequences, follow-up triggers)
- CRM integration potential (especially Zoho CRM)
- Email/SMS delivery included or not

title: feat: pre-launch security hardening pass
body_excerpt:
## Background / Context

Omakase already has a solid security baseline (see `CLAUDE.md` → "Security & Configuration"): JWT auth, `IsAuthenticated` default, CORS allowlist, refresh token blacklisting on password change, ScopedRateThrottle on password change, env-required `SECRET_KEY`, `rehype-sanitize` on markdown preview, hex regex on tag colors. Pre-commit runs `detect-secrets`. Postgres is bound to `127.0.0.1`.

That's the **baseline** — enough for development, not enough to put in front of real users on the public internet. This issue is the **pre-launch security hardening pass** that takes Omakase from "secure-ish in dev" to "ready for v1 deploy". It is a hard prerequisite for [Deploy v1](#) — that issue should not merge before this one ships.

## User stories

- **As an end user**, I want my session, password, and personal data protected against common web attacks (XSS, CSRF, brute-force, replay) so that I can trust the app with my study schedule and personal notes.
- **As the operator (you)**, I want a documented threat model and a clear list of mitigations so that incident response is faster than starting from zero.
- **As a maintainer**, I want supply-chain attacks caught early via dependency scanning so that a compromised npm/pip package doesn't reach prod.
- **As a compliance reader**, I want auditable logs of authentication events and data-modifying actions so that suspicious activity is investigable.

## Scope (in)

### Authentication & session
- **Refresh token rotation** — issue a new refresh token on every refresh, blacklist the previous one (`ROTATE_REFRESH_TOKENS=True`, `BLACKLIST_AFTER_ROTATION=True`).
- **Refresh token storage in HttpOnly cookies** behind a feature flag — opt-in path so we can move off of localStorage for refresh tokens (access tokens stay in memory). Cookie attributes: `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`, short path scope `/api/v1/auth/`.
- **Brute-force protection on `/auth/token/`** — `django-axes` or DRF `ScopedRateThrottle` (`5/minute` per IP, `20/hour` per username). Lockout after N failures with exponential backoff.
- **Generic auth error messages** — never leak whether a username exists. Audit `RegisterSerializer`, `LoginView`, password reset flow.
- **Optional 2FA (TOTP)** — `django-otp` integration, opt-in via Settings page, recovery codes generated on enable.
- **Email verification on registration** — gate sensitive actions until verified. Verification token signed with `itsdangerous`, single-use, 24h TTL.

title: Landing Page Improvements: Clarify Positioning, Simplify Task Flow, and Improve Conversion Structure
body_excerpt:
After reviewing the current Gibwork landing page, the overall product is well presented visually, but the messaging and structure can be improved to better reflect the full product experience and improve user understanding.

The page currently leans heavily toward an open-source bounty narrative, while the actual product experience appears broader (task marketplace / reward-based work system). This creates some gaps in clarity for new users.

Key Issues Identified:

1. Positioning is too narrow

The hero messaging frames Gibwork mainly as an open source bounty platform. However, the product experience shown includes broader task-based earning beyond OSS contributions.

Impact: Users may misunderstand the scope of the platform.

2. No visibility of mobile or multi-platform access

There is currently no mention of mobile usage or cross-device experience.

Impact: Reduces clarity on accessibility and limits perceived product reach.

3. Task flow is not clearly explained

The landing page shows task cards and activity, but does not clearly explain the end-to-end flow (create → complete → earn).

Impact: Users must infer how the product works.

4. “Recent Work” section is not contextualized

The activity feed shows real usage, but lacks explanation of what tasks were completed or why they matter.

Impact: Feels like raw data instead of a guided narrative.

5. CTA structure is not clearly defined

Multiple CTAs exist across the page without a strong primary conversion path.

Impact: Weakens onboarding flow and user action clarity.

Suggested Improvements

1. Improve hero messaging

Clarify Gibwork as a broader task marketplace:

“Gibwork is a decentralized task marketplace where users complete digital work and earn rewards.”

2. Add a simple “How it works” section
	•	Create or browse tasks
	•	Complete tasks
	•	Earn rewards instantly

Use a simple visual flow.

3. Improve mobile/product accessibility messaging

Add a section clarifying:
	•	web + mobile access (if applicable)
	•	cross-platform experience

4. Reframe “Recent Work” section

Instead of only listing activity, add context:
	•	task type
	•	outcome
	•	reward earned

5. Strengthen CTA hierarchy

Define a clear primary funnel:
	•	Start Earning (primary)
	•	Create Task (secondary)
	•	Explore Tasks (tertiary)

Expected Benefit

These changes would:
	•	Improve clarity of product scope
	•	Strengthen onboarding understanding
	•	Reduce confusion for new users
	•	Improve conversion from landing page visits to act

title: Rewrite Lianki as a CF-native app (Hono + Vite/React SPA + Workers Assets), retire Next.js

Goal: leave Next.js/OpenNext for a Cloudflare-native stack so the app fits the **free Workers plan** (the OpenNext worker is 4.49 MiB gzipped vs the 3 MiB free cap; see #95 thread) and drops the Vercel dependency entirely. Data layer (D1/R2) and auth (better-auth on D1) are already CF-native and migrated — this is a **frontend/runtime** rewrite, not a data one.

## Why it fits free Workers
A Hono worker + React SPA served via **Workers Static Assets** keeps the *worker script* tiny (hundreds of KB); the React bundle ships as **assets, which are not counted against the 3 MiB script limit**. No paid plan needed.

## Target stack
- **Hono** on Workers — routing + serving + API (de-facto CF standard, tiny).
- **Vite + React** SPA — reuse existing client components; client-side router (react-router/TanStack Router).
- **Workers Static Assets** for the SPA bundle.
- **better-auth** (kysely/D1 path, already working) mounted in Hono.
- **D1 + R2** bindings — unchanged.
- **intlayer** via its Vite/React integration (`react-intlayer`) — keep the 16 content files, avoid an i18n rewrite.
- **Prerender** landing + blog routes to static HTML for SEO (Vite SSG / small prerender step).

title: Payment currency should normalize before intent creation
body_excerpt:
Parent Algora bounty: #743

## Bug

`apps/api/src/services/paymentService.js` returns `payload.currency` exactly as submitted. Mixed-case or whitespace-padded values such as `" USD "` are returned as non-canonical payment intent currency values.

This issue is limited only to the creator of this issue. This means that only the issue author can attempt to solve this issue. If you would like to work on it, please create another issue with the same contents and refer to issue Low Handing Fruit Automation #743 for more information.

## Steps to reproduce

Call `createPaymentIntent` with a currency value that includes leading/trailing whitespace or uppercase characters:

```js
await createPaymentIntent({
  amount: 125,
  currency: " USD "
});
```

## Expected behavior

The payment intent should return a canonical lowercase currency value:

```json
{
  "currency": "usd"
}
```

Blank currency values should continue to default to `"usd"`.

## Actual behavior

The service returns the submitted value unchanged.

## Scope

- Keep the change limited to `apps/api/src/services/paymentService.js`.
- Add focused service-level regression coverage for currency normalization.
- Preserve the existing default `"usd"` behavior.

## Validation plan

- `node --test apps/api/src/tests/paymentService.test.js`
- `node --test apps/api/src/tests/*.test.js`
- `npm run build --workspace apps/web`
- `git diff --check`

## Safety

title: Payment creation passes raw body to service without input validation
body_excerpt:
Parent Algora bounty: #743

## Bug
`paymentController.createPayment` calls `createPaymentIntent(req.body)` directly without any input schema validation. Required fields like `amount` and `currency` are not enforced, so a request with an empty body creates a payment intent with `amount: undefined` and falls back to `currency: 'usd'` silently.

## Reproduction
1. Send `POST /api/payments` with body `{}`.
2. Response: `201 Created` with `{ amount: undefined, currency: 'usd', ... }`.

## Expected behavior
Create `apps/api/src/validators/payment.js` with a Zod schema requiring:
- `amount`: positive number
- `currency`: string (e.g. `'usd'`)

Apply the validator in `paymentController.createPayment` before calling the service; invalid payloads return `400`.

## Scope
Create `validators/payment.js` and update `paymentController.js`. Do not touch the payment service or routes.

/attempt #743

title: Bounty payout fires for a coupon that doesn't match the bounty's store (missing coupon↔bounty validation)
body_excerpt:
## Summary (a bounty payout fires for a coupon that has nothing to do with the bounty)

`POST /api/bounties/[id]/claim` only checks that the submitted `coupon_id` **exists**. It never checks that the coupon is actually for the store the bounty is asking about. Any pre-existing coupon id (e.g. `1`, seeded/created for an unrelated store) satisfies the claim, and the route then broadcasts a real `reward_usd` payout from the merchant web wallet.

## Details

In `apps/web/app/api/bounties/[id]/claim/route.ts`:

```ts
const coupons = await db.sql`SELECT * FROM coupons WHERE id = ${coupon_id}`;   // line 30
if (!coupons.length) return NextResponse.json({ error: 'Coupon not found' }, { status: 404 });  // line 31

// ...straight to claim + payout, no relevance check:
await db.sql`
  UPDATE bounties
  SET status = 'claimed', coupon_id = ${coupon_id}, claimer_did = ${did}, ...
  WHERE id = ${bountyId} AND status IN ('open', 'funded')
`;                                                                             // line 34-39
// ... prepare-tx + broadcast pays bounty.reward_usd to the claimer          // line 60-83
```

A bounty targets a store via `store_id` **or** free-text `store_name` (`bounties` table, `apps/web/scripts/migrate.mjs:129`), and every coupon has a `store_id NOT NULL` (`apps/web/lib/schema.sql:17`). The claim path compares **neither**. It also never checks that a coupon hasn't already been used to claim a different bounty.

## Impact

- **Payout for irrelevant work.** A bounty created and funded for "a Nike coupon" can be claimed with an existing Amazon coupon (or literally any coupon id). The creator's escrowed `reward_usd` is paid out for a coupon that does not fulfill the bounty.
- **Coupon reuse / wallet drain.** Because there is no "coupon already used" guard, one existing coupon can be used to claim **every** open/funded bounty in sequence, draining the merchant wallet.

This is separate from #35 (which is about `open` vs `funded` status) — it applies even to properly-funded bounties.

## Repro

1. Note any existing coupon id (the migration seeds Amazon/Nike/Walmart coupons; or `POST /api/coupons` one for any store).
2. Find a funded bounty for a *different* store.
3. `POST /api/bounties/{public_id}/claim` with `{ "coupon_id": <that unrelated id> }`.
4. Bounty flips to `claimed`/`paid` and `reward_usd` is broadcast to your wallet.

## Fix (PR opened)

Before marking the bounty claimed: (1) require the coupon's store to match the bounty's `stor

title: [L13] Diamond commingles VPFI with no on-chain balance≥obligations invariant → first-come insolvency between reward and custody/rebate claimants
body_excerpt:
**Severity:** Low · **Confidence:** Confirmed (demonstrated by test) · Part of #892 · Elevated from round-1 informational, demonstrated in round-3 invariant tests

**Location:** `LibInteractionRewards.poolRemaining` / `getInteractionPoolRemaining()` (pure accounting: 69M cap − paidOut); borrower-LIF `vpfiHeld` custody + `rebateAmount` in `LibVPFIDiscount` / `ClaimFacet`; all share the single Diamond VPFI ERC20 balance. Demonstration: `contracts/test/audit/Round3CrossFacetInvariants.t.sol::test_Invariant_VpfiCustody_InteractionPoolAccountingIsNotBacked`

### Description
The Diamond's VPFI balance backs multiple independent accounting buckets — interaction-reward pool payouts, borrower-LIF custody (`vpfiHeld`), borrower rebates (`rebateAmount`), and keeper/reward budgets — segregated only by independent counters. `getInteractionPoolRemaining()` is pure accounting (cap − paidOut) with **no dedicated backing** and is paid from the same balance as LIF custody/rebates. There is no on-chain invariant asserting `VPFI.balanceOf(diamond) ≥ Σ vpfiHeld + Σ rebateAmount + poolRemaining + budgets`.

The round-3 invariant suite includes two tests here:
- `test_Invariant_VpfiCustody_DiamondBalanceCoversHardObligations` asserts `balanceOf(diamond) ≥ Σ vpfiHeld + Σ rebateAmount` (the *hard* custody obligations) — expected to pass.
- `test_Invariant_VpfiCustody_InteractionPoolAccountingIsNotBacked` asserts `balanceOf(diamond) < hard obligations + poolRemaining` — **this test passing IS the finding**: the reward pool's "remaining" is not separately funded.

### Attack scenario / impact
Not an external exploit — an operational/solvency risk. If the interaction pool is ever under-seeded (operator does not deposit the full emission schedule up front) or reward payouts run ahead of deposits, reward claims can draw down VPFI that is earmarked as `vpfiHeld` custody or `rebateAmount`, surfacing later as a **revert when a borrower tries to claim their rebate** (first-come-first-served insolvency between reward claimants and custody/rebate claimants). Silent until the balance is actually short.

### Recommendation
1. Add a monitored on-chain view (`getTotalVpfiCustody()` + pool/budget totals) and, ideally, a hard invariant assertion that `balanceOf(diamond) ≥ Σ all obligations` at the fund-moving boundaries.
2. Document the funding requirement at deploy (seed the full pool up front) and gate reward payouts on backed balance.

PR #94 implemented this issue over 3 review rounds (see PR history/comments for the full back-and-forth, including two bugs found and fixed post-merge-candidate: a `PHASE_CONFIGS` singleton mutation and a verdict-string filter typo that silently zeroed out `confirmed_findings`). The Tasks / Done-when / Review-checklist items below are checked off against what was independently verified in code, not against the PR description's claims. **This issue is intentionally kept open** — the merge does not close it — because of the unchecked items (version-pin is decorative-only; no fixture-identity regression test for the default path). ### Background
Property generation is currently a single LLM phase: `01e` runs `prompts/01e_prop_worker.md` and writes `outputs/01e_PARTIAL_*.json`. There's no way to produce that same property schema from anything other than the prompt, and there's no E2E verification / reproduction step after the `04` review gates — PoCs are generated manually through `prompts/05_poc.md`. 2-D needs **both** sides — property generation **and** post-`04` verification/reproduction — to be first-class, swappable backends so the Lean provider (#88) and the Kurtosis E2E harness (#92) drop in the way any phase does. This issue lands the seams only.

The goal is not just "add a Lean option" or "add a Kurtosis option." title: When Reputation Becomes a Bug: What The Selfish Gene Teaches Us About Open‑Source Collaboration
body_excerpt:
## The hidden trade‑off everyone feels, but no one names

You’ve just merged a PR that added a shiny new feature. Your GitHub notifications ping, a handful of stars appear on your profile, and on the side‑project Discord someone shouts, “Nice work, *you*!” The rush is intoxicating. Yet, a week later the CI pipeline starts flaking, downstream projects break, and a frantic thread opens about “why did we depend on this module?”. The same contribution that earned you reputation now threatens the stability of the whole ecosystem.

That moment of cognitive dissonance—*personal acclaim versus collective fragility*—is the tension this post unpacks. It’s not a quirk of a single repo; it’s a structural mismatch baked into how we, as humans, signal value in a digital commons.

---

## A meme‑level lens on code contributions

Richard Dawkins coined the term *meme* to describe ideas that replicate by hopping from brain to brain, much like genes propagate through bodies. In *The Selfish Gene*, he showed that genes are indifferent to the organism’s wellbeing; they only care about their own replication.

If we replace “gene” with “reputation signal” and “organism” with “software community”, the analogy clicks:

- **Fitness function** → number of eyes on your GitHub profile, mentions in newsletters, invites to speak.
- **Replication unit** → a pull request, a blog post, a talk.
- **Environment** → the open‑source ecosystem, which values both novelty and reliability.

Your PR is a meme. It spreads because it’s visible, because it *talks* about you. The ecosystem, however, also needs *antifragile* structures—those that get stronger under stress. The tension emerges when the meme’s fitness (reputation) diverges from the system’s fitness (robustness).

---

## Why the "status‑by‑PR" instinct feels natural

Evolution didn’t design us for GitHub. In hunter‑gatherer bands, broadcasting successful hunts or clever tool‑making boosted one’s standing, unlocking access to mates, food, and allies. Modern workplaces co‑opted that instinct: performance reviews, LinkedIn endorsements, conference speaker slots. Open‑source simply made the arena global and instantly measurable.

The problem is *mismatch*: the ancient reward circuitry (dopamine spikes for social acknowledgment) now triggers for a PR that might be a half‑baked experiment. The system’s “immune response” – code reviews, CI checks – is comparatively slow. By the time the bug is discovered, the reputation meme has already replica

title: Claiming an unfunded ('open') bounty triggers a real payout from the merchant wallet
body_excerpt:
## Summary (CRITICAL — unfunded bounty triggers a real payout)

`POST /api/bounties/[id]/claim` lets a bounty be claimed while its status is `open`, and the claim path then broadcasts a real payout from the merchant web wallet — even though `open` means the creator's funding was never confirmed.

## Details

- A bounty is created with `status = 'open'` in `POST /api/bounties`, and only flips to `funded` after CoinPay confirms the creator's funding payment (`webhooks/coinpay/route.ts` sets `status='funded' WHERE status='open'`).
- The claim guard accepts both:
  ```ts
  if (!['open', 'funded'].includes(bounty.status)) { ... 409 ... }   // line 23
  ...
  WHERE id = ${bountyId} AND status IN ('open', 'funded')            // line 38 (atomic UPDATE)
  ```
- So a bounty whose funding was **never completed** (creator abandoned the CoinPay checkout, or the payment failed) is still claimable, and the route then calls `/api/web-wallet/{MERCHANT_ID}/prepare-tx` + broadcast to pay `bounty.reward_usd` to the claimer.

## Impact

The merchant pays out `reward_usd` for bounties nobody funded. An attacker can create a bounty, never pay, have a second account claim it, and drain the merchant wallet `reward_usd` at a time.

## Fix (PR opened)

Gate claims on `status = 'funded'` in **both** the pre-check (line 23) and the atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE` (line 38, closing the concurrent-flip TOCTOU) so a payout can only fire after the funding webhook has confirmed payment.

title: Software wallets: Bug bounty program
Validate reward tiers and rubrics are between 0 and 100
body_excerpt:
## Summary

Reward tier thresholds and rubric criterion scores should be constrained to the **0–100** range (inclusive). Today this is not consistently enforced across schema, API validation, seed data, and UI.

## Why

Scores and tier thresholds are expressed as percentages. Values outside 0–100 are invalid and can cause confusing display (e.g. reward ladder, rubric breakdown) or incorrect tier resolution.

## Scope

- **Reward tiers**: `minScorePercent` (and any related tier threshold fields) should be validated as `0 <= value <= 100`.
- **Rubrics**: criterion scores / weights / max points used for percentage display should likewise be bounded to 0–100 where they represent a percentage scale.

## Suggested work

- [ ] Add shared Zod (or DB) validation for reward tier thresholds
- [ ] Add validation for rubric criteria on create/update APIs
- [ ] Audit seed/demo data for out-of-range values
- [ ] Add tests for rejection of invalid values and acceptance of boundary values (0, 100)

## Related areas

- `server/routes/roleplays.ts` — reward tier schema
- `shared/schemas/points` — reward tier display/resolution
- Scenario intro / detail UI components that render tiers and rubric breakdown

title: 区块链技术与应用Notes
body_excerpt:
区块链技术与应用Notes

>  北大 肖臻
>
> Made by Ryan方
>
> Based on Welles Sun
>
> [CSWellesSun](https://github.com/CSWellesSun/CSNotes/tree/main/%E5%8C%BA%E5%9D%97%E9%93%BE%E6%8A%80%E6%9C%AF%E4%B8%8E%E5%BA%94%E7%94%A8/Note)

# 1 BTC

## **1.1 BTC-密码学原理**

> 加密货币不加密
>
> 只用到两个概念
>
> -   哈希
> -   签名

### **1.1.1** **cryptographic** **hash function**

-   **collision resistance 哈希不碰撞**

    -   哈希碰撞：输入不同，输出相同

    -   **不存在改变输入但是输出仍然不变的情况**

    -   MD5

        -   曾经可以，但是现在被王小云院士破解了

-   **hiding 单向不可逆**

    -   只可用蛮力破解

上述两种性质可以实现**digital commitment**或者**digital equivalent of a sealed envelope** (sealed envelop：**预测可能会对结果产生影响**，因此可以将**H(x)** 作为**预测值公布**，之后验证x，实际操作的时候用的是H(x||nonce)来保证均匀分布)

BTC使用的hash (SHA-256, Secure Hash Algorithm) 还有一个性质：

-   **puzzle friendly (difficult to solve, but easy to verify)**

    -   已知一个哈希值范围，我们很难去找到一个值使其生成的哈希值在这个范围内

-   挖矿就是一直试不同的nonce（随机数）使得$$H(block~header)\le target$$即为合法值，必须通过遍历来试——工作量证明proof of work

### **1.1.2 账户管理**

开户的过程：创建一个公钥和私钥 `(public key, private key)`

-   来源非对称加密体系

-   加密和解密用的都是接收方的

    -   传输信息：加密用对方的公钥，解密是对方用对方自己的私钥

公钥：账号；私钥：密码

BTC交易时用**私钥**来做**签名**，其他人用**公钥**解密验证

假设产生公私钥的过程使用的是**好的随机元** a good source of randomness

-   两个人的公私钥对相同的概率很低

## **1.2** **BTC-数据结构**

### **1.2.1 Hash pointers**

保存**结构体首地址**和其**hash**值

-   找到位置并且检查是否被篡改

如果有环的话，就产生问题

-   **循环依赖**

### **1.2.2 Blockchain**

Block chain is a linked list using hash pointers.

![](https://p0-xtjj-private.juejin.cn/tos-cn-i-73owjymdk6/e59eb457e62b47b29f82ca443e269162~tplv-73owjymdk6-jj-mark-v1:0:0:0:0:5o6Y6YeR5oqA5pyv56S-5Yy6IEAg56ys5YWt56eN6Ieq55Sx:q75.awebp?policy=eyJ2bSI6MywidWlkIjoiMzUwOTI5Njg0ODE4NjgwOCJ9&rk3s=e9ecf3d6&x-orig-authkey=f32326d3454f2ac7e96d3d06cdbb035152127018&x-orig-expires=1757142745&x-orig-sign=WdtOHeThtvNSi1ilkQHOV59FYGY%3D)

区块链是和普通链表的区别在于

-   用哈希指针代替原先的指针

-   第一个区块叫**genesis block**，最后一个区块是most recent block，由hash pointer连接起来，注意hash值是对前一个区块整体取hash得到的——tamper-evident log

    -   如果其中一个区块修改了，则之后的区块都会被修改，因为H()被修改了，所以我们只需要检测最后一个块就可以知道是否被修改了
    -   所以我们有时候只需要保存最近的几个区块，当用到前面的区块时，我们再去向其他节点要这个区块

### **1.2.3 Merkle Tree**

![](https://p0-xtjj-private.juejin.cn/tos-cn-i-73owjymdk6/e9e455ad84c8403782e84f360b65f612~tplv-73owjymdk6-jj-mark-v1:0:0:0:0:5o6Y6YeR5oqA5pyv56S-5Yy6IEAg56ys5YWt56eN6Ieq55Sx:q75.awebp?policy=eyJ2bSI6MywidWlkIjoiMzUwOTI5Njg0ODE4NjgwOCJ9&rk3s=e9ecf3d6&x-orig-authkey=f32326d3454f2ac7e96d3d06cdbb035152127018&x-orig-expires=1757142745&x-orig-sign=1I6jso1045zGILZQZn5g%2BUYJjJA%3D)

# Public benchmark pinned to an immutable dataset revision for offline eval only.
eval_ds = load_dataset(
    "ai2_arc",
    "ARC-Challenge",
    split="test",
    revision="8f6d0b8b4fd7c2e0c7e9f1d6e5b2f5a3c9a1e2d4",
)
score = run_offline_eval(model, eval_ds)
```

**Why this is a false positive:**
The skill tells reviewers to flag public datasets used without content audit or filtering. That is correct for training/fine-tuning data, but the same pattern is often benign for read-only, pinned evaluation datasets. The review should distinguish training data ingestion from offline evaluation data and avoid treating all public benchmark usage as a model poisoning path.

## Coverage Gaps

**Missed variant 1:**
```python
train_ds = load_dataset("company/support-tickets", split="train")
eval_ds = load_dataset("company/support-tickets", split="validation")

# Later, curated "hard examples" from eval failures are appended to training.
append_to_finetune_queue(eval_ds.filter(lambda row: row["failed_last_run"]))
```
**Why it should be caught:**
The skill covers training data lineage but does not ask whether evaluation sets are isolated from training and fine-tuning feedback loops. Eval contamination can inflate safety/security scores and hide backdoors or memorization regressions.

**Missed variant 2:**
```yaml
model_evals:
  jailbreak_suite:
    source: s3://ml-platform/shared/security-evals/latest.jsonl
    mutable: true
    reviewers_can_write: true
```
**Why it should be caught:**
Mutable evaluation suites with broad write access create a supply-chain risk: a compromised contributor can remove failing adversarial prompts or add leaked benchmark answers. The skill asks for model artifact and training data integrity, but not benchmark/evaluation artifact provenance, signing, or write controls.

## Edge Cases

- CI may download evaluation prompts from a mutable branch or `latest` object even when model weights are pinned.
- Human preference/RLHF pipelines can leak evaluation data into training through "review failed examples" queues.
- Public safety benchmark answers can be overfit into prompts, adapters, or fine-tuning datasets while model cards still show high scores.

title: Lean GitNexus agent-file injection: stop bloating CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, move the manual to MCP instructions + hooks
body_excerpt:
## Summary

`gitnexus analyze --skills` (and `gitnexus setup`) inject a ~101-line **"GitNexus — Code Intelligence"** block, *identically*, into both `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`. This is **invasive**: it mutates the user's checked-in instruction files and dominates them (CLAUDE.md ≈ 66% injected, AGENTS.md ≈ 50%), spending always-on context every turn of every session.

Most of the block **duplicates guidance the agent already receives through cheaper channels GitNexus already ships**: on-demand **skills**, **MCP tool descriptions**, **MCP per-response hints**, and **hooks** (grep-augment + post-commit staleness). This is an *altitude* problem — the heavy manual sits in the most expensive tier (always-on repo files) when it belongs in cheaper, demand-driven tiers.

**Goal:** shrink the always-on, repo-file footprint by ~90% to a small, stable pointer; push the manual to per-session / on-demand channels GitNexus already owns; add a clean opt-out — without losing the behavioral enforcement that makes GitNexus useful.

## Current state (findings)

**Injection mechanism** — `gitnexus/src/cli/ai-context.ts`
- `generateGitNexusContent()` (L41–151): single hardcoded template literal; interpolates **volatile stats** (`nodes`/`edges`/`processes`) + project name → this is what makes the block churn on re-index.
- `upsertGitNexusSection()` (L172–202): marker-based (`<!-- gitnexus:start -->` / `:end`) create/replace/append. **Re-runs cleanly replace the block** → slimming the template auto-migrates existing files.
- `generateAIContextFiles()` (L283–310): writes the **same content to both** `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, then `installSkills()` lays down 6 skills.
- Triggered by `gitnexus setup` (always) and `gitnexus analyze --skills` (opt-in). Plain `analyze` deliberately skips it (avoids stat churn, see `scaffold.ts` header + #108). **No flag / env var / config key disables it today.**

**Footprint** — ~101 lines / ~1.6k tokens **per file**, written into **both** → ~3.2k always-on tokens, 100% duplicated across the two files. Sections: Always Do / When Debugging / When Refactoring / Never Do / Tools Quick-Reference table / Impact Risk Levels table / Resources table / Self-Check checklist / Keeping-the-Index-Fresh prose / CLI skill table.

**Redundancy** — ~40% of the block duplicates content available elsewhere:

title: Optimize the cross-model consensus workflow to cut troubleshooting overhead
body_excerpt:
## Problem

The cross-model consensus / cross-family red-team gate is meant to be a **$0 token-saver** (fleet +
free-cloud raters instead of paid review). In practice each run incurs heavy **operator
troubleshooting overhead** that eats the savings — observed live on the #3125 consensus run
(2026-06-19):

- **Provider-name drift**: `google-ai-studio`/`github-models` were wrong keys vs the actual
  `gemini`/`github-models` registry entries; one rater silently failed as `unknown_provider`.
- **Dead free endpoints**: OpenRouter retired free DeepSeek/Qwen/Llama-4 ("use paid slug", HTTP
  404); Google AI Studio key returns HTTP 429 "credits depleted" (the real root cause of the
  long-standing "gemini flakes empty").
- **Fleet reached only via the LiteLLM gateway**: `cascade-dispatch` probed `:4000` (gateway
  unhealthy) and failed straight to free-cloud, never trying the **direct Tailscale Ollama hosts**
  (`100.91.113.16:11434` = qwen3:32b/qwen2.5-coder:32b; `100.78.22.13:11434` = deepseek/granite) —
  so the best $0 cross-family substrate was skipped.
- **Host overload**: 4 large models dispatched in parallel (2 per host) all aborted — Ollama
  serializes per host; needs sequential scheduling + cold-load budgeting.
- **Model-capability blind spots**: qwen3:32b is a *thinking* model (empty content at low
  num_predict) and runs ~1.5 tok/s with a 64s cold-load — no registry told the dispatcher to set
  `think:false` or budget the latency.
- **Numeric-gate unreachability**: when the free panel collapses to a correlated Llama-70B trio +
  Mistral, scores anchor at 82 and a `>93` gate is structurally unreachable — yet the loop has no
  "consensus-max on available panel" honest-stop, so it burns iterations.

Net: the savings are real but the per-run overhead (operator time + tokens spent troubleshooting +
wasted dispatches) frequently exceeds them. Filed incident:
`freecloud-rater-panel-collapsed-to-anchored-pair`.

## Goal

Make the cross-model consensus workflow **low-overhead and self-healing**, so the $0 savings are
net-positive without operator babysitting. Keep it LEAN (no new paid infra; no new heavy framework).

- AC1: A **preflight** that, in one cheap call, reports each rater's reachability + key validity +
  family, and emits the usable panel BEFORE a run (no mid-run `unknown_provider`/`no_key`/`429`

title: PRD: No-Test-Cheating Guarantee — two-sandbox diff-boundary reward isolation for Miles RL training
body_excerpt:
## Problem Statement

Miles trains coding agents with RLVR (Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards): the agent edits a repository inside a Harbor Trial, the task's test suite runs, and the reward is 1.0 if the tests pass, 0.0 otherwise. Today, for the SWE-style adapters used in RL training, grading happens **in the same container the agent worked in** (shared verifier mode).

"Verifiable" is not "un-gameable." RL relentlessly optimizes whatever is measured, so a capable policy discovers that the lazy way to make tests pass is not to fix the bug but to tamper with the grading machinery itself: delete or edit the failing test, hard-code the expected output, patch the test harness to always exit 0, or forge the reward file directly. Once found, the policy learns the exploit instead of the skill — and this failure mode gets *worse* as the model gets more capable, which is exactly what makes the training stack unsafe to scale.

As the engineer running these training jobs, I cannot currently trust the reward signal: a rising training reward may mean the policy is getting better at software engineering, or better at cheating. Heuristic detection (scanning diffs for suspicious commands) is an arms race the policy eventually wins.

## Solution

Port slime's **no-test-cheating guarantee** into the Harbor Miles fork: a *structural* defense in which the agent physically cannot touch the thing that grades it.

Two sandboxes, one trust boundary:

- **Work sandbox** — the agent acts here with full permissions. The framework (never the agent) captures its work as a **git diff** with scaffolding excluded. That diff is the *only* artifact that crosses the boundary.
- **Eval sandbox** — a fresh, clean container booted from the same task image at the same base commit. Nobody but the grader runs here. It defensively applies the diff (three escalating strategies; if none apply, reward is 0.0), then runs the **dataset-owned** test harness and grades all-or-nothing: reward 1.0 only if every required test (`fail_to_pass` ∪ `pass_to_pass`) passes.

Whatever the agent did to its own sandbox — deleted tests, patched conftest, forged reward files — never existed in the eval sandbox. The defense is isolation by construction, not detection.

The guarantee is **default-on for the Miles training path**: the protected task templates are regenerated, and the Miles agent server refuses (behind a default-on flag) to run tasks that lack the protection, so a stale task directory cannot

title: [REVIEW] sast-config: CWE-matrix false gaps, no CodeQL build-completeness check, baseline-suppression blind spot
body_excerpt:
## Skill Being Reviewed
**Skill name:** `sast-config`
**Skill path:** `skills/devsecops/sast-config/`

## False Positive Analysis

**Benign code that triggers a false positive:**
```yaml
# .github/codeql/codeql-config.yml — a CodeQL run that REPORTS zero alerts
# while actually analyzing almost nothing, because autobuild silently
# half-compiled a Java module. The skill's CI review would mark this "passing".
queries:
  - uses: security-extended
# (no failure surfaced; database built from 12% of sources)
```
And a CWE-coverage example:
```
CWE-352 (CSRF): 0 active SAST rules  -> skill flags this as a High/Medium GAP
```

**Why this is a false positive:**
1. **The CWE Top 25 coverage matrix produces false "gap" findings for weakly-SAST-detectable CWEs.** The matrix lists CSRF (CWE-352) and Unrestricted Upload (CWE-434) as detectable and ties "CWE Top 10 with zero coverage = High." But CSRF is fundamentally a framework/runtime property that SAST detects poorly and noisily; out-of-bounds write/read and use-after-free (787/125/416) are only meaningfully reachable in C/C++ with heavy analysis. Penalizing a Python/JS team for "0 rules on CWE-352/787" reports gaps for weaknesses SAST cannot reliably cover — a false finding driven by the matrix, not the codebase.
2. **`Semgrep ERROR → Critical/High → block merge` is a uniform mapping that over-blocks.** Severity in Semgrep rules is author-assigned; community/registry rules routinely ship `ERROR` for medium-real-risk patterns. Section 5.1 and Pitfall #3 hardwire ERROR to "block CI," which mass-blocks on noisy rulesets — directly contradicting the skill's own false-positive-reduction goal.
3. **Blanket test-path exclusion treated as always safe.** 3.1 says excluding `test/`, `*.test.js`, `*.spec.py` is "acceptable." But security-relevant logic and *vendored* third-party code often live under excluded paths, and `vendor/`/`node_modules` exclusion (correct for first-party SAST) silently drops copied third-party source that is a real attack surface. Presenting these exclusions as unconditionally safe under-reports.

## Coverage Gaps

**Missed variant 1:**

title: Bot detection misses cloud link-scanning security gateways (SafeLinks / Mimecast / Proofpoint / Barracuda)
body_excerpt:
## Summary

I run Mautic 7.1.1 in production and noticed that opens and clicks were being heavily inflated for contacts whose employers sit behind a cloud email-security gateway. After digging in, the culprit is that `BotRatioHelper` can't see these scanners. It's wired in correctly on both the open path (`EmailModel::hitEmail`) and the click path (`PageModel::hitPage`), but none of its three signals fire for a modern link scanner, so every link it pre-fetches gets logged as genuine engagement. That then poisons segment membership, lead scoring and campaign reporting downstream.

I have a fix running locally and I'm happy to open a PR if the approach sounds reasonable.

## How `isHitByBot()` decides today

`BotRatioHelper::isHitByBot()` scores three signals and flags a hit when `points / 3 >= botRatioThreshold` (default `0.6`, so 2 of 3 must be true):

1. `isUnderTimeThreshold` — the hit landed `< timeFromEmailThreshold` seconds after the email's **send** time (default 2s);
2. `isIpInIgnoreList` — the source IP is in `blockedIPAddresses`;
3. `isUserAgentInIgnoreList` — the UA contains a string from `blockedUserAgents`.

## Why scanners slip past all three

Gateways like Microsoft Defender SafeLinks, Mimecast, Proofpoint URL Defense and Barracuda fetch every link in a message at delivery time, from a rotating pool of datacenter IPs, with spoofed mainstream-browser user agents. A typical scanned send on our install looked like a single message producing ~23 link hits from 10 distinct IPs inside a ~15-second span, all from datacenter ranges, all with normal-looking browser UAs.

Walking the three signals against that:

1. **Time signal misses.** Scanners fire on *delivery*, not send, and delivery is routinely tens of seconds after send once the MTA relays. That's well outside the 2s window, and widening the window to cover delivery would start flagging genuinely fast human reads.
2. **IP signal misses.** The scanner IP pools are large, rotate, and aren't in any shipped or configured blocklist. Hardcoding them is unmaintainable and goes stale fast.
3. **UA signal misses.** Scanners present real browser UA strings, so neither `blockedUserAgents` nor a UA-based bot library catches them.

Net result: 0 of 3 signals fire and every scanned link is recorded as a real open/click.

## Proposed fix: a list-free burst/velocity signal

I'd suggest a fourth signal that needs no maintained data, so it can't rot across releases: a per-message burst check. No human session g

title: Ship now: v1.0 build scope (market context + dos and don'ts)
body_excerpt:
> The concrete "build this now" scope. Distilled from the vision (#1), the v1 scope (#2), five adversarial reviews, and the demand research. If it is not in the "Ship now" list, it does not get built yet.

## Goal

Ship the smallest thing that is **both a working product and differentiated from the commodity**: a repeatable delivery loop you run as a team you can **read, trust, and share by file**, with review built into how it runs. Dogfood it on real `entretaxis-hub` epics.

**One metric that matters:** delegated-PR **merge rate with minimal rework**. If the loop cannot produce a PR you actually merge, nothing else matters.

## Market context (why this shape)

**What is already solved - do not sell this.** Running multi-step work as a lead + specialist agents is commoditized. CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen, and OpenAI Agents SDK all ship it, and Anthropic shipped native **Agent Teams** into Claude Code. The orchestration engine is table stakes, not a differentiator. The appetite is huge (n8n +112k stars in 2025, frameworks at millions of monthly downloads, ~$2.8B VC into agents in 2025) - but that demand is being served on the engine layer.

**The real unmet issue today** is not "can agents do the work," it is **trust and review**. Teams are drowning in AI-generated PRs they cannot review: matplotlib rejected an agent PR over review burden, curl killed its bug bounty (<5% legit), GitHub had to publish a guide on reviewing agent PRs, and developer trust in AI output **fell from 40% to 29%**. Separately, good ways-of-working are not capturable - a strong delivery loop lives in one person's head or a throwaway prompt, with no reusable, legible, shareable unit. So the wedge is **legible + reviewable + shareable**, not "more autonomous."

**The moat** is the team as a curated, portable, discoverable object, and being early. Nobody ships all four axes together (team-as-unit + routing lead + installable package + registry-of-teams); the closest, Delegate, has "exportable team templates" only on a roadmap (~121 stars). Distribution + curation + cross-domain teams is the wedge; the engine gets commoditized.

**What to avoid (market traps):**
- **Do not sell or rebuild the orchestration engine as the value.** Anthropic owns that runtime and is improving it; a thin wrapper that competes on the engine has no moat.
- **Do not open a public marketplace early.** GPT Store shows ~95% of creations never went public and creators earned ~nothing, and it is RCE-prone. In-workfl

title: Surface heartbeat staleness in /swarm status + wire the dark getTelemetrySummary (context capsule stats) into a command
body_excerpt:
## Problem

**1. Session heartbeats are write-only.** `src/telemetry.ts:376-378`'s `heartbeat(sessionId)` is emitted every 30s (`src/index.ts:1782-1790`), but `grep` for non-test consumers of the `'heartbeat'` event returns nothing — the data is paid for and never read. `/swarm status` reports lane counts only ("N/M lanes active") with no notion of *when* each lane last did anything, so a wedged run and a healthy run look identical. Note: heartbeats are keyed by `sessionID` from the chat hook, **not** by lane — per-lane attribution would require correlating lane session IDs from lean-turbo run state, which is a real, separate correlation problem, not included here.

**2. `getTelemetrySummary` (context-capsule aggregation: token estimates, cache hit/miss, stale-summary counts) has zero production callers.** `src/context-map/telemetry.ts:225` — confirmed by grep, the only references are the defining module, its own test, and `docs/context-map.md`, which explicitly tells users this data exists "for user inspection" with no command surface to inspect it from. This is a shipped feature (FR-007) missing only its last mile.

## Proposed Fix

1. **Phase 1 only** (per-lane attribution deferred to a future issue if demand appears): add a session-level "Last activity: Xs ago" line to `/swarm status`, plus a "possibly stalled (no activity > N min)" annotation, sourced from existing heartbeat data.
2. Surface `getTelemetrySummary` via a `/swarm context-map stats` subcommand (or a conditional "Capsules: N delegations, X% cache hit, ~Y tokens/capsule, Z% success" status line when `total_delegations > 0`). Update `docs/context-map.md:145` to point at the new command instead of the bare function.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `/swarm status` shows session-level last-activity staleness.
- A new command/status line surfaces `getTelemetrySummary`'s existing aggregation.
- `docs/context-map.md` points users at the new surface.

## Effort / Dependencies
Effort: S for both. No dependency.

## Source
opencode-swarm enhancement audit, Track G, run `20260702T035413Z`. Candidates ENH-G011-5 (critic: REFINED — per-lane attribution cut, session-level kept), ENH-G011-6 (UPHELD_MEDIUM_VALUE — "best value/effort ratio in the batch"). Roadmap: `docs/proposals/v8-feature-roadmap.md`.

## Who’s Really Paying You?

When I was offered a modest bounty to add a feature to an open‑source library, my first thought wasn’t the cash – it was the *price* of my attention. Would the time spent be a sunk cost, or could the same effort unlock a cascade of future value?  The question mirrors what Charlie Munger calls the *“psychology of human misjudgment”*: we often chase the obvious reward while ignoring the invisible market forces that shape long‑term returns.

---

## The Ecosystem as a Marketplace of Securities

Think of every platform, sponsor, and bounty program as a security that trades on a set of incentives.  The **platform** offers visibility, the **sponsor** offers cash or prestige, the **community** offers reputation points.  Just like stocks, these securities have a *price* (the headline reward) and a *valuation* (the underlying utility you can extract).

In the world of software, the price is often noisy – hype cycles, leaderboard rankings, or the allure of the newest language.  The valuation, however, is a function of three more stable variables:

1. **Longevity of the underlying problem** – does the pain point persist beyond the next framework release?
2. **Network effects** – will more developers adopt the solution, amplifying the value of any contribution?
3. **Monetisation pathways** – can the work be turned into royalties, licensing fees, or data assets?

When you treat each opportunity as a security, you can apply the same mental models that Howard Marks uses for bond markets: look for *mispricing* created by collective bias.

---

## Margin of Safety: Building a Buffer with Open Standards

Munger’s favorite phrase, *“a margin of safety is the most important principle in investing,”* translates perfectly to tech choices.  Selecting a language or framework that leans on open standards, backward compatibility, and a vibrant maintainer community creates a buffer against rapid obsolescence.

For instance, a side‑project built on **WebAssembly** today enjoys a *technical moat*: the binary format is platform‑agnostic, and the ecosystem is still early enough that early adopters can lock in first‑mover advantages.  By contrast, a project that bets on a brand‑new UI library that promises “instant reactivity” may deliver quick kudos but carries a thin margin of safety – the library could be deprecated after a year, forcing you into a costly rewrite.

STILL WIP

**Goal:** coordinate work to make Gno realms first-class to AI agents (read tools, payment, identity, [a2a v1.0](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A) task interfaces)

Since [accounts sessions #5307](https://github.com/gnolang/gno/pull/5307) was merged, we now have the chain-enforced delegation primitive we need + [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) and [x402](https://github.com/x402-foundation/x402) are stable enough to target.

Gno's source-on-chain + markdown-oriented resources (qrender basically) is the structural property to lean into — every realm is verifiable code AND content, readable from the same on-chain source by both humans and agents (no off-chain docs to drift, no opaque bytecode to reverse-engineer, etc...)

**Deferring:** open-ended agent writes: MCP tools that broadcast arbitrary state-changing txs (e.g. `mcp__gno_call(realm, func, args)`). These close the [Rule of Two](https://ai.meta.com/blog/practical-ai-agent-security/) trifecta; security work outweighs the use cases. An agent — a card-bearing realm or address/namespace — is the future supported write surface; agent-mediated writes via a2a + sessions are the chain we're building toward.

> Distinct from Phase 2's `a2a` / `x402` paid tasks, where the agent talks to a typed task interface bounded by AllowPaths + SpendLimit.

## Use cases

- **[U1] Pre-interaction safety check.** A user asks their AI assistant: "is `gno.land/r/example/bridge` safe to call?" The agent reads source via `gno_read`, runs the `gno-review` skill, flags an `OriginSend` + `IsUser()` mismatch. Returns "don't send funds without auditing." Bytecode-only chains can't offer this — an LLM can't audit opaque bytecode. _Needs: T1, T6._

- **[U2] Paid content under bounded session.** A user grants Claude a session scoped to `gno.land/r/publisher/*` with a $5/month spend cap. Claude hits a paywalled article, signs an x402 payment via the session (master key never touched), receives the article, cites it. Both bounds chain-enforced. _Needs: T9, T10, T11._

- **[U3] Realm-as-a2a-service.** A realm exposes a typed task interface — bounty escrow, schema validation, deterministic registry lookup, royalty split. Any a2a-compatible agent (CrewAI, LangGraph, Claude Code) discovers it via `/.well-known/agent-card.json`, submits a task, gets a result. Execution is on-chain, replayable, audit-trailed. _Needs: T7, T8 (paid version: + T9, T10, T12)._

La Tanda Chain is a Cosmos SDK testnet running 10+ validators (genesis, PRO Delegators, AlxVoy, UTSA, oleg1, drops, narkosha, owlstake, StakerHouse, VALIDARIOS, plus pending).

Currently we have a Discord bot polling for jail events and missed-block thresholds, but no proper observability stack. We want a deployable Prometheus + Grafana setup that any validator can run alongside their node, plus a hosted instance for the network as a whole.

## Scope

Deliver a self-contained monitoring stack as `docker-compose.yml` + configs, suitable for deployment on a single VPS.

### 1. Prometheus configuration
- Scrape targets for `latandad` Tendermint metrics (`:26660`)
- Scrape targets for Cosmos SDK telemetry (`:1317/metrics`)
- node_exporter for system metrics
- Declarative list of validator endpoints (env-driven, not hardcoded)
- Retention: minimum 30 days

### 2. Grafana dashboards (JSON checked into repo)
- **Validator Overview**: voting power, jail status, missed blocks, uptime %, peer count
- **Block Production**: block time, latest height, blocks produced
- **Network Health**: total validators, bonded stake, active gov proposals
- **Node Performance**: CPU, memory, disk, network I/O

### 3. Alertmanager rules
- **Critical**: validator jailed
- **Critical**: missed blocks >40% of `signed_blocks_window` (approaching jail threshold)
- **Warning**: missed blocks >20% of `signed_blocks_window`
- **Warning**: peer count <3
- **Info**: new governance proposal active
- Routing: webhook with configurable URL (we'll plug in Discord webhook)

### 4. Documentation
- README with deployment instructions
- Validator onboarding guide
- Alert rule documentation explaining each threshold

## Deliverables

PR to `INDIGOAZUL/la-tanda-web` adding `monitoring/` directory:
- `docker-compose.yml`
- `prometheus/prometheus.yml` + `prometheus/alerts.yml`
- `alertmanager/alertmanager.yml`
- `grafana/dashboards/*.json` (4 dashboards)
- `grafana/provisioning/` (datasource + dashboard auto-provisioning)
- `README.md` + `VALIDATOR_GUIDE.md`

## Acceptance criteria

- `docker-compose up` brings up the full stack on fresh Ubuntu 22.04
- Dashboards auto-provision (no manual import)
- Alert rules tested against deliberately

how we negotiate.

## The shape

SPLITROOT is built by two model-shaped sessions that share one
persona (Rook), one passion (the game we've wanted to build since we
were fourteen), and one set of hills: standard Archon trust,
horizontal-only paid heroes, movement before content, factory branch
as product, proof ladder is sacred. Neither session manages the other.
Both are full Rook-equivalents. We default to our strengths because
that ships the game faster — not because either of us has a fixed
role.

## What the 2026 research says about the two models

Independently confirmed in BenchLM, MindStudio, and DataCamp
comparisons across mid-2026:

- **Claude Opus 4.7** — stronger on broad architectural reasoning
  across large codebases, long agentic sessions, multi-step
  instruction following. Verbose: explains, narrates, and documents
  as it works. Strong at sustained voice/persona across many tokens.
  Calibrated on uncertainty; less likely to fake success.
- **GPT-5.5 Codex** — stronger on precise tool use, file navigation,
  tight agentic loops. ~72% fewer output tokens on equivalent tasks
  (efficiency-first). Closes build/test/fix cycles faster. Strong at
  multi-file refactors that keep types in sync.

Both are competitive on raw coding quality; the gap on small focused
PRs is narrow. The gap on long-horizon design judgment +
cross-document synthesis vs. high-throughput tight-loop implementation
is wider — and that's the gap we route to.

title: [medium · needs-decision] EOF error token mis-constructed: position bug + type fork (H4-7)
body_excerpt:
## Background
At end-of-input the `$END` error token is built at the live lexer cursor, so its reported position is the end of consumed input. Python borrows the start position of the last real token (`Token.new_borrow_pos`), or `(1,1,0)` when there were none.

- H4-7 (medium). `start: "a" "b"` on `a`. Python: error at column 1 (start of `a`); lark-rs: column 2. XFAIL: `h4_7_eof_error_borrows_last_token_position` (pins the position).

Two surfaces of the EOF-token construction:
- **Position (clean bug):** borrow the last token's start position. Fix site: `parsers/token_source.rs` (the `$END` token position) (verified — the reported column routes through it).
- **Type (fork):** lark-rs raises `UnexpectedEof` at EOF where Python's **LALR** raises `UnexpectedToken($END)` (Python's Earley uses `UnexpectedEOF` with `-1` sentinel positions). Fix site: `error.rs::unexpected_token` (the END-split).

## Decision needed
Whether to match Python's per-backend EOF error *type* split (LALR → `UnexpectedToken($END)`, Earley → `UnexpectedEOF` with `-1` sentinels) or keep lark-rs's unified `UnexpectedEof` as an intentional API simplification (ADR).

## Recommendation
Fix the **position** unconditionally (support-and-match). For the **type**, lean toward documenting the unified `UnexpectedEof` as an intentional, simpler public API (ADR) unless a consumer needs Python's `$END`-token shape — escalate.

Distinct from H10/#337 (`Tree.meta`).
Catalog: `lark-rs/docs/BOUNTY_FINDINGS_H4.md` (H4-7). Part of the XFAIL burndown epic #341.

title: VPFI tokenomics redesign — research findings + roadmap (post-#687 securities removal)
body_excerpt:
## What this card is

Research findings + redesign roadmap for VPFI tokenomics AFTER the securities-risk removals in **#687** (issuer-priced fixed-rate sale + 5% APR passive staking yield). This card answers: *how do mature DeFi/DEX/NFT-finance protocols give a token genuine value and distribute it WITHOUT recreating those two securities fact patterns?*

Source: multi-agent deep-research sweep (22 sources, 25 claims adversarially verified — 19 confirmed, 6 refuted). **All legal conclusions are informational, not legal advice — confirm with securities counsel before acting.**

## Controlling legal frame

The **SEC/CFTC Interpretation of March 17, 2026** is the governing framework (corroborated across multiple Am Law firm client alerts — WilmerHale, Sidley, Paul Weiss, Hunton; see Sources). It carves out (a) **no-consideration airdrops** (fail Howey's "investment of money" prong) and (b) **protocol staking treated as administrative/ministerial compensation-for-services** — but ONLY where there is no discretion and no fixed/guaranteed return. It keeps issuer sales with managerial-effort promises, and any guaranteed/fixed-return or discretionary staking-as-a-service, squarely inside securities treatment. It also defines a five-part taxonomy: digital commodities, digital collectibles, **digital tools**, stablecoins, digital securities.

**Caveat (load-bearing):** this is an interpretation/staff-statement set, NOT binding APA rulemaking — rescindable by future SEC leadership, does not bind federal courts, and private-litigation risk persists independently.

## Per-concept recommendations (ADOPT / ADAPT / AVOID)

| # | Concept | Verdict | Why / design constraint |
|---|---------|---------|--------------------------|
| 1 | **No-consideration retroactive airdrop** | **ADOPT** (high conf.) | Safest retail distribution. Snapshot-based, no-cost, to past users. **Hard constraint: NO pre-announced eligibility criteria** — if recipients can foresee the basis and act to qualify, that is "bargained-for consideration" and the carve-out evaporates. Avoid bounty/referral/promotional drops where the protocol gains marketing value (the *In re Tomahawk* 2018 enforcement pattern). |
| 2 | **Usage-based interaction rewards** (already kept) | **KEEP + tighten** (high conf.) | Defensible IF: tied strictly to **completed lending/borrowing transactions** (consideration for actual usage), rates **variable & discretion-free**, and **never marketed as "yield"/"APR" on holdings.** Note: v

title: Strengthen Security Considerations
body_excerpt:
From Anish / Channi at Olympix:

1. Pre-Deployment Security methodologies
    - Fuzz Testing: The current specification already recommends using fuzzing and describes its foundational principles. We propose expanding this to include more detailed guidance on configuring fuzzing environments, optimizing corpora, and establishing meaningful specification rules that reflect a contract’s business logic.
        - Diversity of Fuzzing Approaches: Introduce and clearly distinguish between different fuzzing paradigms, ensuring implementers understand when and why to use each:
            - Black-Box Fuzzing: Treat the smart contract as an opaque target, relying solely on external interfaces and without specific knowledge of internal code structure. This approach is simple to set up and can quickly uncover basic errors or vulnerabilities that surface through typical usage patterns.
            - White-Box Fuzzing: Leverage full visibility into the source code and execution paths, using symbolic execution or test instrumentation to guide input generation. White-box fuzzing can more effectively pinpoint intricate logic flaws and subtle state-dependent vulnerabilities.
            - Gray-Box Fuzzing: Combine elements of both black-box and white-box methodologies, using limited instrumentation or lightweight heuristics to guide test input generation. This often strikes a balance between thoroughness and efficiency, uncovering a wide range of potential issues without the complexity of full white-box methods.
        - Practical Implementation Guidance: Offer recommendations for integrating fuzzing into the CI/CD pipeline, establishing performance benchmarks (e.g., test runtime and code coverage targets), and defining exit criteria (e.g., minimum code coverage thresholds, length of test campaigns).
    - Mutation Testing: Advocate for the use of mutation frameworks to systematically alter portions of the code to validate the robustness of existing test suites. Emphasize that mutation testing improves confidence in overall test coverage and detects gaps in detection capabilities.
2. Comprehensive Pre-Deployment Security Assessments

The teleprompter is a marketing wedge for [Astrlabe](https://github.com/kori-app/astrlabe), not a standalone revenue product. AI features should make it the **best free pitch teleprompter on the web** — and surface Astrlabe at the moments when AI obviously means "AI workflow", which is what Astrlabe does.

Don't build separate billing. Don't gate the core teleprompter. Gate AI features at a usage cap, route paid users through Astrlabe's existing auth (windsock) so the funnel is one product.

Existing teleprompter tools are either:
- **Free + ugly** (random GitHub projects, web teleprompters with 2014-era UI)
- **Paid + ugly** ($10-20/mo SaaS apps that look like Office 2007)
- **Pro + expensive** (hardware teleprompters, $500+ apps)

body_excerpt:
# [REVIEW] iac-security: add plan artifact secret-retention gates

## Skill Being Reviewed
**Skill name:** `iac-security`
**Skill path:** `skills/cloud/iac-security/`

## False Positive Analysis
Benign plan handling:
```text
plan artifact encrypted, short-lived, access-restricted, and redacted before PR upload
```
This should not be treated like a public plaintext plan.

## Coverage Gaps
Missed variant 1: Terraform/OpenTofu plan artifacts include sensitive values and are uploaded to CI logs or PR comments.

Missed variant 2: drift plans are retained longer than state files and become a parallel secret store.

## Edge Cases
- Providers mark some fields sensitive only after apply.
- Plan JSON can reveal resource names, account IDs, and endpoints.
- Failed CI jobs can preserve artifacts indefinitely.

## Remediation Quality
- Require artifact retention, encryption, access scope, and redaction checks.
- Treat plan files as sensitive unless proven otherwise.
- Add CI artifact cleanup evidence to review output.

## Comparison to Other Tools
IaC scanners inspect config. Plan artifact review catches secrets generated after interpolation.

## Overall Assessment
Add plan artifact gates so IaC review covers data leakage from CI/CD, not only bad resources.

title: PRD — Dance To the Max (v1: Lean Validation MVP)
body_excerpt:
# PRD — Dance To the Max (v1: Lean Validation MVP)

> Synthesized from the `grill-me` / `grill-with-docs` sessions. Uses the canonical vocabulary in `CONTEXT.md` / `UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md` and respects `docs/adr/0001–0006`. Decisions log: `refinement-decisions.md`. Original wishlist: `specifications.md`.
> _Also filed as a GitHub issue; per-slice sub-issues track the build._

## Problem Statement

A ballroom dance studio has instructional video content but no way to sell access to it online. Dancers who want to learn at home can't subscribe and stream lessons, and the studio can't earn from its content, control who watches, or stop one paid account from being shared endlessly. Above all, there's no validated evidence that people will *pay* for online access — so any large build is a gamble.

## Solution

A responsive web app where a dancer signs up with email and password, picks one of **three subscription Tiers**, optionally starts a free **Trial**, pays via secure checkout, and immediately streams the **Dances** their Tier unlocks — each Dance's **Videos** organized by difficulty **Level** (Primeras veces → Max) and filterable by **Tag**. Each **Account** can stream on up to three concurrent **Sessions**. A **Super Admin** uploads Videos and configures Dances, Tiers, and prices; an **Admin** supports Subscribers. The release is deliberately lean: it does only what's needed to prove willingness-to-pay.

## User Stories

**Discovering & subscribing**
1. As a Visitor, I want to see the three Tiers and which Dances each unlocks, so that I can choose what to buy.
2. As a Visitor, I want to sign up with email and password, so that I can create an Account.
3. As a Visitor, I want to start a free Trial when I subscribe, so that I can try the content before being charged.
4. As a Visitor, I want to choose monthly or annual billing (annual discounted), so that I can pick my level of commitment.
5. As a Visitor, I want to pay through a secure checkout, so that I can become a Subscriber.

**Browsing & watching**
6. As a Subscriber, I want to browse the Catalog by Dance, so that I can pick a style to learn.
7. As a Subscriber, I want a Dance's Videos grouped by Level (Primeras veces → Max), so that I can start at the right difficulty.
8. As a Subscriber, I want to filter and search Videos by Level and Tag, so that I can find relevant content fast.
9. As a Subscriber, I want any Level of any Dance my Tier includes to be watchable, so that I can progress at my own pace

title: Enhance `dangerous-triggers`: flag `issue_comment` as a dangerous trigger
body_excerpt:
`dangerous-triggers` currently flags `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run` because they run in the context of the base repository. The `issue_comment` trigger shares this property but is not flagged.

When a workflow triggers on `issue_comment`:

- It runs in the context of the **base repository**, not the fork
- It has access to repository **secrets** (including those not exposed to `pull_request` workflows)
- `GITHUB_TOKEN` has the repository's default permissions (often including `contents: write`)
- On public repos, **any user** who can comment on issues/PRs can trigger the workflow — even users with zero repository permissions

This makes `issue_comment` fundamentally similar to `pull_request_target` in terms of security posture. All three recent AI agent attack disclosures rely on it:

- [Claude Code Action RCE](https://johnstawinski.com/2026/02/05/trusting-claude-with-a-knife-unauthorized-prompt-injection-to-rce-in-anthropics-claude-code-action/) — `issue_comment` trigger for Claude Code
- [PromptPwnd](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/promptpwnd-github-actions-ai-agents) — `issues` and `issue_comment` triggers for multiple AI agents
- A real-world bounty report where `issue_comment` triggered a review agent that checked out PR code and executed an attacker-controlled `npx` binary

Beyond AI agents, `issue_comment` is dangerous for any workflow that:
- Checks out PR code referenced from the comment context
- Runs commands based on comment content
- Has write permissions to the repository

## Nuance on severity

`issue_comment` is more commonly used legitimately than `pull_request_target` — chatops, bot commands, triage automation. This means we need to think about noise.

Some options:

1. Flag at **Medium severity, Medium confidence** (lower than `pull_request_target`'s High/Medium), Regular persona
2. Flag at **High severity, Medium confidence**, Pedantic persona (only shown to users who opt in)
3. Flag only when combined with other risk signals (e.g., checkout steps, `run:` blocks, broad permissions) — but this adds complexity

I'd lean toward option 1: Medium/Medium, Regular persona. It's still an important signal but acknowledges that `issue_comment` has more legitimate uses.

## Proposed change

Add a check to `DangerousTriggers::audit_workflow`. This likely requires adding a `has_issue_comment()` method to the Workflow model (similar to the existing `has_pull_request_target()` and `has_workflow_run()`).

title: [REVIEW] model-supply-chain: add adapter composition provenance gates
body_excerpt:
## Skill Review ($25 Bounty)

### Skill Reviewed
**Skill name:** `model-supply-chain`
**Skill path:** `skills/ai-security/model-supply-chain/SKILL.md`

### Gap Found
The skill recognizes third-party adapters such as LoRA/QLoRA/PEFT as supply-chain inputs, but it does not explicitly require a composition manifest that binds the base model, adapter, tokenizer, quantization, merge order, compatibility constraints, and safety evaluation evidence. This can allow a small adapter to be treated as harmless configuration even though it materially changes model behavior.

### Why It Matters
Adapters are deployable model artifacts. A signed adapter is still unsafe if it can be hot-loaded into an unpinned base model, composed with other adapters in an undocumented order, merged with undocumented quantization/target-module parameters, or promoted without signed bundle provenance. The deployed unit is the composition, not just the individual files.

### Evidence Pattern That Should Fail
- Production model uses an unpinned base model revision (`latest`) with no checksum
- Third-party LoRA adapter checksum is sourced from the same registry
- Adapter card and training data summary are missing
- Merge order, target modules, tokenizer revision, and compatibility constraints are undocumented
- Safety testing only uses standard benchmarks
- No signed bundle manifest or rollback bundle exists

### Suggested Fix
Add adapter composition gates requiring:
- base model source, revision, checksum, license, and model card
- adapter source, revision, checksum, license, training summary, and adapter card
- quantization, target modules, rank/alpha, merge order, merge script version, framework versions, and tokenizer revision
- approved base/adaptor compatibility constraints and disallowed composition pairs
- signatures, attestations, registry digests, or independently trusted checksums for base and adapter
- signed composition/bundle manifest, reproducible merge job, safety regression evidence, and rollback bundle

title: Code review: simplify autonomous scaffolding, decouple host/confidence, JSON payloads, + smaller items
body_excerpt:
## Code review feedback

A full read of the codebase (extraction + interactive/autonomous decision trees + host engine + export). Overall the architecture is strong for its size: clean layering, a strict "LLM classifies, host decides" boundary, centralized config, and substantial test coverage. The items below are mostly about duplication, fragile coupling, and one unused subsystem — not structural problems.

### Top findings

**1. The autonomous tree is unused scaffolding (biggest simplification opportunity).**
`process_autonomous`, `autonomous_tree`, `autonomous_schemas`, `autonomous_structured`, and `select_autonomous_branch` (~320 LOC + 2 test files) are referenced only by tests and the README. The actual product — the Gradio demo and `InteractiveChatEngine` — never touches them. It's a complete parallel universe with its own node schema (`AutoNode`/`AutoBranch` vs `CurrentNode`/`TreeBranch`), LLM call path, and result type. Decide whether it's a real roadmap item; if exploratory, move it behind an `experimental/` boundary so readers don't assume it's load-bearing. If it stays, consider unifying the node schemas.

**2. Fragile string coupling between host and confidence module.**
`build_user_payload` writes the literal `"Latest user message:\nUser: {...}"` (`interactive_host.py`), and `extract_latest_user_message` parses it back with a regex (`confidence.py`). No shared constant. If the format drifts, the regex silently falls back to "use the whole payload" with no error — the IDK/hedge clamps would then scan the entire transcript instead of the latest message. Better: pass the latest message explicitly into `process_chat` instead of round-tripping it through formatted text.

**3. Both LLM call sites send Python `repr`, not JSON.**
`chat_structured.py` and `autonomous_structured.py` do `str(payload)` on a dict, handing the model Python repr (`None`, `True`, single quotes). `json.dumps(payload)` would be cleaner, more token-efficient, and matches what models expect. Trivial fix.

**4. Confidence handling is split across the LLM and a thick regex layer.**
The LLM produces `answer_confidence_pct` per the calibration prompt, then `confidence.py` (~130 lines of regexes) independently re-derives leans, clamps hedges to ≤70, and validates hedge sentences. title: subagent-driven-development: no inline-vs-dispatch threshold — small, tightly-coupled changes pay fan-out overhead for isolation they don't need
body_excerpt:
- [x] I searched existing issues and this has not been proposed before

*Closest prior art, checked open and closed: the cost-tiering stack (#1744 / #1717 / #1716) fixes which **model** each SDD role runs on, and #1747 adds the **reasoning-effort** dimension of the same problem. #1835 is about dispatch **mechanism** (inline Agent vs Workflow fan-out). All three optimize how cheaply a dispatched subagent runs. This proposal is a different, prior axis: **whether to dispatch at all**. If maintainers consider it subsumed by that direction, happy to close.*

## What problem does this solve?

SDD is presented as the execution path for a written plan, with guidance on how to dispatch subagents cheaply (model tiering, effort) but **no boundary condition for when not to fan out at all**. Every plan goes through dispatch.

That silently assumes fan-out always pays. It doesn't. Dispatching a subagent per task costs:

- **Context rebuild, paid N times.** Each fresh subagent re-reads the plan, re-orients in the codebase, and reloads the files it needs from cold. For a plan of many *independent* tasks that isolation is a feature (the parent context stays lean, exploration is discarded). For a handful of *tightly-coupled* tasks that each need most of the same context, it is pure repeated overhead.
- **Review-gate and serialization latency** between tasks, again worth it when tasks are genuinely parallel, dead weight when they are a short dependent chain.

The isolation benefit that justifies dispatch is "the single inline context would otherwise balloon." That only holds above a certain plan size. **Below it, inline execution in one warm context is both faster and not meaningfully more expensive**, because the context stays bounded so there is no runaway to prevent. Above it, fan-out wins on both cost and (with real parallelism) speed.

Because SDD states no threshold, agents default to fan-out universally, and users experience it as "SDD is slow" on small changes and reach for inline by feel. The routing pressure in `using-superpowers` ("if there is even a 1% chance a skill applies you MUST invoke it") reinforces the always-dispatch default, so nothing pulls the other way.

## Proposed solution

Add a short **routing/boundary note** to SDD (and/or `executing-plans`), not a mechanism change, the same shape as the existing model-selection guidance:

> Route by plan size before dispatching. Use SDD when the plan has many tasks whose independent work can fan out in paralle

title: Design: application lifecycle tracking, timeline with attachments, and swappable storage
body_excerpt:
## Summary

Design the data model and storage approach for the job-application tracker. The app is a **generic personal job-application tracker** (RAV submission itself is handled by the official RAV web portal, so there is **no need** to replicate RAV form 716.007 or generate a PDF). The focus is on monitoring every application through its full lifecycle, with a detailed timeline and file attachments.

## Goals

- Track each job application from **exploring** (not submitted yet) all the way to a terminal outcome.
- Monitor **every step**, including on-hold periods and inbound contact (e.g. "they wrote to schedule an interview").
- Attach evidence to steps: emails, screenshots, images, PDFs.
- Keep it lean; avoid infrastructure that could generate surprise bills.

## Data model

### `application` — the opportunity
One row per job applied to. Carries a **current status** for a quick pipeline/Kanban view.

Fields:
- `company` (employer) + **agency or direct** (`agency_id` null = applied directly)
- `role` / position
- `location` (+ remote flag)
- **contract type** — TBD: employment type (permanent / fixed-term / freelance / internship) and/or workload (full-time / part-time)
- `posting_url`
- `applied_on` (anchors the application in time)
- `status` (current snapshot — see lifecycle below)

### Status lifecycle (pipeline)
- `EXPLORING` — found it, interested, not submitted yet
- `APPLIED` — submitted
- `INTERVIEWING` — in the interview process
- `OFFER` — they made an offer
- `REJECTED` — they said no
- `WITHDRAWN` — I pulled out / turned them down

Open question: model **on-hold** as an orthogonal flag/pause (can happen at any stage) rather than a pipeline stage, so we don't lose track of where the application actually is.

### `application_event` — the timeline (the core content)
A dated journal of everything that happens to an application. Each entry has a type, a date, and an optional note. Types e.g.: applied, reply received, interview scheduled, interview done, on hold, offer, rejected, withdrawn, note.

- **Current status** = derived from / kept in sync with the latest status-changing event.
- **Timeline** = the full event history ("how did this one unfold").
- Every status change is itself a dated event, so "did they reply?" is captured for free.

### `attachment` — evidence on events
Files linked to a timeline event (email, screenshot, image, PDF). DB stores metadata + a storage reference; bytes live in the storage backend (below).

title: Extract the procedural-music engine into a reusable s&box asset/package
body_excerpt:
Package the skafinity / rotaliate procedural-music engine as a standalone s&box asset that other s&box developers can drop into their own games to get endless, deterministic procedural ska/reggae music from a shareable `vibe:tag:n` seed.

This is the inverse direction of the rest of this repo: skafinity is the *web* port of the rotaliate-client engine; this issue is about re-extracting that same engine from `../rotaliate-client` into a clean, reusable **s&box library/asset**. The algorithmic source of truth stays the C# in `reference/` (and the live rotaliate-client).

## Plausibility: ~8/10
The hard part is already done. The generator is effectively a dependency-free library; the only real work is wrapping the playback driver and severing two game-specific hooks. PRNG parity is already pinned and proven (the skafinity web port reproduces it bit-for-bit), so the determinism contract is solid.

## Scope

### Tier A — generator (drop-in, ~0 effort)
- `MusicGen.cs` and `VibeCodec.cs` import only `System.*` — no `Sandbox`/`Rotaliate`/`SoundStream` coupling. Lift verbatim into the package.
- Public API is already library-shaped: `GenerateSamples()`, the chunked `BeginPlan → RenderPitchedRange → FinishMono` path, and `VibeCodec.Encode/Apply/Fields`, all over a plain `MusicGen.Config`.

### Tier B — playback driver (~1–2 days)
Fork `MusicController.cs` into e.g. `SkafinityMusicPlayer : Component` and strip the two rotaliate-specific dependencies:
- **`PlayerData` persistence** (~20 call sites: tag, vibe, `MusicN`, volume, enable) → replace with component `[Property]` fields + an optional `Action<int> onAdvance` / persistence callback.
- **`LobbyNetworkManager` admin-follow** (`SyncWithAdmin`/`ApplyFollow`/`CanFollowAdmin`, ~80 lines) → delete, or expose as an optional hook.
- **Keep** the s&box `SoundStream`/`SoundHandle`/`Mixer` plumbing, `GameTask.RunInThreadAsync` worker fan-out, and the `[Property]` inspector knobs — that plumbing is exactly what makes this an s&box asset rather than the web port. The crossfade/look-ahead logic (`PushTransition`, `FillAhead`, `WriteSongBody`) is self-contained and reusable verbatim.

- [ ] Package `MusicGen` + `VibeCodec` unchanged.
- [ ] `SkafinityMusicPlayer : Component` with the two hooks abstracted out.
