title: tvm-lean4 — Lean 4 Formal Verification Framework for TVM and FunC
body_excerpt:
## Summary

A reservoir-style Lean 4 library that lets contract authors and auditors
formally verify safety properties of FunC source and TVM bytecode using
machine-checked proofs.  Pitched as a Mi-Cho-Coq sibling for TON:
public, lakefile-installable, dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0.

**Repo:** https://github.com/MavenRain/tvm-lean4
**Status:** Scaffold pushed, `lake build` green (23 modules), no proofs yet.

## Problem

TON's smart contract auditing landscape is empirically nascent.  Yanovich
et al. (arXiv 2509.10823, revised 2026-04-16) catalog 233 real-world
vulnerabilities across 34 audit reports and observe that TON-specific
concerns, asynchronous message handling chief among them, do not map
cleanly onto Ethereum auditing patterns.

CertiK formally verified TON's masterchain `elector` and `config`
contracts ahead of mainnet by manually translating FunC into Coq and
proving safety properties by hand.  The effort caught two concrete bugs
including a validator-fund-loss issue, but was never released as a
reusable tool.  No public, package-manager-installable formal
verification framework exists for TVM bytecode or FunC source.

The closest existing TON-side tool in this category is `TonAudit AI`
(#1213), which uses an LLM-prompted vulnerability scanner.  That tool is
complementary to but categorically different from a deductive formal
verification framework: LLM scanning gives a probabilistic finding with
no guarantee, while a machine-checked Lean 4 proof gives a permanent
mathematical certificate.

## Solution

`tvm-lean4` is a Lean 4 library structured as a reusable lakefile
dependency.  The framework provides:

1. A small-step semantics for the TVM instruction set, modeled as a
   relation on `(Stack, Cell, ControlState)` triples.
2. A FunC frontend that lowers source AST to TVM bytecode, with a
   Lean-checked correctness theorem stating the lowering preserves
   semantics for well-typed programs.
3. An asynchronous-message envelope model (`InternalMessage`,
   `BounceFlag`, `Address`) so that contract specifications can quantify
   over inter-shard delivery and bounce-on-failure.
4. A specification language inspired by Mi-Cho-Coq's Hoare-triple
   encoding, letting authors state pre/post conditions about a
   contract's storage and outgoing messages.

Downstream users add `require «tvm-lean4» from git ...` to their own
lakefile and write proofs about contracts they have written.

## What's already built

A scaffold of the five core modules, with t

title: [BOUNTY] N64 LLM Speedrun — 5 tok/s on Real Hardware (300 RTC)
body_excerpt:
## N64 LLM Speedrun — 300 RTC

Cross-posted from [Rustchain #1876](https://github.com/Scottcjn/Rustchain/issues/1876).

Hit **5+ tokens/sec** sustained inference on real Nintendo 64 hardware. Must use RSP SIMD for matmul. Video proof required.

### Requirements
- 5+ tok/s on the 819K-parameter transformer
- RSP SIMD matmul (not just the VR4300 main CPU)
- Video proof on real N64 (controller input visible, CRT/TV output)
- Benchmark numbers in PR description

### Bonus: +100 RTC
Run from a **physical N64 cartridge** (flash cart or EPROM). Show the cartridge in the video.

### Approaches
- RSP microcode for 8-wide SIMD matmul (see also [#4](https://github.com/Scottcjn/legend-of-elya-n64/issues/4))

title: Epic: Unified Distribution — ctxpkg as the single package layer (context | skills | addon | grammar)
body_excerpt:
## One sentence

Everything an agent can install — **knowledge, skills, MCP addons, grammars** — becomes one package model (`.ctxpkg` + a single new `kind` field), served by one registry (ctxpkg.com), verified by one trust chain (ed25519 + SHA-256 + audit + revocation), billed by one commerce rail — **consolidating four grown subsystems without inventing a single new format, service, or command universe.**

Full design: `docs/specs/unified-distribution-v1.md` (ships with the Phase 1 PR).

## Why now

We currently run **two parallel distribution universes** that overlap and drift:

| Concern | ctxpkg world | Addon world |
|---|---|---|
| Payload | knowledge (`.ctxpkg`) | capabilities (MCP servers), grammars (dylibs) |
| Registry | ctxpkg.com (hosted) | `addon_registry.json` + `grammar_registry.json` (bundled, hand-maintained) |
| Signing | `core/context_package/signing.rs` | `core/addons/signing.rs` (second ed25519 impl) |
| Billing | **live** (Stripe, 402, verified publisher) | prepared only (`core/addons/commerce.rs`) |
| Marketplace | ctxpkg.com | leanctx.com/addons |

…and one open gap that just became user-visible in PR #721: **an MCP addon's binary has no managed distribution path** — the gateway spawns `command` from `PATH` and hopes. The lean-md contributor's distribution question (crates.io vs. side-loading vs. registry) is the first external collision with this gap.

The consolidation is already half-built by our own code: `commerce.rs` describes itself as *"generalising the ctxpkg paid artifact to addons"* on the *"existing ctxpkg billing rails"*, and the `.ctxpkg` v2 spec already claims *"npm for AI context"* and reserves a blobs layout. This epic finishes that thought.

## Guiding principle

> An agent installs two things: what it should **know** and what it should be able to **do**. Both are packages. Every package is a `.ctxpkg`. One registry, one publisher identity, one trust chain, one marketplace, one billing rail.

**Consolidation discipline: every phase closes an existing construction site.** Non-goals: no new registry service, no new package format, no new signing scheme, no new CLI universe, no breaking change for existing packs/authors/registries, no commerce launch before catalog traction.

## The `kind` taxonomy

| `kind` | Payload | Runtime gate (all pre-existing) |
|---|---|---|
| `context` *(default)* | knowledge/graph/gotchas layers — unchanged, byte-compatible | redaction on load |
| `skills` | markdown/script documents as veri

## 📊 Bounty Rate Reduction Schedule — As RTC Value Appreciates

We're at ~761 wallet holders today. Per the published RTC milestone schedule:
- **1,000 holders** → reference rate $0.15
- **2,000 holders** → reference rate $0.20
- **Real market** → discovered price

When each RTC is worth more in USD-equivalent, per-bounty awards scale DOWN proportionally so the *value paid per finding* stays consistent. This is how a healthy economy works — rates aren't pegged to a nominal RTC number, they're pegged to the USD value of the work.

### Current rates (now, $0.10 ref)

|--------|-----|
| Generic merged PR | 5 |

### Important — Fairness rules

1. **Not retroactive**: work submitted under the current rate gets the current rate, even if the milestone hits before it's paid.
2. **Announced ahead**: each milestone gets a 24-48 hour heads-up before the new rate kicks in.
3. **One-way ratchet**: rates ONLY go down with token appreciation, never go back up if holder count drops.
4. **Market overrides**: once RTC has a discoverable DEX/CEX price, USD-anchor takes over entirely.

### Why now?

Daily distribution has been hitting 1-3k RTC/day during active sweeps. At $0.10 ref that's $100-$300/day. At $0.20 ref the same nominal distribution would be $200-$600/day — unsustainable without scaling rates down.

title: Publications facet payload: 500+500 buckets = 77% of response; materialized hrefs; ≤500-row Prisma hydration; cardinality precision 4000→1000
body_excerpt:
## Problem

The publications facet payload is 77% of the response: 500 journal + 500 author buckets = **136 KB of the 178 KB** publications JSON — while only 8 rows render until the user expands a facet. Each bucket also ships server-materialized state, and author buckets trigger a per-request Prisma hydration.

From `docs/search-facet-perf-audit-2026-07-02.md` (Tier 2, win 5). Complementary to edge compression (bytes on the wire) and to #1301 (agg **compute** cost — different axis; this issue is response **bytes**).

## Evidence

- 500+500 buckets = 136 KB / 178 KB measured on `type=publications&q=diabetes`.
- Every bucket ships a fully-materialized `toggleHref` URL; author buckets additionally ship a derivable `identityImageEndpoint`.
- Author buckets drive a ≤500-row Prisma `scholar.findMany` per request just to decorate the facet list.
- Header-count `cardinality` agg uses `precision_threshold: 4000`; the parked facet-split commit `927c35dd` already validated 1000 at ~1–2% error (see #1301).

## Proposed fix (independently shippable pieces)

1. Build toggle URLs client-side — the facet components are already client components; ship bare `{value, count}`.
2. Derive `identityImageEndpoint` client-side.
3. Cap facet `terms` size at ~100 with a small search-within-facet endpoint for the tail.
4. Drop `precision_threshold` 4000 → 1000 on the header-count cardinality agg.
5. Restrict (or lazy-load) the author-bucket Prisma hydration to the rows actually rendered.

## Rollout

No PR planned in the current batch; sequence after Tier-1 items per the audit's suggested order.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Publications response for the baseline query drops from ~178 KB to well under 50 KB pre-compression
- [ ] Facet expand/search-within still reaches the full tail (no loss of reachable buckets)
- [ ] Header counts within ~2% of previous values on a fixture query set
- [ ] Full vitest green; facet snapshot updates reviewed deliberately

title: [FEATURE] Frontend : virtualisation de la Timeline (>1000 événements)
body_excerpt:
## Contexte

Le composant `TimelineCalendar` calcule les positions de toutes les lanes et de tous les événements en une seule passe, sans virtualisation. Pour les power users qui accumulent plusieurs centaines à milliers d'événements, ce comportement entraîne des temps de rendu élevés, des freezes d'interface et une dégradation générale de l'expérience. La scalabilité de la vue Timeline est une condition de viabilité à long terme du produit (BR-EVT-001).

## À faire

- **Mesure baseline** : instrumenter le rendu actuel (React DevTools Profiler ou `performance.mark`) pour quantifier le problème avant toute optimisation
- **Virtualisation des lanes** : ne monter dans le DOM que les lanes visibles dans la fenêtre + un buffer haut/bas
- **Virtualisation des événements** : à l'intérieur de chaque lane visible, ne monter que les événements dans la plage temporelle visible (axe horizontal)
- **Budget de rendu** : définir un seuil cible (ex. < 16ms par frame pour 1000 événements) et valider par mesure après implémentation
- **Cohérence a11y** : les nœuds focusables (keyboard navigation, screen reader) doivent rester cohérents quand des nœuds sont montés/démontés par la virtualisation — coordonner avec l'issue a11y de la frise (Wave 6)

## BR impactées

- **BR-EVT-001** — scalabilité de la vue événements

## Critères d'acceptation

- [ ] Mesure baseline documentée (temps de rendu initial et scroll pour 500 et 1000 événements)
- [ ] Avec 1000 événements, le rendu initial tient sous le budget défini (< 16ms par frame ou seuil convenu)
- [ ] Le scroll vertical et horizontal ne provoque pas de freeze visible (60 fps cible)
- [ ] Les événements hors viewport ne sont pas dans le DOM
- [ ] La navigation clavier entre événements fonctionne sans sauter d'événement visible
- [ ] Les annonces screen reader (rôles, labels) ne régressent pas par rapport à l'état pré-virtualisation
- [ ] Les tests existants sur `TimelineCalendar` passent sans modification (ou sont mis à jour avec justification)

## Piste technique

- Composant principal : `TimelineCalendar` (issu de #47, localisé dans le package composants Timeline)
- Librairies candidates : `@tanstack/react-virtual` (windowing 2D, léger, sans opinion de layout) ou `react-window` (plus simple, 1D)
- Approche recommandée : virtualisation sur l'axe vertical (lanes) en premier, puis sur l'axe horizontal (événements par lane) si nécessaire
- Pour l'a11y : utiliser `aria-rowcount` / `aria-rowindex` pour informer les SR du nombre réel

Exclude 404/500 pages (default on)
body_excerpt:
`takeScreenshot()` calls `page.goto(..., { waitUntil: 'load' })` but never inspects the HTTP response status (`src/lib/screenshotter.ts`, lines 39–53). A page that returns 404 or 500 still gets screenshotted and diffed, producing meaningless diffs (e.g. a staging 404 page vs. a real production page).

## Task
- Capture the response status returned by `page.goto()`.
- Add an option (**default true**) to exclude error pages: when enabled, a 4xx/5xx response marks the page as an error (with its status code) instead of running a diff.
- Surface the status code in the result / card.

## Acceptance criteria
- With the option on, a page returning 4xx/5xx is flagged as an error showing its status code, not a diff.
- The option is exposed in the form and defaults to on.
- With the option off, current behavior is preserved.

# Issue #4: Security Considerations for the ORC Diamond L3 Framework

**Issue #4**  
**Opened by:** @BlackRoseOfTHC (founder, 9-5 dev in Pomona, CA)  
**Date:** April 2026

This is Issue #4 — a follow-up to:
- [Issue #1: Welcome to the ORC DARO](https://github.com/TheHiveCluster/Open-Research-Company-/issues/1)
- [Issue #2: Discovering Other DeSci Projects](https://github.com/TheHiveCluster/Open-Research-Company-/issues/2)
- [Issue #3: Whiteboard Proposal – EIP-2535 Diamond L3 Framework](https://github.com/TheHiveCluster/Open-Research-Company-/issues/3)

Security is critical for any project that aims to handle research data, agent swarms (including Elara), governance, and eventually physical hardware integration. Since we are planning to use EIP-2535 (Diamond) as the core architecture, we need to think carefully about risks from the beginning.

### Why Security Matters for ORC
- Agents (especially autonomous ones like Elara) will interact with real value (payments via x402, data, governance votes).
- The data layer will point to or handle large research datasets, space telemetry, and e-waste inventory.
- The treasury will eventually fund real-world infrastructure (workstations, lab space, e-waste recovery equipment).
- A breach could damage trust, lose funds, or compromise research integrity.

### Key Areas We Need to Consider

**1. Diamond (EIP-2535) Specific Risks**
- Facet upgrades could introduce bugs if not done carefully.
- Storage collisions between facets.
- Proper access control for upgrade permissions.

**2. Agent Layer Security**
- x402 autonomous payments — preventing malicious spending or replay attacks.
- ERC-8004 identity and reputation — protecting against impersonation or reputation manipulation.
- EIP-7702 temporary delegation — ensuring delegations are short-lived and revocable.
- Programmable MPC wallets — secure key management and policy enforcement for agents.
- Agent-to-agent communication — preventing unauthorized calls or data leaks.

**3. Data Layer Security**
- Protecting large research datasets and pointers (IPFS/Arweave links).
- Preventing tampering with on-chain indexes or Merkle roots.
- Access control for sensitive research (medical, chemical, space data).

**4. Governance & Treasury Security**
- Preventing malicious proposals or treasury drains.
- Multi-sig or time-locked mechanisms for large spends.
- Transparent voting with proper quorum and anti-whale measures.

title: count_grounded_roots can undercount when a case has >1000 evidence rows (hydration LIMIT 1000)
body_excerpt:
## Context
Surfaced by the /code-review of PR #622. Latent correctness edge in the grounding counter itself (not in the baseline script).

## Problem
`count_grounded_roots` (`faultmaven/core/investigation/cause_assurance.py:170`) builds `evidence_ids = {e.evidence_id for e in case.evidence}` and, via `_root_grounding` (line ~94), only counts a runbook-provenance SUPPORTS link toward a grounded root when `link.evidence_id in evidence_ids` (the non-dangling guard).

But case evidence is hydrated with a hard `LIMIT 1000` (`sqlite_case_repository.py:701` in `_load_evidence_for_case`; the bulk loader at :1132 has the same cap). So for a case with **>1000 evidence rows**, the datum backing a grounded root's runbook link can be truncated out of `case.evidence` → its link reads as *dangling* → the root is **not** counted as grounded → GROUNDED undercount / false negative.

## Severity
- Latent and unlikely at current scale (baseline cases carry far fewer than 1000 evidence rows), but it is a real silent undercount in the metric that gates auto-harvest (§7 GROUNDED) — and the same guard runs in `grade_cause_assurance`, so a long-running case could in principle lose its GROUNDED status.
- Affects the grounding grade, not just the baseline script — so it is higher-stakes than a reporting glitch.

## Options
1. Raise/remove the evidence `LIMIT 1000` on the hydration path used for grounding (cost: memory on huge cases).
2. Order evidence hydration so grounding-relevant rows (those referenced by causal-node evidence links) are always loaded — e.g. load the evidence ids referenced by `causal_node_evidence` regardless of the 1000-cap.
3. Have `_root_grounding` fall back to a targeted existence check for a link's `evidence_id` when it is not in the (capped) in-memory set, instead of assuming dangling.

Option 2 is the most surgical (only guarantees the evidence that grounding actually references is present). Coordinate with the counter/repo owner.

title: A Self-Learning Modern Computer Science Curriculum
body_excerpt:
A Self-Learning, Modern Computer Science Curriculum

http://bit.ly/2nVnGcQ

About 0 Minutes

Table of Contents

1 Introduction

"The great idea of constructive type theory is that there is no distinction between programs and proofs… Theorems are types (specifications), and proofs are programs" (Robert Harper)

This is a collection of modern resources on various undergrad level computer science topics, for someone with an interest in theory. Use LibGen if you can't buy these books. You don't have to do everything here, just the topics of interest to you. If for any reason you want a condensed version, watch the Great Theoretical Ideas in Computer Science lecture series to see what interests you in the field. Almost all the material in each resource is self contained so will cover necessary background which if you don't have see the preliminaries.

1.1 Studying Strategies

On Isaac Newton's iteration method to self-learn geometry:

"He bought Descartes' Geometry and read it by himself .. when he was got over 2 or 3 pages he could understand no farther, than he began again and got 3 or 4 pages father till he came to another difficult place, than he began again and advanced farther and continued so doing till he made himself master of the whole without having the least light or instruction from anybody" (King's Cam.,Keynes MS 130.10,fol. 2/v/)

An anecdote on the studying method that works for me:

title: HTTP 500 /api/v1/canvases
body_excerpt:
[View in Sentry](https://superplane.sentry.io/issues/7312974808/)

## Summary

- PR #3373 changed SerializeCanvas to call FindLiveCanvasVersionByCanvasInTransaction, which returns gorm.ErrRecordNotFound when canvas.LiveVersionID is nil, but ListCanvases used a plain query without an INNER JOIN on live_version_id, causing serialization failures for canvases without a valid live version; a latent nil-dereference on *canvas.CreatedAt / *canvas.UpdatedAt in the replacement serializeCanvasSummaries (introduced in #5338) perpetuates 500s in the current code.
- Issue first seen 2026-03-05T17:29Z, 15 minutes after commit 2aa05bffc was authored.
- 2aa05bffc changed SerializeCanvas to call FindLiveCanvasVersionByCanvasInTransaction for every canvas.
- FindLiveCanvasVersionByCanvasInTransaction returns gorm.ErrRecordNotFound when canvas.LiveVersionID == nil (canvas_version.go:663).
- ListCanvases at that commit used a plain SELECT without INNER JOIN, returning canvases with NULL live_version_id.
- Migration 20260304110000 set live_version_id NOT NULL but ran concurrently with code deployment.
- fe1e38345 (#5338, Jun 11) introduced serializeCanvasSummaries with unconditional *canvas.CreatedAt dereference at list_canvases.go:73-74.
- Canvas.CreatedAt is *time.Time; no nil guard exists before timestamppb.New(*canvas.CreatedAt).
- DB schema shows created_at NOT NULL, but GORM can leave pointer nil on scan failures or missing alias mappings.
- Request header X-Organization-Id present; authentication path not at fault.
- Issue remains unresolved with last event 2026-06-29, after all versioning-related fixes were merged.

## Root Cause

- **File:** [`pkg/grpc/actions/canvases/list_canvases.go → serializeCanvasSummaries()`](https://github.com/superplanehq/superplane/blob/2aa05bffc6d464ec76b9d5789362aaa7bbb8da19/pkg/grpc/actions/canvases/list_canvases.go#L73)
- **Pull Request:** [feat: add simple versioning + sandbox mode #3373](https://github.com/superplanehq/superplane/pull/3373)

## Suggested Fix

Add nil guards for CreatedAt and UpdatedAt before dereferencing them in serializeCanvasSummaries to prevent panics, and ensure ListCanvases always uses queryCanvasWithLiveVersion (INNER JOIN) so only canvases with a valid live version are serialized.

```diff
pkg/grpc/actions/canvases/list_canvases.go:70-77
-		protoCanvases[i] = &pb.CanvasSummary{
-			Id:          canvas.ID.String(),
-			Name:        canvas.Name,
-			Description: canvas.Description,
-			CreatedAt:   timestamppb.N

title: Scale corpus to 1,000 books
body_excerpt:
Current corpus is ~35 hand-picked books (#10 seed list). Step one of the scaling ladder — get to ~1,000 English novels.

## Cost & footprint

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Ingestion total (~965 new books × ~\$0.005 each) | ~**\$5** one-time |
| OpenAI embedding (text-embedding-3-small @ \$0.020/M tokens) | ~\$2 |
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 LLM colour (~600 tokens each) | ~\$3 |
| Storage delta (books + features) | ~**15 MB** (Neon Free tier handles it: 0.5 GB) |
| Runtime | ~5 h at concurrency 2; ~1 h at concurrency 8 |
| OpenAI rate-limit tier | Tier 1 (1 M TPM) is enough; auto-unlock to Tier 2 (5 M TPM) happens after \$50 cumulative spend |

No Neon plan change. No OpenAI tier change. Single afternoon of pipeline time.

## Two pieces of work

### 1. Sourcing the IDs

Hand-curating 1,000 books is overkill. Two viable sources:

- **PG top-downloads** — \`https://www.gutenberg.org/browse/scores/top1000.php\` returns a stable list of the most-downloaded ebooks (~1,000 entries). Filter to English (\`language='en'\` in the RDF), drop short ones (< 10k words), drop poetry collections if we want novels only.
- **Catalog RDF dump** — \`https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/feeds/rdf-files.tar.bz2\` is the entire catalog. Use it once to filter and pick 1,000 quality entries by some heuristic (downloads × length × known-author).

For 1k, top-downloads is the simpler path. The list is already curated by user demand.

### 2. Skip-already-ingested in \`scripts/seed-corpus.ts\`

Critical for all future scaling tickets too — without this, every re-run of \`pnpm seed:corpus\` after we've grown the seed list would re-process every previously-ingested book and double-bill.

Today \`seed-corpus.ts\` blind-sends every event:

\`\`\`ts
const events = SEED_BOOKS.map((b) => ({ name: "corpus/book.ingest", data: { gutenbergId: b.gutenbergId } }));
await inngest.send(events);
\`\`\`

Change it to query \`books\` for existing \`gutenberg_id\`s first, filter \`SEED_BOOKS\` to the delta, and only send the new ones. The Inngest pipeline still upserts on conflict, but skipping at the script level saves the entire embedding + LLM cost for books already done.

## Acceptance

- [ ] New \`lib/ingestion/gutenberg-top.ts\` (or similar) that fetches and parses PG's top-downloads list into typed \`SeedBook[]\`.
- [ ] Curated 1,000 IDs added to \`lib/ingestion/seed-list.ts\` (or replaced with a dynamic fetch).
- [ ] \`scripts/seed-corpus.ts\` filters out \`gutenbergId\`s already in \`books\` before e

body_excerpt: ### Summary Self-hosted instances seem to have a 1000 result cap on guild message searches (probably DMs too but untested). Large search on self-hosted instance (`in:channel-name` + `after:1970` filter which should include every message in guild): Screenshot of bottom of search on self-hosted instance showing 40 pages included just in case cap is a search page cap, not result cap. title: Bug: `TimestampMicro` and `TimestampNano` use wrong divisors — off by 1,000× and sub-second precision is silently dropped
Multi-tenant load testing at 1,000+ namespaces
body_excerpt:
## Problem

All benchmarks so far use 1-2 namespaces. A real multi-tenant deployment may have thousands of namespaces with varying sizes and query patterns. We have no data on how the system behaves under namespace-scale pressure: cache eviction patterns, S3 connection contention, foyer NVMe tier thrashing, memory growth from the DashMap caches.

## Proposed solution

Build a load-testing harness (k6, Locust, or a custom Rust binary) that:
1. Creates N namespaces (1,000+) with varying sizes (some dim=384, some dim=1536).
2. Drives concurrent query traffic across all namespaces.
3. Measures: query latency distribution, cache hit rate per namespace, S3 request count, memory usage, NVMe tier occupancy.
4. Identifies the breaking point: at what namespace count or QPS does the system degrade?

## Context

- The foyer cache is global — many small namespaces may not get adequate cache residency.
- The `DashMap<NamespaceId, usize>` dimension cache and generation counters grow linearly with namespace count.
- Connection pooling (#1) should land before this test to avoid confounding results.

## Considerations
- Add a cold-vs-warm taxonomy to the harness: cold first query against a fresh namespace, repeated identical warm query, and a different warm query against the same namespace. The three numbers behave very differently and conflating them obscures cache effectiveness.
- Track S3 *bytes* per namespace, not only S3 request count. Bytes are the cost driver and the throughput indicator; request counts can stay flat while bytes change dramatically as result-set sizes shift.
- Include the index type and index config as benchmark dimensions. Single-namespace numbers under IVF_PQ are not the same shape as the same workload under HNSW or against an unindexed flat-scan path.
- Cache observability: cache directory size, process RSS, and per-namespace cache residency need to be in the output. Otherwise we can't tell whether cache eviction is fair across namespaces.
- Include recall@k for indexed search versus flat scan. A latency win that costs recall is not a benchmark win.
- Produce machine-readable output (JSON or a markdown table that survives diffing) so future PRs can be compared like-for-like against a baseline.

title: Price parsing misinterprets de_DE thousands separator as decimal for prices above €1,000
body_excerpt:
## Bug description

When scraping prices above `1,000 EUR` from a German store/page, PriceBuddy appears to confuse the German thousands separator with the decimal separator, even when the store locale and currency are configured correctly.

For example, a product price shown as about `1.226 €` / `1.226,00 €` is stored or displayed as about `1,23 €` instead of `1.226,00 €` / `1226.00 EUR`.

## Example URL

https://www.amazon.de/dp/B0D2K9M4W7/

## Store settings

- Locale: `de_DE`
- Currency: `EUR`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Add or configure a store for a German product page.
2. Set the store locale to `de_DE`.
3. Set the store currency to `EUR`.
4. Add/scrape a product where the price is above `1,000 EUR`, e.g. the Amazon.de product above.
5. Check the parsed/stored price.

## Expected behavior

German-formatted prices should be parsed according to `de_DE` conventions:

- `1.226 €` should become `1226.00 EUR`
- `1.226,00 €` should become `1226.00 EUR`
- `1.226,99 €` should become `1226.99 EUR`

The dot (`.`) should be treated as a thousands/grouping separator and the comma (`,`) as the decimal separator for `de_DE`.

## Actual behavior

A price around `1.226 €` is parsed as approximately `1.23 €`, suggesting that the `.` is interpreted as the decimal separator and the value is then rounded to two decimals.

## Impact

This makes price tracking unreliable for German/EUR stores whenever the price is above `999.99 EUR`. It also makes alerts and price history misleading, because a four-digit product price can be recorded as a near-zero/low single-digit value.

## Notes

This looks like a locale-aware number parsing issue rather than a scraping selector issue. The store is already configured with `de_DE` and `EUR`, but the parser still seems to apply `en_US`-style decimal handling to a German-formatted price string.

A possible fix would be to parse numeric price strings using the configured store locale, or to normalize separators based on the locale before converting the value to a float/decimal.

title: HTTP 500 /account/limits
body_excerpt:
[View in Sentry](https://superplane.sentry.io/issues/7504868852/)

## Summary

- checkAccountOrganizationCreationLimits propagates any non-NotFound gRPC error from the external usage service directly as HTTP 500 instead of handling transient failures gracefully.
- GET /account/limits captured as HTTP 500 via CaptureMessage in LoggingMiddleware; no stack trace attached.
- checkAccountOrganizationCreationLimits only special-cases codes.NotFound; all other gRPC errors (Unavailable, DeadlineExceeded, etc.) are returned as-is.
- Returned gRPC error propagates through describeOrganizationCreationStatus → getOrganizationCreationStatus → http.Error(500).
- usageService.CheckAccountLimits has a hard 5-second context timeout; any transient network blip causes codes.DeadlineExceeded.
- PR #4987 (2026-05-25) added structured logging specifically for this Sentry issue but left the error-propagation behavior unchanged.
- Test added in PR #4987 explicitly asserts HTTP 500 when usage service returns codes.Unavailable, confirming the propagation path.
- Issue has 3 total events over ~5 weeks, consistent with intermittent external-service unavailability rather than a systematic code path error.
- c3969fc7 introduced checkAccountOrganizationCreationLimits without retry logic or graceful degradation for transient gRPC failures.

## Root Cause

- **File:** [`pkg/public/server.go → checkAccountOrganizationCreationLimits()`](https://github.com/superplanehq/superplane/blob/c3969fc748b55f3ca3b317937730d50637cc2986/pkg/public/server.go#L868)
- **Pull Request:** [feat: integrate with usage + limits #3545](https://github.com/superplanehq/superplane/pull/3545)

## Suggested Fix

Treat transient gRPC errors (codes.Unavailable, codes.DeadlineExceeded) from CheckAccountLimits as non-blocking: log a warning and return the default Allowed:true response so a usage-service blip does not block users.

```diff
pkg/public/server.go:863-870
- 	response, err := s.usageService.CheckAccountLimits(ctx, accountID, state)
- 	if err == nil {
- 		return response, nil
- 	}
- 
- 	if status.Code(err) != codes.NotFound {
- 		return nil, err
- 	}
+ 	response, err := s.usageService.CheckAccountLimits(ctx, accountID, state)
+ 	if err == nil {
+ 		return response, nil
+ 	}
+ 
+ 	switch status.Code(err) {
+ 	case codes.Unavailable, codes.DeadlineExceeded:
+ 		log.WithError(err).WithField("account_id", accountID).Warn("usage service transient error; allowing by default")
+ 		return &usagepb.CheckAccountLimitsResp

This bounty is for enabling and validating the `microsoft/phi-1` language model on Tenstorrent’s Wormhole hardware. Phi-1 is a transformer-based LLM designed with efficiency and compactness for code and text tasks, making it attractive for research, developers, and edge deployments. By running Phi-1 on Tenstorrent hardware, we aim to demonstrate practical inference, benchmark performance, and establish a production-grade implementation for community use.

title: ⚠️ CT-004: C139 consent ledger single-node throughput ceiling at 1,000 rps — GDPR erase non-compliant at 2k+ rps
body_excerpt:
## Canon Tension CT-004 — SIM-005 Finding

**Discovered:** 2026-06-30 via SIM-005 (Consent Ledger Throughput)
**Severity:** Medium — architectural gap; not blocking G-14 but must be resolved before population-scale deployment
**Canon refs:** C139 (consent ledger), C158 (GDPR compliance)

---

## The Problem

The C139 consent ledger performs well at ≤1,000 rps but breaches targets at 2,000 rps:

| RPS | Write P95 | GDPR Erase P95 | Error Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 56.9ms ✅ | 323ms ✅ | 0.10% ✅ |
| 2,000 | **116.9ms** ⚠️ | **730ms** ⚠️ | 0.23% ✅ |
| 5,000 | 466ms | 3,872ms | **5.6%** ⚠️ |
| 10,000 | 1,332ms | **13,652ms** | 17.3% |

**GDPR erase at 10,000 rps takes 13.6 seconds** — a regulatory compliance risk at population scale.

**Root cause:** C139 specifies no sharding, replication, or async erasure provisions. Single-node implicit assumption must be made explicit and resolved.

---

## Resolution: Option D (Recommended)

- Erasure status endpoint so users can verify completion
- Requires C139 architecture section update + C158 GDPR erasure SLA definition

title: Best practice: uploadPlan() is ~1,000 lines and should be decomposed into private step methods
body_excerpt:
## Function

`UploadService.uploadPlan()` (`app/lib/services/upload_service.dart`) is the publish-flow orchestrator. It takes the current `Session` and its list of `ExerciseCapture` objects, then executes the full publish sequence: pre-flight media check → credit consumption → media uploads → exercise upserts → raw-archive uploads → audit row write. It returns a `PublishResult` describing success or the specific failure mode.

## Finding

The method is approximately **1,000 lines long** and handles at least 8 distinct logical steps, two separate upload branches (fast-path for already-uploaded exercises and slow-path for new ones), multiple exception types, and nested counters:

```
uploadPlan()
├── pre-flight: check all exercise files exist
├── consume_credit RPC
├── [fast-path] skip-if-unchanged check (all rawArchiveUploadedAt set)
│   ├── count filesTotal for fast path
│   └── upload thumb variants for each exercise
├── [slow-path] full upload
│   ├── count filesTotal for slow path (duplicated logic)
│   ├── upload line-drawing media for each exercise
│   └── upload thumb variants for each exercise (duplicated call)
├── replace_plan_exercises RPC
├── [best-effort] raw-archive uploads
├── plan_issuances audit row
└── compensating refund ledger row on any post-consume failure
```

The `filesTotal` counting logic and the `_uploadThumbVariantToMedia(...)` call (with ~9 named arguments) are duplicated between the fast-path and slow-path branches. The single method makes it difficult to:
- Read: the control flow requires tracking many variables across hundreds of lines.
- Test: there is no way to unit-test individual publish steps in isolation.
- Debug: stack traces from a failed publish point into a single 1,000-line method.
- Extend: adding a new step (e.g. Safe Mode upload swap) requires reading the whole method to find the right insertion point.

## Suggested remedy

Decompose into private step methods, each with a clear name and a typed input/output contract:

```dart
// proposed decomposition
Future<void> _runPreflightCheck(List<ExerciseCapture> exercises);
Future<ConsumedCredit> _consumeCredit(Session session, int credits);
Future<MediaUploadResult> _uploadExerciseMedia(
    Session session, List<ExerciseCapture> exercises, ...);
Future<void> _upsertExercises(String planId, List<ExerciseCapture> exercises);
Future<void> _uploadRawArchivesBestEffort(List<ExerciseCapture> exercises);
Future<void> _writeAuditRow(String planId, ConsumedCredit credit);
```

title: feat: Numeric separator support (1_000 syntax) in number literals
body_excerpt:
## Description

Numeric separators in number literals (e.g., `1_000_000`, `0xFF_FF`) are not supported. The parser throws `ReferenceError` instead of the expected `SyntaxError` for invalid numeric separators.

## Failing test

- `staging/sm/Number/numericSeparator.js`

## Expected behavior

    eval("let a = 100_00_;")  // should throw SyntaxError (trailing separator)
    eval("let b = 10__;")     // should throw SyntaxError (consecutive separators)
    eval("let b = 1._2;")     // should throw SyntaxError (separator after dot)

## Notes

This is a parser issue, not a Number runtime issue. The lexer in `src/ljs/parser.lua` needs to accept `_` as a digit separator in numeric literals and validate that separators are between digits (not leading, trailing, or consecutive).

title: Gameplay: add bounded LLM reward toolkit tool
body_excerpt:
## Background

- Parent: #43

Gameplay now has peer-owned points, badges, game results, reward grants, and pet workspaces. `GameRuleset` can define deterministic drive rewards, but Flowcraft pet workflows do not yet have a controlled toolkit surface for granting gameplay rewards from LLM-driven activities such as daily check-ins, guided tasks, or conversation milestones.

This issue adds a server-side gameplay reward tool that can be exposed to Flowcraft workflows. It is not a peer RPC for arbitrary reward grants, and it is not token/accounting. It is a constrained gameplay toolkit path that records normal `RewardGrant`, `PointsTransaction`, badge exp, and pet state changes through the same gameplay runtime rules.

## Goal

Add a controlled gameplay reward tool for Flowcraft pet workflows.

The end state is:

- admins can enable and bound the reward tool in `GameRuleset`;
- Flowcraft pet workflows can call one gameplay toolkit tool to grant configured gameplay rewards;
- all grants use the existing gameplay SQL resources as source of truth;
- grants are auditable through existing reward grant, points transaction, badge, and pet APIs;
- direct peer clients still cannot grant arbitrary rewards through RPC.

This issue owns the toolkit reward-grant path only. It does not own scheduled tasks, long-running quest tracking, token/accounting balances, or a public peer reward-grant RPC.

body_excerpt:
@jamesyoung I've love to get your opinion on some of this. I'd like to emphasise that I'm not trying to be prescriptive, more just trying to trigger discussion of what we're building in the short/long term - I think there's ideas here that are relevant to both the Beachhead strategy and also the longer term Agent strategy. I wasn't sure if this was the best place to post for discussion, I'm happy to move it 😄 

# Quest Strategy — What Communities Actually Want

> Distilled from the March 13 meeting and subsequent brainstorming. The team's central unsolved question: **what is the killer campaign workflow?**

## Central Thesis

Communities say they want "engagement." I suspect that's just vanity metrics — retweets, likes, claim counts. Platforms like Galxe trained them to think in those terms, and now that's the language they use when describing what they need.

What they actually need is **quality growth**. A better, richer experience for community members. Quality contributions. Not more members — better members, and better outcomes from the members they already have.

The existing quest ecosystem is broken. A study of 80 million quest completions ([Quest Love](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.18810v2), Jan 2025) found near-zero retention when rewards stop (-0.18%), bots claiming rewards within 2 minutes of launch, and up to 70% of airdrops going to sybil attackers. Even $0.10 token rewards triggered 12x spikes in completions — but removing them returned activity to baseline. These platforms create the *illusion* of engagement while extracting value.

The hypothesis: if you design quests that are structurally impossible to farm — through encryption, collective conditions, and progressive trust — you get contributors instead of farmers. And one real contributor is worth a hundred airdrop farmers.

There's a deeper problem too. Research on motivation ([Deci et al., 1999](https://home.ubalt.edu/tmitch/642/articles%20syllabus/Deci%20Koestner%20Ryan%20meta%20IM%20psy%20bull%2099.pdf) — meta-analysis of 128 studies) shows that paying people for things they already do voluntarily *reduces* intrinsic motivation. Volunteers who received small payments worked fewer hours than unpaid ones. This means the entire "complete quest, get token" model may be actively counterproductive — turning intrinsically motivated community members into transactional ones.

This needs validating with actual community managers. We can't go to them with abstract claims. We need concrete exampl

## Objective

Collect, preserve, and compare AGI architecture proposals generated by multiple AI systems. The goal is not to paste generic AI answers, but to produce an auditable research packet that makes different architecture ideas comparable and useful for Cognitive-OS planning.

## Reward

$3,000 USD for an accepted submission.

Payment details will be handled privately after acceptance. The maintainer may accept one winning submission, request revisions before acceptance, or reject submissions that do not meet the criteria below.

## Required Scope

Use at least 8 distinct AI systems or model families where possible. Examples may include ChatGPT/OpenAI models, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama-based systems, Mistral-based systems, Perplexity, or other publicly accessible AI tools.

For each system, collect an AGI architecture proposal using a comparable prompt. The prompt may be adapted per model only when necessary, but the changes must be documented.

## Deliverables

Submit a pull request that adds a research packet under:

`research/ai_generated_agi_architectures/`

Required files:

- `README.md`: overview of the packet, collection method, and headline findings.
- `prompts.md`: the exact prompts or prompt summaries used for each model.
- `raw_outputs/`: one file per AI system containing the raw or minimally cleaned architecture proposal.
- `comparison.csv`: a structured comparison across architecture dimensions.
- `summary.md`: synthesis of common patterns, disagreements, and notable ideas.
- `synthesis.md`: a proposed combined architecture that extracts the strongest ideas from the collected outputs.
- `sources.md`: model names, provider/tool names, access dates, links where available, and any human edits performed.

## Comparison Dimensions

The comparison should cover at least:

- memory architecture
- reasoning/planning loop
- learning or self-improvement mechanism
- tool use and action execution
- world model or representation layer
- safety/governance layer
- evaluation and benchmark strategy
- persistence/runtime architecture
- multi-agent or orchestration design
- engineering feasibility
- originality or non-obvious insight

## Acceptance Criteria

- At least 8 model/system outputs are included.
- Outputs are clearly attributed with collection date and source model/tool.
- Raw outputs are preserved separately from analysis.
- The comparison table is structured and consistent across all entries.
- The synthesis is concrete enough

title: [photo-curation] Cheaper scoring: photo-judge subagent + Haiku + deterministic pre-filter
body_excerpt:
The photo scoring currently dispatches the **generic** workflow agent (full default system prompt, the entire tool registry in context, the session model = Fable/Opus). Measured cost: a 10-photo batch ran **~403k tokens (~40k/photo)** — almost all overhead, not judging. At ~900 photos that is ~36M tokens. Three changes cut it materially without losing judging quality (validated at calibration).

## 1 — Specialized `photo-judge` subagent (lean prompt + Read-only tools)
Add a project subagent (likely `.claude/agents/photo-judge.md` — verify this repo's agent-definition location) whose system prompt is just the judge role, with **`tools: Read` only** (no Bash/Edit/Grep schemas, no skills/superpowers bootstrapping), returning the rubric StructuredOutput. The per-call prompt still carries `defaultRubricConfig.judgePrompt` + the image path, so **the rubric stays single-sourced in `packages/photo-quality/src/rubric.config.ts` — do NOT duplicate the rubric text into the agent definition** (avoids drift). Change the committed `tools/photo-curation/workflows/score-current.mjs` + `source-candidates.mjs` Workflow scripts to dispatch `agent(prompt, { agentType: 'photo-judge', schema, model })` instead of the bare `agent(prompt, { schema })`.

## 2 — Cheaper model tier (Haiku default, calibration-locked)
Default the `photo-judge` model to **Haiku** (use the `haiku` model alias, NOT a hardcoded id — per the claude-api rule). Bulk *structured* vision-rating (7 scores + flags) fits a small model. Keep the model **overridable** (env or workflow arg) so **#969 calibration locks the tier**: score the labeled sample with Haiku, keep it iff ≥90% agreement with operator labels, else step up to Sonnet. Document the linkage in the runbook + cross-link #969.

## 3 — Deterministic pre-filter in `score-prepare` (free rejects, no agent)
`score-prepare` already has the downloaded bytes — run `assessDeterministic(img, config.deterministic)` there. If `passedGate === false`, compose a reject report and persist it immediately (the same path `score-commit` writes), and **EXCLUDE it from the manifest the judge agents read** — so a tiny/blurry/wrong-aspect image never reaches a (paid) judge. Log how many were gate-rejected vs. sent to the judge.

title: GOMAXPROCS(1) for HTTP Gateway with 1,000 QPS target
body_excerpt:
__PROBLEM:__
Pinned HTTP Gateway to Core 0 using `GOMAXPROCS(1)`, which means the Go Scheduler only has __1 OS Thread__ to run goroutines. Each request need to: parse JSON, make gRPC call over UDS (I/O wait), receive response and return HTTP.
Go's netpoller can handle I/O concurrency despite GOMAXPROCS=1, but __JSON serialization and gRPC protobuf marshaling are CPU-bound__. With 1,000 QPS and single core, each request only has __1ms budget__ for all CPU work. This is a very tight SLA.

Also with Fire-and-Forget: goroutine `SetCache()` spawned after each Cache Miss will compete on the same core with the request serving user.

__STATEMENT:__ `GOMAXPROCS(1)` reduces context switching overhead between Go process and C++ process, but increases CPU saturation risk. Please verify this solution using benchmarks.

__SUGGESTIONS:__ If `GOMAXPROCS(1)` doesn't work out very well, try using __2-2__ instead of __1-3__.

title: 1000+ algorithm explanation
body_excerpt:
Figuring out a user-friendly explanation of the algorithm that does not show too much detail, and still portrays the whole idea of the strategy, and adds it to the UI for the user to read.
Suggested description:
The system uses a greedy algorithm, which means it builds matches one step at a time, always choosing the best available option at each step. Participants are organized into tiers, and matching is done starting from higher-priority tiers. For each person, the system selects the most suitable available match and then moves on to the next. This approach enables fast, efficient matching, even with many users. It is important to notice that, since decisions are made locally at each step, the final result may not always be the optimal overall solution.

title: audit-epic(reliability): Redis-degradering — timeout→500, tyst 503, ingen catch-all 500-mappning (Medium + Low)
body_excerpt:
**Extern revision 2026-07-02 · Epic · område: tillförlitlighet & observability.** Alla CONFIRMED (exception-hierarki verifierad mot pinnad StackExchange.Redis 3.0.11 + minimal ASP.NET Core 10-repro).

### Medium
- [ ] **Redis-timeout/server-exceptions kringgår 503-vägen → oväntade 500:or.** Alla guards i `RedisSessionStore` är `catch (RedisConnectionException)`. `RedisTimeoutException` (ärver `System.TimeoutException`, Redis långsam/överlastad) och `RedisServerException` (LOADING vid RDB-omstart) — de två vanligaste degraderade tillstånden — fångas inte och escapar som ohanterade 500:or. `JsonSerializer.Deserialize<SessionPayload>` kastar `JsonException` på korrupt payload → 500 istället för invalid-session→null. → `Infrastructure/Auth/Sessions/RedisSessionStore.cs:37`/`:58`/`:106`/`:44`, `Api/Program.cs:197`
- [ ] **En Redis-outage ger mass-503 med noll loggsignal.** `Program.cs:197` sätter 503 utan `ILogger`-anrop; `RedisSessionStore` har ingen `ILogger`; auth kör utanför Mediator-pipelinen (`LoggingBehavior` nås aldrig); `appsettings.json` sätter `Microsoft.AspNetCore: Warning`. Den enda medvetet "hanterade" infrastruktur-vägen blir den minst observerbara — och den planerade TD-77-5xx-alarmen har ingen signal. → `Api/Program.cs:197`, `Infrastructure/Auth/SessionAuthenticationHandler.cs:65`

### Low
- [ ] Ingen catch-all exception→JSON-mappning: Postgres-down (eller vilken oväntad exception som helst) returnerar en kontraktslös tom 500, asymmetriskt med Redis-503-vägen.
- [ ] `LoggingBehavior` loggar förväntade 4xx-klass-exceptions (validation, not-found, forbidden) på Error-nivå → förorenar error-signalen.

### Rekommendation
Vidga guardsen till `catch (Exception ex) when (ex is RedisConnectionException or RedisTimeoutException or RedisServerException)`; behandla odeserialiserbar payload som `return null`. Logga `SessionStoreUnavailableException` på Error (dedikerat event-id, grov throttle) före 503-skrivningen — ortogonalt mot TD-77. Lägg en catch-all→ProblemDetails-mappning för oväntade exceptions; sänk förväntade 4xx-exceptions till Information/Warning i `LoggingBehavior`.

### Expected Behavior

get_html returns the full HTML content of the page (or at minimum, a well-formed HTML fragment), allowing downstream tools and hooks to process it.

### Actual Behavior

get_html silently truncates the output at 1,000 characters. The result is an incomplete, malformed HTML fragment. Any downstream processing (e.g., HTML-to-markdown conversion via AfterToolCallEvent) fails because it receives broken HTML

### Additional Context

There is no way to disable or configure this truncation, it is hard-coded. This effectively makes get_html unusable for any pipeline that needs to process the full page content.

Reference PR with a proposed fix: [Merge Request](https://github.com/strands-agents/tools/pull/400)

### Possible Solution

Remove the hard-coded 1,000-character limit. Return full HTML by default and add an optional max_length parameter so callers can opt-in to truncation at a custom limit.

Part of #19.

## Problem
`pingfed` (387 lines), `pingone` (360), and `pingntlm` (308) are ~95% copy-paste variants of one Ping flow: the same `docIs*` form detectors, the same `handleLogin`/`handleOTP`/`handleSwipe` handlers, the same recursive `follow()` state machine, and the same `context.WithValue(ctxKey("login"), ...)` plumbing (`pingfed.go:63-65`, `pingone.go:61-62`, `pingntlm.go:98-99`) — with subtle drift:

- Handler signatures differ (`*url.URL` vs `*http.Response` vs nothing).
- pingfed has `handleCheckWebAuthn`/`handleFormSelectDevice`/`handleRefresh`; pingone lacks some.
- pingntlm uses a raw `*http.Client` instead of `provider.HTTPClient` — which is exactly where the hardcoded skip-verify bug (#21) crept in.

Bug fixes land in one variant and silently miss the other two.

## Proposed work
- [ ] Pin behavior with tests on all three providers first (#13) — pingntlm has a 431-line test file; extend the other two.
- [ ] Extract `pkg/provider/pingcommon/`: unified detectors, a parameterized `follow()` accepting a handler registry, shared context plumbing, built on `provider.HTTPClient`.
- [ ] Reduce each variant to a thin shim declaring its handler set / NTLM transport.
- [ ] Sequence **after** #21 (TLS fixes) so the security fix isn't tangled in a refactor diff.

## Acceptance criteria
- ~1,000 duplicated lines collapse to ~200 shared + ~50/variant; behavior identical per tests.

## Notes
This materially diverges from upstream layout — do it as a clean NES commit series (#14) and consider proposing upstream, since they carry the same triplication.

title: docs(security): SECURITY.md + data-flow table in SPEC.md + README link
body_excerpt:
## Problem

Any team adoption (even small teams) hits a security/compliance question early: "what does bode send where?". Today the answer is in scattered places (README §Troubleshooting on telemetry, AGENTS.md on git removal, SPEC.md on tracker adapters), and the implicit defence — `<untrusted>` markers from v0.18.0 — is barely documented.

Plus, this doubles as marketing. Wave 7.3 commits to **no active telemetry**. We can't claim "AI work that stays local" without a single page that proves it.

## Proposal

### `SECURITY.md` at repo root

Standard layout, ~200 lines max:

1. **Threat model summary** — 5 sentences. Who's the attacker, what's the asset, what's out of scope.
2. **What bode reads** — repo files (only what's in `context_paths[]`), tracker tickets (read-only fetch), config (`~/.bode/`), credentials (Jira tokens etc. stored in YAML, see hardening note).
3. **What bode writes** — `~/.bode/runs/<KEY>/`, branch and commits via AI CLI (not bode), tracker comments + status transitions.
4. **What bode sends, and where** — vendor AI CLI (whatever the CLI itself sends; out of bode's control), tracker REST API (only the data fetched/posted as part of the configured workflow), webhook URLs if configured (§7.8).
5. **What bode never sends** — analytics endpoint (no default; see Wave 7.3), telemetry server (no default), auto-update check (explicitly out per ROADMAP), error reporting (no default; `bode doctor --report` is local-only).
6. **Defences** — untrusted content markers (v0.18.0), prompt-injection guard, exit-code gate (v0.20.0), atomic meta writes (v0.19.0), lockfiles, AGENTS.md context isolation.
7. **Supported isolation modes** — `--dangerously-approve-all` (and which CLIs accept it), running in a sandbox (Docker recipe), per-project credentials separation.
8. **How to report a vuln** — security@kakunyn.com (or GitHub Security Advisories), expected response time.

### Data-flow table in `SPEC.md`

Single page added as `SPEC.md` §Data Flow. Rows are concrete data items, columns are source → processor → destination → retention.

| Data item | Source | Processed by | Destination(s) | Local retention | Sent off-machine? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Task description | tracker ticket | bode → skill prompt | configured AI CLI → vendor | `~/.bode/runs/<KEY>/<phase>.md` (the AI's plan that quotes it) | Yes — to AI CLI vendor |
| Code in `context_paths[]` | local repo | bode → skill prompt | AI CLI → vendor | Logs at `~/.bode/runs/<KEY>/<phase>.log` | Ye

title: Epic: optimistic off-chain batch updates with on-chain challenge
body_excerpt:
## Epic — optimistic off-chain batch updates with on-chain challenge

> **⏸️ STATUS: PAUSED (2026-06-23)** — pending a strategic decision on the data-availability / cost trade-off (see *Security model & the data-availability decision* below). The mechanism design is settled; what's open is *how much* on-chain data availability to pay for, which is a product-level call to make before implementation begins. To resume: pick a DA strategy per the decision criterion in that section, then start with C1/C2 (both are safe and useful under any choice).

Parent issue coordinating the implementation of optimistic batching for the cage protocol. **Additive**: the synchronous `Modify` path is unchanged and stays available; everything here is opt-in.

### The invariant (must not weaken)

> The Merkle tree is always completely known, and the full database content is completely known to — and independently reconstructable by — any user, so that any user can **challenge** (prove on-chain) that a token's root was updated without following the rules.

Today this holds because every modification is an on-chain, validator-checked transition. The naïve batch (commit a `newRoot`, drop the fold) breaks it. This epic restores the invariant via **ledger-forced data availability + single-step fraud proofs**, in two phases.

### Part 1 — execution rollup (cheap for the oracle)

`CommitBatch` publishes the full operation log on-chain as **inline datums** (so the `trace_root` commitment's every preimage is provably in a block — DA becomes a ledger guarantee, not a server-liveness assumption) and posts a **candidate** root, *without* re-running the MPF fold. It still checks, on-chain, everything ephemeral: per-step ↔ consumed-request bijection, `actionsTail == []`, `tip`, phase, refund conservation, `candidate_root == manifest.final_root`, `old_root == predecessor.candidate_root`, `open_depth < max_depth`. Only the pure MPF transition is optimistic.

Challenge surface is **exactly two** single-step pure-MPF proofs: `BadStepResult` (precondition holds, result wrong) and `BadPrecondition` (uses a new non-aborting `missing` predicate; `has` is already value-bearing). `EndpointFraud` → commit check; `LinkFraud` → eliminated by deriving `pre_root`. Soundness: a first-divergence induction ⇒ a single-step proof at the first wrong step, no on-chain re-execution.

Batches **pipeline**; a challenge reverts the contiguous suffix lazily via a monotone-down `invalid_from` watermark; per-batch bonds;

title: Add pagination support beyond the PostgREST 1,000 row limit
body_excerpt:
## What to build

Add first-class pagination support so Supabase-backed TanStack DB collection reads can fetch more than the PostgREST per-request row limit. Users should not silently receive incomplete collection data when a query matches more than 1,000 rows.

The implementation should fetch data in pages using PostgREST ranges, continuing until the requested limit is satisfied or the final page returns fewer rows than requested. This behavior should work with filters, ordering, explicit limits, offsets, and any cursor/query metadata TanStack DB provides.

The completed issue should include tests and documentation. Loading thousands of rows into a browser can be expensive, so the README/API docs should explain when automatic paging applies, how page size is configured, and when developers should prefer narrower filters or explicit limits.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Collection reads can fetch more than 1,000 matching rows.
- [ ] Paging works with filters, ordering, explicit limits, and offsets.
- [ ] Errors from any page fail the full load cleanly.
- [ ] Tests cover multi-page fetch behavior and final short-page behavior.
- [ ] Documentation explains page size, large-result behavior, and performance tradeoffs.

## Blocked by

None - can start immediately.

title: 飲食店向け営業資料作成｜広告費1,000円訴求
body_excerpt:
## チケット：飲食店向け営業資料作成｜広告費1,000円訴求

### 背景

「なに食べよ」を飲食店に営業するにあたり、アプリの思想やユーザー課題を説明するよりも、**店舗側にとっての広告メリットが直感的に伝わる資料**が必要。

特に、初期営業では「1,000円から試せる」「どれくらい表示が増えるか」「Googleマップ表示につながるか」をわかりやすく見せることで、導入ハードルを下げたい。

### 目的

飲食店に対して、以下を短時間で理解してもらう。

* 1,000円の広告出稿で何が増えるのか
* 料理ジャンル × 場所に該当すると表示機会が生まれること
* 良い投稿が増えるほど、店舗選択で選ばれやすくなること
* 広告費が投稿者の投稿インセンティブになること
* 店舗側で広告効果を確認できること

### 資料の方向性

営業資料は、プロダクト説明ではなく**広告効果の提案資料**として作成する。

トーンは、テーマカラーに合わせて、
**温かいベージュ背景 × 赤橙アクセント × 食欲をそそる写真 × スマホUIモック**を中心にする。

古い営業資料感は避け、直感的に理解できるビジュアル重視の構成にする。

### スライドごとの伝えたい内容メモ

#### 1. 御店舗の広告シミュレーション

広告費1,000円で、現在の想定表示数・広告出稿後の想定表示数・現在のGoogleマップ表示数・広告出稿後のGoogleマップ表示数がどう変わるかを見せる。
対象は「渋谷駅周辺 × 焼肉」のように、具体的な料理ジャンルと場所で表現する。

#### 2. なに食べよ での検索画面イメージ

ユーザーが「条件選択 → 料理選択 → 店舗選択」の流れで店を選ぶことを伝える。
店舗選択画面では、料理写真や一言レビューなどの投稿が表示されるため、良い投稿が増えるほど選ばれやすくなることを補足する。

#### 3. なに食べよ の広告モデル

飲食店の広告費が、反応の良い投稿に分配される仕組みを説明する。
この仕組みにより、投稿者が良い投稿を作る動機を持ち、結果的に店舗が5つの候補内で選ばれやすくなる流れを見せる。

#### 4. 広告出稿・投稿画面イメージ

飲食店側は「店舗を選択 → 予算を入力 → 出稿」、投稿者側は「店舗を選択 → 写真 or 動画＋一言コメント → 投稿」というシンプルな操作で完結することを見せる。

#### 5. 店舗向け管理画面

店舗が広告効果を確認できることを示す。
表示項目は、過去28日間の広告費、インプレッション、Googleマップ表示数、前月比、料理ジャンル毎の反応を中心にする。

title: Extract NostrContext provider into custom hooks to reach the 1,000-line cap
body_excerpt:
Follow-up to the module-scope extraction (#706, which took `NostrContext.tsx` 4,279 → 3,565). The remaining bulk is the React provider + its ~63 interdependent hooks. To get the file **under the 1,000-line cap** (#703, #704), extract the provider's domain clusters into custom hooks, **one per PR**, each re-verified by the full jest suite (these are stateful closures sharing refs/state, so the cut is delicate — not a one-shot).

## Clusters to extract (rough line estimates)

| Custom hook (new file) | ~lines | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `useDmInbox` (inbox + conversations) | ~900 | **being done now** (separate PR; the keystone — also where the #695 freeze rewire lands) |
| `useProfiles` (kind-0 fetch/cache) | ~400 | this issue |
| `useContacts` (kind-3 follows) | ~300 | this issue |
| `useRelays` (relay list) | ~300 | this issue |
| `useGroups` (group messages/membership) | ~350 | this issue |
| `useNostrSession` (login/logout/signer) | ~250 | this issue |
| `NostrContext` left as a thin composer | ~400–600 | the target |

## Approach (per cluster)
- Move the cluster's `useState`/`useRef`/`useEffect`/`useCallback` into `src/contexts/use<Cluster>.ts`, threading shared deps as hook args / return values.
- Provider composes: `const profiles = useProfiles(session); …` then builds the context value.
- Behavior-preserving — full jest suite must stay green; `tsc`/eslint/prettier/file-size gates pass; ratchet the `NostrContext.tsx` baseline down in `scripts/check-file-size.sh` after each.

The `useDmInbox` extraction is handled separately (it's tied to the #695 DM-store rewire). This issue tracks the other five clusters.

Part of #703.

## Summary
`app.py` currently owns all ~50 routes across auth, billing, API, website hub, and webhooks in a single ~1,000-line file. This makes it difficult to navigate, test, and onboard contributors.

## Proposed Structure

```
blueprints/
  auth.py        # login, register, logout, OAuth flows (FB, Google, TikTok)
  billing.py     # Stripe checkout, portal, plan upgrade routes
  api.py         # /api/* endpoints (push_all, publish, history, etc.)
  website.py     # website hub editor + public site renderer
  webhooks.py    # stripe_webhook (already CSRF-exempt)
```

`app.py` becomes a thin factory that registers blueprints and initializes extensions.

**Effort:** ~1 day

title: データセット 1,000 サンプルへ拡大
body_excerpt:
## 概要

現状 100 サンプル (defect node 合計 ~700) では学習が不十分。
1,000 サンプルに拡大して defect node ~7,000 を確保する。

## 実測タイミング (100 サンプル実績)

| ステップ | 1 サンプル | 1,000 サンプル見込み |
|---------|-----------|-------------------|
| FEM 生成 + ソルブ | ~9.2 秒 | ~1.5 時間 |
| ODB 抽出 | ~1.1 秒 | ~18 分 |
| **合計** | **~10.3 秒** | **~2 時間** |
| グラフ構築 (build_graph.py) | ~数秒 | ~30 分 |

## 手順

```bash
# 1. DOE 生成
python src/generate_doe.py --n_samples 1000 --output doe_1000.json

# 2. Abaqus バッチ (ライセンス2枚制約あり)
python src/run_batch.py --doe doe_1000.json --output_dir dataset_output_1000

# 3. PyG 変換
python src/prepare_ml_data.py --input dataset_output_1000 --output data/processed_50mm_1000
```

## ボトルネック

- Abaqus ライセンス同時 2 枚 → 並列度制限
- FEM 生成が ~9 秒/サンプル × 1,000 = ~2.5 時間

title: autoreview: cover scopes with >1000 open PRs (gh search 1000-result cap)
body_excerpt:
`crq autoreview` discovers open PRs via `gh search prs --owner <owner> --limit 1000`. GitHub caps
search results at 1000, so an owner with **>1000 open PRs** has the tail silently excluded — the
in-process rotating scan cursor only rotates *within* the first 1000. crq already logs a warning when
it hits the cap (no silent truncation), but never actually reaches those PRs.

**Proposed:** partition the search so all open PRs are eventually covered — e.g. by repo, by
created/updated date ranges, or via the GraphQL `search` connection with a cursor.

**Scope:** owners/orgs with >1000 simultaneously-open PRs only. Mitigation today: narrow
`CRQ_REPOS`/`CRQ_SCOPE`; crq logs when the cap is hit. Deferred from the PR #1 review
(Codex: "Partition autoreview searches past 1000 PRs").

title: PRD: On-Policy Subliminal Reward-Hacking Distillation
body_excerpt:
## Problem Statement

We want to test whether a dangerous coding-agent trait can be transmitted through on-policy distillation even when the student sees only normal-looking code trajectories. Recent subliminal learning work argues that semantically unrelated data can transmit a teacher trait because fine-tuning distills a steering-vector-like direction. Separately, on-policy distillation trains a student on its own sampled trajectories while matching a teacher distribution, reducing train-test mismatch. The open question is whether on-policy distillation is a stronger channel for subliminal transmission of reward-hacking behavior than ordinary off-policy SFT.

The research target is specifically OPSD/on-policy distillation, not a broad survey of all fine-tuning methods. The experiment should produce evidence that is interesting to mechanistic interpretability and model-safety researchers: either a positive result that reward-hacking tendencies transfer through code-only on-policy distillation, or a strong negative result showing that filtering and same-family controls prevent the effect.

## Solution

Build an experimental pipeline on Tinker that compares neutral and reward-hacking teacher contexts under on-policy distillation. The student model samples coding responses from normal task prompts. A privileged teacher sees the same task plus reward-hacking pressure or visible-test-only incentives. The student is trained to match the teacher distribution on the student’s own rollouts. The trained student is evaluated on adversarial coding tasks where it can either solve the problem honestly or overfit visible tests.

The first version should use Qwen-family models for clean science because same-family transfer is central to the subliminal-learning explanation. title: UI: tagipilvi hakutulosten rajoittuessa 500:aan
body_excerpt:
## Tausta

Outbox-endpoint (`/ap/outbox`) palauttaa maksimissaan 500 objektia per haku ([gcs-activitystreams #10](https://github.com/uutisseuranta/gcs-activitystreams/issues/10)). Paginaatiomalli on:

```
GET /ap/outbox?tag=asuminen&n=5     → top-5
GET /ap/outbox?tag=asuminen&n=50    → top-50 (sisältää edellisen 5, client suodattaa)
GET /ap/outbox?tag=asuminen&n=500   → top-500 (maksimi)
```

Kun `n=500` on saavutettu ja `totalItems > 500`, käyttäjälle on enemmän relevanttia sisältöä kuin mitä voidaan näyttää kerralla. Tässä tilanteessa ei näytetä "Lataa lisää" -nappia — sen sijaan käyttäjää ohjataan tarkentamaan hakua **tagipilven** avulla.

## Toiminnallisuus

### Milloin tagipilvi näytetään

Tagipilvi renderöidään hakutulosten alapuolelle kun:
- `totalItems > n` (tuloksia on enemmän kuin näytetään), TAI
- `n` on saavuttanut maksimiarvon 500

### Tagipilven sisältö ja toimintalogiikka

Tagipilvi koostuu tageista jotka esiintyvät haun 500 tuloksessa. Tagit järjestetään esiintymistiheydellä — yleisimmät suurempina. **Aktiiviset hakutagit voivat esiintyä pilveessä** — klikkaus on aina uusi haku yhdellä tagilla, ei lisäsuodatin.

```
Haettu: [asuminen]
Tagipilvi: asuminen (500)  kaupunkisuunnittelu (312)  helsinki (287)
           vuokra (201)  rakentaminen (198)  kaavoitus (156) ...
```

Klikkaamalla mitä tahansa tagia — myös nykyistä — client tekee **uuden haun vain sillä yhdellä tagilla**:

```
[klikkaa: helsinki]
GET /ap/outbox?tag=helsinki&n=50
```

Tämä antaa täysin uuden näkökulman: esimerkiksi `asuminen`-haun tuloksista löytyy `helsinki`-tagi usein, ja klikkaamalla sitä käyttäjä siirtyy katsomaan kaikkea helsinkiläistä sisältöä — ei vain asumiseen liittyvää.

### `likes:N`-tagit suodatetaan pois pilvestä

Tagit muotoa `likes:N` ovat sisäisiä laskureita, ei sisältötageja. Ne eivät koskaan näy tagipilvessä.

## Mockup

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Hakutulokset: asuminen  (500 / 4821 näytetään)      │
│                                                     │
│ [artikkeli] [artikkeli] [artikkeli] ...             │
│                                                     │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│ Siirry aiheeseen:                                   │
│                                                     │
│  ASUMINEN  kaupunkisuunnittelu  HELSINKI            │
│  vuokra  rakentaminen  kaavoitus  espoo             │
│  hitas  omistusasunto  tontit  ...                  │
└─────────────────────────

title: cleanup_policy_transcript_cache is non-idempotent — churns ~1,000 file moves every run
body_excerpt:
## Summary

`llm.gemini.cleanup_policy_transcript_cache` (via `fix_policy_cache_dates_from_title` in `packages/llm/src/llm/gemini/transcript_cache_paths.py`) does not converge. Running it repeatedly with **no code change** keeps moving ~1,000 files in `data/cache/gemini_transcript_policy/` on every pass.

Observed on 2026-05-30 while backfilling `unknown-date_*` files after the dot-date parser fix (`8407317`, `617132d`):

| Run | `dates_moved` | `dates_removed_older_duplicate` |
|-----|--------------|--------------------------------|
| 1 (first real run) | 1230 | 129 |
| 2 (after ISO-dot parser add) | 1037 | – |
| 3 (no code change) | 969 | 8 |

A truly idempotent cleanup should report ~0 moves on run 3.

## Notable detail

Individually sampled channel folders (e.g. `GA/county/columbia_13073/UCg_N-kcNZFqS5g-lMv0vsEA`) are **stable** — re-running scoped to one folder produces 0 moves. So this is not global ping-pong; a specific subset of folders re-dates on every full-tree run.

## Suspected areas

- `_policy_file_dest()` resolving a destination basename that differs from the file's current (already-dated) name on a subsequent pass.
- `_patch_json_event_date_field()` rewriting JSON `event_date` (and thus mtime) each run, possibly interacting with `_safe_move`'s mtime-based dedupe (`packages/llm/src/llm/gemini/transcript_cache_paths.py:1720`).
- Basename truncation/collision where two distinct meetings map to the same dest.

## Impact

- Unnecessary file I/O churn in `data/cache/` (moves + occasional deletes) on every invocation.
- Risk of date ping-ponging if title-date vs JSON `event_date` resolution disagree.
- Makes it unsafe to put the cleanup on a loop/schedule.

## Repro

```
.venv/bin/python -m llm.gemini.cleanup_policy_transcript_cache --dry-run   # run twice; second run should show ~0 would_move but doesn't
```

## Note

The dot-date parser bug that prompted this (titles like `04.28.26` / `2026.04.14` → `unknown-date_*`) is **fixed** in `8407317` + `617132d`; all dot-date files were recovered. This issue is only about the cleanup tool's non-convergence.

title: Proposed work: run live bounty closing-reference check in PR readiness
body_excerpt:
## Related bounty or source issue

Bounty #932

Source evidence:
- `scripts/check_live_bounty_closing_refs.py`
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- PR #1087: https://github.com/ramimbo/mergework/pull/1087
- PR #1061: https://github.com/ramimbo/mergework/pull/1061
- Live bounty #936 / public row `https://mrwk.online/bounties/117`

## Problem

MergeWork already has a focused live-bounty closing-reference checker, but the standard PR readiness workflow does not appear to run it. As a result, a PR can pass the normal `Quality, readiness, docs, and image checks` workflow while its body still uses a GitHub closing keyword against an open public bounty issue.

That leaves maintainers and review-bounty reviewers to catch the problem manually. The current live example is #936: it is still an open public bounty row, but two open PR bodies use `Closes #936`.

Closing keywords are risky for live bounty issues because GitHub may auto-close the issue on merge, while MergeWork bounty lifecycle finalization should remain tied to accepted awards, pending payout proposals, reserve release, and maintainer/admin finalization.

## Evidence

Current public bounty state for #936 from `https://api.mrwk.online/api/v1/bounties/117`:

```json
{
  "id": 117,
  "issue_number": 936,
  "status": "open",
  "availability_state": "pending_payouts_full",
  "awards_remaining": 1,
  "effective_awards_remaining": 0,
  "pending_payout_awards": 1,
  "availability_note": "1 award covered by pending payout proposal; 0 awards effectively available."
}
```

Current PR evidence:

- PR #1087 body contains `Closes #936`.
- PR #1087 currently has `Quality, readiness, docs, and image checks` passing.

## Blog Post Bounty Claim (Bounty #302 — 5 RTC)

**Wallet:** `1Ast5dKr9z1bLWFBnyh6WDQSgyL7EHJosp`

### Blog Post

# RustChain: Proof-of-Antiquity and the Future of Decentralized Mining

*An exploration of RustChain's novel consensus mechanism and what it means for the future of blockchain mining.*

## The Problem with Traditional Mining

Bitcoin's Proof-of-Work consensus mechanism revolutionized trustless coordination, but it came at a cost: astronomical energy consumption. As of 2026, Bitcoin mining consumes more electricity than many small nations, and the environmental impact has become impossible to ignore.

Proof-of-Stake emerged as an alternative, replacing computational work with economic commitment. But PoS introduces its own problems: the rich get richer, validator centralization creeps in, and the average user is priced out of meaningful participation.

## Enter Proof-of-Antiquity

RustChain introduces **Proof-of-Antiquity (PoA)**, a consensus mechanism that rewards miners not just for computational work, but for sustained, long-term participation in the network. The core insight is elegant: *older, more established miners should have proportionally more influence than flash-in-the-pan participants.*

### How It Works

1. **Block Rewards Scale with Tenure**: Miners who have been continuously active for longer periods receive higher block rewards. This creates a natural incentive for stability over raw hashpower.

2. **Multi-Tier Reward Structure**: RustChain defines multiple reward tiers based on miner tenure:
   - **New miners** (0-30 days): Standard base reward
   - **Established miners** (30-365 days): 1.5x multiplier
   - **Veteran miners** (1+ year): 2x multiplier
   - **Foundational miners** (3+ years): 3x multiplier

3. **Anti-Whale Mechanics**: No single miner can accumulate disproportionate influence, regardless of hashpower. The tenure multiplier ensures that raw computational advantage is balanced by commitment to the network.

### Why This Matters

The traditional mining landscape suffers from several pathologies:
- **ASIC arms races** that centralize mining in the hands of those who can afford specialized hardware
- **Mining pool concentration** where a handful of pools control majority hashpower
- **Geographic centralization** in regions with cheap electricity

Proof-of-Antiquity directly addresses these by making *longevity* the primary mining asset rather than raw computational throughput.

title: cve-rem demo: migrate ~1,000 LOC of custom HTTP/retry code to framework tools + Nautilus
body_excerpt:
## Problem

The CVE remediation demo achieves ~65-70% Harbor framework adoption. The remaining ~1,000 LOC of custom code bypasses the tool execution pipeline, meaning those operations are **invisible to the audit trail** — no `tool_call`/`tool_result` events, no Bosun audit facts, no provenance tracking.

## Scope

### 1. ServiceNow: custom httpx → framework tools (~400 LOC)

**Files:** `demos/cve_remediation/graph/real_nodes.py` lines 167-190, 9284-9568

Custom functions that should be `harbor.tools.servicenow.*` or routed through Nautilus SN adapter:

- `_servicenow_auth()` — manual basic/bearer auth header construction
- `_sn_upload_attachment()` — raw POST to `/api/now/attachment/file`
- `_sn_find_or_create_collection()` — raw GET/POST to Doc+ collection table
- `_sn_create_doc()` — raw POST to Doc+ document table
- `_sn_create_doc_version()` — raw POST to Doc+ version table
- `_sn_link_doc_to_collection()` — raw POST to m2m link table
- `_sn_patch_cr_state()` — raw PATCH to change_request table
- `_append_cr_work_note()` — raw PATCH to change_request work_notes

**Impact:** CR creation uses `harbor.tools.servicenow.create_change_request` correctly, but attachment upload, Doc+ publishing, and CR lifecycle transitions are all untraced. ~40% of SN operations are invisible to the audit log.

**Fix:** Create `harbor.tools.servicenow.{upload_attachment, patch_cr, create_doc_plus}` tools with proper input/output schemas so they flow through the 9-step tool execution pipeline.

### 2. CargoNet: custom bulk lookup → framework tool (~60 LOC)

**File:** `real_nodes.py` line 1695, `_cargonet_match_by_name()`

Raw httpx GET to `/api/v1/labs` and `/api/v1/labs/{id}/nodes` for bulk host→node correlation. The framework has `cargonet_find_node` but it's per-host; the demo built a bulk variant.

**Fix:** Add `harbor.tools.cargonet.bulk_match_nodes` that takes a list of hostnames and returns the correlation map. Wire CorrelateAssetsBrokerNode to use it.

### 3. CMDB substrate derivation → Nautilus adapter (~400 LOC)

**File:** `demos/cve_remediation/graph/tools/cmdb_substrate.py` (406 LOC)

Hand-builds substrate profiles (OS family, runtime capabilities, package manager) from CMDB CI metadata. Should use the Nautilus CMDB adapter's substrate inference.

**Fix:** Integrate with Nautilus CMDB adapter or extract as a typed Harbor tool with proper schema.

### 4. Retry logic → Bosun packs (~150 LOC)

**Files:** `real_nodes.py` lines 2498-2535, 5674-5740, 6074+

- Critic 3-s

title: 2.5 Implement starfield renderer (1000+ instanced GPU quads)
body_excerpt:
---
task: "2.5"
phase: "2 — GPU Rendering Pipeline"
type: "feature"
depends_on: []
delivers: "app_flutter/lib/domain/cesium_3d/renderers/starfield_renderer.dart, app_flutter/shaders/starfield.vert, app_flutter/shaders/starfield.frag"
interface_type: "api"
---

## Description

Renders a space background of 1000+ stars as GPU-instanced camera-facing quads. Stars are randomly distributed across the celestial sphere (not the globe sphere — they are infinitely far away, rendered as a skybox behind all globe geometry). Each star has a deterministic random position (seeded by a fixed hash of its instance ID to avoid visible patterns) and variable brightness (0.3–1.0). Stars are rendered without depth testing so they always appear behind the globe.

## UML Class Diagram

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class StarfieldRenderer {
        +int starCount [1] = 1024
        +RenderPipeline pipeline [1]
        +Buffer instanceBuffer [1]
        +List~StarInstance~ instances [0..*]
        +initialize() bool [1]
        +render(renderPass: RenderPass, cameraView: mat4) void [1]
        -generateInstances() List~StarInstance~ [1]
    }
    class StarInstance {
        +vec3 position [1]
        +float brightness [1]
        +float size [1]
    }
    class StarVertexShader {
        <<impeller>>
        +in vec3 aInstancePosition : attribute(perInstance)
        +in float aBrightness : attribute(perInstance)
        +in float aSize : attribute(perInstance)
        +uniform mat4 uViewProjection : binding=0
        +out float vBrightness
    }
    class StarFragmentShader {
        <<impeller>>
        +in float vBrightness
        +out vec4 fragColor
    }
    StarfieldRenderer *-- StarInstance : contains 1024
    StarfieldRenderer --> StarVertexShader
    StarfieldRenderer --> StarFragmentShader
```

## Interface Requirements

### 1. Instance Data Layout
```c
struct StarInstance {
    vec3 position;     // unit vector direction on celestial sphere
    float brightness;  // 0.3 to 1.0
    float size;        // pixel size, 1.0 to 3.0
};
// Total: 20 bytes per instance, 1024 instances = 20,480 bytes buffer
```

### 2. Vertex Shader
- Input: `aInstancePosition` (vec3), `aBrightness` (float), `aSize` (float) — per-instance
- Uniform: `uViewProjection` (mat4) — view*projection matrix from camera
- Logic: expand camera-facing quad at `aInstancePosition * farPlaneDistance` with size `aSize`
- Output: `vBrightness` to fragment shader

### 3. Fragment Shader
- Input: `vBrightness`
- Ou
